blurb: Peru's capital sits on cliffs above the Pacific and is the food capital of South America: ceviche at lunch, sunsets over the ocean.
fun_fact: Lima is one of the driest capitals on Earth: it gets less than 2 cm of rain a year, yet a grey sea mist, the garúa, hangs over it for months.

blurb: A desert peninsula where the sand runs into the sea, and a short boat ride to the Ballestas Islands: sea lions, Humboldt penguins and huge bird colonies.
fun_fact: On the way to the islands you pass the Candelabro, a figure about 170 m tall carved into a sandy hillside. Nobody knows for sure who made it, or when.

blurb: A tiny palm-fringed lagoon surrounded by giant sand dunes, made for dune buggies, sandboarding and sunsets from the crest.
fun_fact: For years Huacachina was printed on the back of Peru's 50-sol banknote.

blurb: The White City, built from pale volcanic stone under the snowy cone of El Misti, with one of the best colonial centres in South America.
fun_fact: The Santa Catalina Monastery is a walled town inside the town, about 20,000 m² of lanes and cloisters. It stayed closed to the outside world for almost 400 years and opened to visitors only in 1970.

blurb: A huge canyon lined with pre-Inca terraces, where Andean condors glide past the viewpoint in the early morning.
fun_fact: At about 3,270 m at its deepest, Colca is almost twice as deep as the Grand Canyon.

blurb: Peru's port on Lake Titicaca, the base for the floating reed islands of the Uros and the weaving island of Taquile.
fun_fact: The Uros islands are made of totora reeds: as the bottom layers rot in the water, the islanders keep adding fresh reeds on top.

blurb: The old Inca capital at 3,400 m: Spanish churches and balconies built straight on top of perfect Inca stone walls.
fun_fact: The Inca walls fit without any mortar. The famous Twelve-Angled Stone in Hatun Rumiyoc street locks into its neighbours on all twelve sides.

blurb: The green valley of the Urubamba river below Cusco, lined with Inca terraces, salt pans and market villages.
fun_fact: People still live in Ollantaytambo on its original Inca street plan, with stone water channels running along the lanes.

blurb: The village at the foot of Machu Picchu, reached only by train or on foot, and the start of the bus up to the citadel.
fun_fact: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 and the Spanish conquerors never found it. It became world famous only after Hiram Bingham's visit in 1911.

blurb: Tango, steak and grand boulevards: a European-looking capital on the River Plate that eats dinner at ten.
fun_fact: Avenida 9 de Julio is listed by Guinness as the widest avenue in the world: about 110 m and 16 lanes of traffic.

blurb: A small town on the turquoise Lago Argentino and the base for the Perito Moreno glacier, where towers of ice crash into the lake.
fun_fact: The town is named after the calafate bush. Local legend says that whoever eats its berries will come back to Patagonia.

blurb: Argentina's trekking capital: a village of hikers right under the granite spires of Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre.
fun_fact: El Chaltén is one of the youngest towns in Argentina: it was founded in 1985, partly to settle a border dispute with Chile.

blurb: A windy fishing town on a fjord, the base for Torres del Paine, with mountain views straight from the waterfront.
fun_fact: In a cave nearby, settlers found the skin and bones of a giant ground sloth, the mylodon. A scrap of that skin inspired Bruce Chatwin's book In Patagonia.

blurb: Granite towers, glaciers and blue lakes: one of the great treks of the world, walked in four or five days.
fun_fact: 'Paine' means 'blue' in the language of the Tehuelche people, so the name means roughly 'Towers of Blue'.

blurb: One of the southernmost cities in the world, on the Strait of Magellan, with penguin colonies a boat ride away.
fun_fact: Before the Panama Canal opened in 1914, ships between the Atlantic and the Pacific sailed past here, and the port grew rich on them.

blurb: The northernmost capital in the world: colourful houses, geothermal pools and the rocket-shaped Hallgrímskirkja church.
fun_fact: Almost every home in Reykjavík is heated with natural hot water piped in from geothermal fields.

blurb: Iceland's classic loop: the rift valley of Þingvellir, the spouting Geysir field and the double waterfall of Gullfoss.
fun_fact: At Þingvellir you walk in the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates, which move apart by about 2 cm a year.

blurb: A village on the south coast with black sand beaches, basalt columns and sea stacks rising out of the Atlantic.
fun_fact: Legend says the Reynisdrangar sea stacks are trolls who were turned to stone by the sunrise while dragging a ship to shore.

blurb: A green oasis between glacier tongues in Vatnajökull National Park, with Svartifoss, the waterfall framed by black basalt columns.
fun_fact: Vatnajökull, the ice cap above you, is the largest in Iceland and covers about 8% of the country.

blurb: Vietnam's capital: lakes, a thousand-year-old centre and street food on every pavement.
fun_fact: Old Quarter streets are named after what they used to sell: Hàng Bạc is Silver Street, Hàng Gai is Hemp Street.

names: Ha Long and Lan Ha Bay
blurb: Around 1,600 limestone islands rising out of emerald water, best seen from a boat with a night on board.
fun_fact: Ha Long means 'descending dragon': legend says the islands are jewels that dragons spat into the sea to defend the coast.

blurb: Rice fields and limestone peaks you explore by rowing boat along the river, often called Ha Long Bay on land.
fun_fact: Many of the Tam Coc boat rowers row with their feet, leaning back and pushing the oars with their legs.

blurb: The old imperial capital on the Perfume River, with a walled citadel and the royal tombs of the Nguyễn emperors.
fun_fact: Hue was the capital of Vietnam from 1802 to 1945, under the Nguyễn, the country's last royal dynasty.

blurb: A lantern-lit old trading port with yellow merchant houses, and tailors who make you clothes overnight.
fun_fact: Its Japanese Covered Bridge, from the late 16th century, is printed on Vietnam's 20,000-dong banknote.

blurb: Vietnam's biggest city, still called Saigon by most people: motorbikes, markets and rooftop bars.
fun_fact: The Cu Chi tunnels, a day trip away, once ran for more than 200 km underground during the war.

blurb: Nepal's capital in a green valley ringed by hills: temple squares, prayer flags, stupas and the busy lanes of Thamel, where most Himalayan treks begin.
fun_fact: The city's name is linked to the Kasthamandap, a wooden pavilion in Durbar Square that legend says was built from the timber of a single tree.

blurb: The Inca citadel on a ridge above the Urubamba canyon: terraces, temples and stone walls fitted without mortar, with Huayna Picchu rising behind.
fun_fact: The Spanish never found it. It was built around 1450, left a century later and only became world-famous after Hiram Bingham's visit in 1911.

blurb: Thousands of limestone islands rising out of green water in northern Vietnam, best seen from a boat overnight, with caves and kayaking between the karsts.
fun_fact: Hạ Long means 'descending dragon'. Legend says dragons came down to defend Vietnam and spat out jewels that turned into the islands.

blurb: A huge collapsed volcano whose grassy floor is packed with wildlife: lions, elephants, buffalo and one of the last refuges of the black rhino.
fun_fact: The Maasai named it after the sound of their cowbells: 'ngoro ngoro'.

blurb: The world's biggest city that still feels orderly: neon districts, quiet shrines, tiny bars and some of the best food on the planet.
fun_fact: Until 1868 the city was called Edo. Its new name, Tokyo, simply means 'eastern capital'.

blurb: An Inca town at the end of the Sacred Valley, below giant stone terraces and a temple hill, where the train to Machu Picchu leaves.
fun_fact: People still live in its Inca-built houses: they are some of the oldest continuously occupied homes in South America.

blurb: Endless savannah in northern Tanzania and the classic safari: big cats, elephants and, for part of the year, the herds of the great migration.
fun_fact: About 1.5 million wildebeest and 250,000 zebras circle the Serengeti every year, the largest animal migration on land.

blurb: Japan's old imperial capital: wooden temples, Zen gardens, geisha streets in Gion and thousands of red torii gates on the hills.
fun_fact: Kyoto was on the shortlist for the atomic bomb in 1945. The US Secretary of War, Henry Stimson, had it taken off because of its cultural value.

blurb: A maze of narrow tunnels outside Saigon used by the Viet Cong during the Vietnam War. You can crawl through a stretch of it.
fun_fact: Underground there were kitchens, sleeping rooms, hospitals and command posts, and the tunnels served as a base for the 1968 Tet Offensive.

blurb: Marrakech's great square: juice stalls and snake charmers by day, smoke from food stalls, storytellers and musicians by night.
fun_fact: The square inspired UNESCO's list of oral and intangible heritage: it was one of the first places named on it, in 2001.

blurb: A green, busy town under Mount Meru and the starting point of most northern Tanzania safaris and Kilimanjaro climbs.
fun_fact: Arusha sits almost exactly halfway between Cairo and Cape Town, and its clock tower is often said to mark the midpoint.

blurb: Tokyo's oldest temple, reached through the huge red Thunder Gate and a street of snack and souvenir stalls, with incense drifting over the main hall.
fun_fact: With more than 30 million visitors a year it is called the most visited religious site in the world.

blurb: Japan's loud, friendly food city: neon canals in Dotonbori, street food at every corner and a castle in a big park.
fun_fact: Osaka's nickname is 'the nation's kitchen', and its own word for its food culture, kuidaore, means 'eat until you drop'.

blurb: Islands woven from totora reeds on Lake Titicaca, where Uros families still live, cook and fish on the water near Puno.
fun_fact: The islands rot from below, so families add fresh layers of reeds on top every few weeks to keep them afloat.

blurb: The green maze where the Mekong reaches the sea: floating markets, fruit orchards, rice fields and slow boats along palm-lined canals.
fun_fact: The river splits into many branches here, which is why the Vietnamese call it Cửu Long, the 'Nine Dragons' river.

blurb: Old Tokyo on the Sumida River: Senso-ji temple, rickshaws, craft shops and small eateries, with the Skytree just across the water.
fun_fact: Asakusa is Tokyo's oldest geisha district, and dozens of geisha still work there.

blurb: A 60 m curtain of water dropping off old sea cliffs in south Iceland. Walk right up to the spray or climb the stairs to the top.
fun_fact: Legend says the first settler of the area hid a chest of gold behind the falls, and that its ring is now in a local museum.

blurb: The 'Golden Falls': the Hvítá river drops in two steps into a deep canyon, a highlight of the Golden Circle drive.
fun_fact: The story that a farmer's daughter, Sigríður, saved the falls from a power plant by threatening to jump in is famous in Iceland, but not true.

blurb: The best preserved of the Kathmandu Valley's royal cities: brick squares, pagoda temples, potters at work and almost no cars in the centre.
fun_fact: Bhaktapur was the capital of all Nepal until 1482, when the valley split into three rival kingdoms.

blurb: A fortified village of red earth towers on a hill above a river, on the old caravan road from the Sahara to Marrakech.
fun_fact: It has starred in many films and series, including Gladiator and Game of Thrones.

blurb: Tokyo's famous scramble crossing: when the lights turn, crowds pour across from every side at once under giant video screens.
fun_fact: It is called the world's busiest pedestrian crossing: up to 3,000 people can cross on a single green light.

blurb: Kyoto's Golden Pavilion: a Zen temple covered in gold leaf, mirrored in a pond with pines and small islands.
fun_fact: What you see is a copy: a young monk burned the original down in 1950, and the pavilion was rebuilt in 1955.

blurb: A calm walled temple to Confucius in central Hanoi, with courtyards, ponds and old trees. It was the country's first university.
fun_fact: Stone tablets on the backs of stone turtles carry the names of the scholars who passed the royal exams over more than 300 years.

blurb: Nepal's holiest Hindu temple on the Bagmati River, with sadhus, monkeys and open-air cremation ghats on the riverbank.
fun_fact: Only Hindus may enter the main temple, so visitors watch from the terraces on the opposite bank of the river.

blurb: Thousands of bright orange torii gates forming tunnels up a wooded hill on the edge of Kyoto. Go early, or walk higher up, to have them to yourself.
fun_fact: Each gate is a gift from a person or company, whose name is written on its back. Inari is the god of rice and business.

blurb: A huge, deep-blue lake high in the Andes, shared by Peru and Bolivia, with reed islands, island villages and Inca legends.
fun_fact: At about 3,800 m it is often called the highest navigable lake in the world, and it is the largest lake in South America.

blurb: A port town between snowy mountains and the Beagle Channel at the bottom of the Americas, where ships leave for Antarctica.
fun_fact: Ushuaia calls itself the southernmost city in the world, and its museum is set in an old prison for repeat offenders.

blurb: One of the largest stupas in the world, a giant white dome with painted eyes, circled by pilgrims spinning prayer wheels.
fun_fact: It is the heart of Tibetan Buddhism in Nepal: dozens of monasteries were built around it by refugees who came from Tibet after 1959.

blurb: Japan's first permanent capital, where more than a thousand tame deer roam a park full of ancient temples and a giant bronze Buddha.
fun_fact: The deer are considered sacred messengers of the gods. Many have learned to bow to visitors to get a rice cracker.

blurb: The green lake in the heart of Hanoi, with a red bridge to a temple islet. The streets around it close to cars at weekends.
fun_fact: Its name means 'Lake of the Returned Sword': legend says a golden turtle took back the magic sword that freed Vietnam from the Ming.

blurb: The Inca Empire's most important temple, dedicated to the sun. A Spanish convent was built on top, but the perfect Inca walls are still there.
fun_fact: Spanish chroniclers wrote that its walls were covered in sheets of gold, and its garden held plants and animals made of gold and silver.

blurb: A hilltop stupa above Kathmandu, reached by a steep stairway, with views over the whole valley.
fun_fact: Travellers call it the 'Monkey Temple' because of the hundreds of monkeys that live around it and steal food from visitors.

blurb: A rift valley where you walk between the American and Eurasian plates, and the site of Iceland's open-air parliament.
fun_fact: The Alþing first met here in 930, which makes it one of the oldest parliaments in the world.

blurb: A small Saharan village at the foot of the Erg Chebbi dunes, the place to ride a camel into the sand and sleep in a desert camp.
fun_fact: A local legend says the area was once green, until God buried a family under the dunes for refusing to help a poor woman.

blurb: Zanzibar's old town: a maze of alleys, carved wooden doors, spice markets and sunset on the seafront at Forodhani.
fun_fact: Its buildings mix Arab, Persian, Indian and European styles, and the big carved doors are among its most famous features.

blurb: A city poured into a deep canyon on the Altiplano, with snowy Illimani above it and cable cars gliding over the rooftops.
fun_fact: At about 3,600 m it is the highest seat of government in the world, and its cable car network is one of the largest in the world.

blurb: A lively market town at the foot of the Rift Valley wall, on the road to Lake Manyara, Ngorongoro and the Serengeti, with banana farms all around.
fun_fact: Its Swahili name means 'river of mosquitoes'.

blurb: Namibia's great safari park around a vast white salt pan, where elephants, lions and rhinos gather at the waterholes in the dry season.
fun_fact: The salt pan is so big it can be seen from space. It was proclaimed a game reserve in 1907.

blurb: A lagoon full of icebergs broken off the Vatnajökull glacier, drifting out to the sea past seals. Boat tours go among the ice.
fun_fact: The lake did not exist a century ago: it formed as the glacier retreated, and it is now the deepest lake in Iceland.

blurb: A slender 60 m waterfall right by the Ring Road in south Iceland, with a path that goes behind the falling water.
fun_fact: Its water comes from the glacier on top of Eyjafjallajökull, the volcano whose 2010 eruption stopped flights across Europe.

blurb: A narrow canyon in the High Atlas where red cliffs rise about 300 m on both sides of a stream, popular with climbers and walkers.
fun_fact: At its narrowest point the gorge is only about 10 m wide, just enough for the river and the road.

blurb: A mountain road between Hue and Da Nang that climbs above the sea, with sweeping views of beaches and jungle.
fun_fact: Jeremy Clarkson called it 'one of the best coast roads in the world' on Top Gear's Vietnam special.

blurb: A seaside town between the Namib dunes and the Atlantic, with German colonial buildings, cool sea fog and sandboarding and quad trips into the desert.
fun_fact: Founded in 1892 as the main port of German South West Africa, it still has German bakeries, street names and buildings.

blurb: A sacred island near Hiroshima, famous for its giant red torii gate that seems to float on the sea at high tide.
fun_fact: It is one of Japan's 'Three Views' listed in 1643, and the shrine was built over the water so that ordinary people would not walk on the holy island.

blurb: Morocco's biggest sea of sand dunes on the edge of the Sahara, glowing orange at sunrise and sunset.
fun_fact: Some of its dunes rise to about 150 m above the surrounding stony desert.

blurb: The walled palace of Vietnam's last emperors, with gates, throne halls, temples and gardens beside the Perfume River.
fun_fact: Built from 1804, it once had 160 buildings. After the 1968 battle of Hue only 10 major ones were left standing.

blurb: Tokyo's skyscraper district: the world's busiest train station, tiny bars in Golden Gai, neon in Kabukicho and a big garden park.
fun_fact: Shinjuku Station is the busiest railway station in the world, used by more than three million people a day.

blurb: A green, lively city rebuilt after 1945, with the Peace Park and Atomic Bomb Dome at its heart and its own style of layered okonomiyaki.
fun_fact: Hiroshima was the first city ever hit by a nuclear weapon, on 6 August 1945. It was founded in 1589 as a castle town on a river delta.

blurb: Morocco's oldest imperial city: a huge car-free medina of alleys, tanneries, mosques and craftsmen that feels unchanged for centuries.
fun_fact: Its University of al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859, is often called the oldest university in the world still teaching.

blurb: The red city at the foot of the Atlas: souks, riads with hidden gardens, palaces and the great square of Jemaa el-Fnaa.
fun_fact: Its nickname is the 'Red City', from the colour of its walls and buildings, made of local red clay.

blurb: A white clay pan ringed by some of the highest red dunes on Earth, in the Namib Desert. Climb one at sunrise.
fun_fact: Many of the dunes are over 200 m high. The tallest here, nicknamed Big Daddy, reaches about 325 m.

blurb: Osaka's neon canal street, packed with giant signs, takoyaki stalls and late-night crowds. The Glico running man sign is the classic photo.
fun_fact: By 1662 this street already had six kabuki and five bunraku puppet theatres: it was Osaka's entertainment district long before the neon.

blurb: Kyoto's old geisha district: wooden teahouses, lantern-lit lanes and, with luck, a geiko or maiko hurrying to an appointment at dusk.
fun_fact: It grew up in front of Yasaka Shrine to serve its visitors, and became one of the most exclusive geisha districts in Japan.

blurb: Spice islands in the Indian Ocean: white beaches and turquoise water, dhows, spice farms and the old alleys of Stone Town.
fun_fact: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 is the shortest war in recorded history: it lasted about 40 minutes.

blurb: The geothermal valley of Haukadalur, where Strokkur shoots boiling water 20 m into the air every few minutes.
fun_fact: Every geyser in the world is named after this one: the English word 'geyser' comes from Geysir.

blurb: Morocco's big modern city on the Atlantic, with Art Deco streets, a seafront corniche and the Hassan II Mosque standing over the ocean.
fun_fact: The Hassan II Mosque has the second tallest minaret in the world, about 210 m, and part of its floor is built out over the sea.

blurb: Tokyo's electric town: floors of electronics, retro games, anime and manga shops, and maid cafés.
fun_fact: The name comes from Akiba, a fire-fighting shrine built after a great fire destroyed the area in 1869.

blurb: The largest salt flat in the world, a white plain to the horizon at 3,650 m. After rain it turns into a giant mirror of the sky.
fun_fact: It holds a large share of the world's lithium, the metal in phone and car batteries.

blurb: A seven-storey pagoda on a hill over the Perfume River, the unofficial symbol of Hue. Arrive by dragon boat from the city.
fun_fact: Legend says a 'celestial lady' appeared here and foretold that a lord would build a pagoda for the country's prosperity. It was built in 1601.

blurb: A seaside town south of Tokyo full of temples, shrines and hiking trails, home to the Great Buddha.
fun_fact: From 1185 Kamakura was the seat of Japan's first military government, the shogunate, while the emperor stayed in Kyoto.

blurb: A relaxed lakeside town under the Annapurna range, the base for the Annapurna treks, paragliding and boating on Phewa Lake.
fun_fact: The Machapuchare peak above the town is sacred and closed to climbers: its summit has never officially been reached.

blurb: The old royal square of Kathmandu, full of pagoda temples, palace courtyards and the house of the Kumari, the living goddess.
fun_fact: One of its palaces, the Nautalle Durbar, has nine storeys and was built to celebrate the unification of Nepal.

blurb: Nara's great temple, whose huge wooden hall shelters a 15 m bronze Buddha. Tame deer wait at the gate.
fun_fact: Its Great Buddha Hall was for centuries the largest wooden building in the world, even though today's hall is smaller than the original.

blurb: Norway's capital at the head of a fjord: a striking opera house you can walk on, Viking ships, Munch's Scream and forest trails a metro ride away.
fun_fact: Every year the city sends a Christmas tree to London's Trafalgar Square, a thank-you for Britain's help in the Second World War.

blurb: The grand capital of the Habsburgs: palaces, coffee houses, cake and the music of Mozart, Strauss and Beethoven.
fun_fact: Until the early 20th century Vienna was the largest German-speaking city in the world, with two million people.

blurb: The classic four-day trek to Machu Picchu along a stone Inca road, through cloud forest and ruins, arriving at the Sun Gate.
fun_fact: Only 500 permits a day are issued, and just 200 of them for trekkers: the rest go to guides and porters.

blurb: Huge zigzag Inca walls on a hill above Cusco, built of boulders cut to fit so tightly that no mortar was needed.
fun_fact: Some of the stones weigh more than 100 tonnes. Every 24 June it hosts Inti Raymi, the Inca festival of the sun.

blurb: Tokyo's youth fashion district: crowded Takeshita Street, crêpes, vintage shops, and Meiji Shrine's forest next door.
fun_fact: In the Edo period Harajuku was a small post town on the road to Kamakura.

blurb: A lively Arctic city on an island, with old wooden houses, a striking Arctic Cathedral and the northern lights overhead in winter.
fun_fact: It is the third largest urban area north of the Arctic Circle in the world, after Murmansk and Norilsk.

blurb: The 1960s presidential palace of South Vietnam, kept as it was: war rooms in the basement, reception halls and tanks in the garden.
fun_fact: On 30 April 1975 a North Vietnamese tank crashed through its gate, the moment that marked the end of the Vietnam War.

blurb: A mountain town near the Chinese border, among rice terraces and Hmong and Dao villages, and the base for climbing Fansipan.
fun_fact: The French built it as a hill station to escape the summer heat, and the area is nicknamed the 'Tonkinese Alps'.

blurb: The oldest barrio of Buenos Aires: cobbled streets, antique shops, tango in the squares and a big Sunday street market.
fun_fact: It is one of the birthplaces of tango, and was the bohemian quarter of painters and jazz clubs in the mid 20th century.

blurb: A calm Shinto shrine hidden in a forest in the middle of Tokyo, steps from Harajuku, dedicated to Emperor Meiji.
fun_fact: Its forest was planted by hand: about 120,000 trees were donated from all over Japan when the shrine was built.

blurb: A black sand beach where chunks of glacier ice wash up and glitter in the sun, just across the road from Jökulsárlón.
fun_fact: The ice that lands here has broken off the glacier, drifted across the lagoon and been rolled smooth by the ocean.

blurb: A park of baobab trees and big elephant herds along the Tarangire River, at its best in the dry season.
fun_fact: The oldest elephant known to have given birth to twins lives in Tarangire.

blurb: The 'door of the desert' at the edge of the Sahara, with a kasbah and big film studios, on the way to Aït Benhaddou and the gorges.
fun_fact: Its Atlas Studios are among the largest film studios in the world by land area.

blurb: A black sand beach near Vík with basalt columns, a cave and sea stacks offshore. The waves are dangerous: stay well back from the water.
fun_fact: Legend says the sea stacks are trolls who were turned to stone when the sun rose as they dragged a ship to shore.

blurb: A red shrine built over the sea on Miyajima, with its famous torii gate standing in the water.
fun_fact: The shrine is said to date back to 593. At high tide the gate and halls seem to float.

blurb: Overgrown brick temples of the Cham kingdom in a jungle valley near Hoi An, built between the 4th and the 14th century.
fun_fact: The temples were built with bricks fitted without visible mortar, and how exactly the Cham did it is still debated.

blurb: Namibia's small, tidy capital in the highlands, with German colonial buildings, craft markets and good restaurants before the road trip.
fun_fact: It lies at about 1,700 m, close to the geographical centre of the country.

blurb: Iceland's huge ice cap, covering about 8% of the country, with ice caves, glacier walks and volcanoes beneath it.
fun_fact: Under the ice lie active volcanoes, and its edge holds Iceland's highest peak, Hvannadalshnúkur.

blurb: The old port barrio of Buenos Aires with brightly painted houses on Caminito, tango in the street and Boca Juniors' stadium.
fun_fact: The houses are so colourful because Italian immigrants painted them with leftover paint from the shipyards.

blurb: Hundreds of waterfalls on the Argentina-Brazil border thundering into a jungle gorge. Walk the catwalks right to the Devil's Throat.
fun_fact: A Guaraní legend says a god, enraged when the woman he wanted fled in a canoe with her lover, split the river to create the falls.

blurb: The channel at the end of the world, between Argentina and Chile: boat trips past sea lion colonies, cormorants and the red-and-white Les Eclaireurs lighthouse.
fun_fact: It is named after HMS Beagle, the ship that later carried Charles Darwin around the world.

blurb: Granite peaks rising out of the flat Namib desert, with rock arches, ancient San rock paintings and starry campsites.
fun_fact: The granite is more than 120 million years old, and the peaks are nicknamed the 'Matterhorn of Namibia'.

blurb: A quiet park of memorials, museums and the Children's Peace Monument in the centre of Hiroshima, on the spot where the bomb fell.
fun_fact: The park stands on an open field created by the explosion: before 1945 this was the city's busiest commercial district.

blurb: Rocky islands off Paracas covered in seabirds, sea lions and Humboldt penguins, reached on a short speedboat trip.
fun_fact: They are sometimes called the 'poor man's Galápagos', and the seabird droppings, guano, were once worth more than gold to Peru.

blurb: The best preserved Roman town in Morocco: mosaics, a triumphal arch and columns standing in open farmland near Meknes.
fun_fact: People went on living here for some 700 years after the Romans left, first as a Christian community and then as an early Islamic town.

blurb: A Sacred Valley town with a big craft market below one of the most impressive Inca sites: terraces curving around a mountainside.
fun_fact: The hillside above the ruins hides the largest known Inca cemetery, with hundreds of tombs cut into the cliff.

blurb: A white clay pan with black, 600-year-old dead camelthorn trees under towering orange dunes. One of the most photographed places in Africa.
fun_fact: The trees died around 600 to 700 years ago but never rotted: the air is too dry for them to decompose.

blurb: A wooden temple on the hillside of eastern Kyoto, with a huge veranda on stilts over the trees and the city below.
fun_fact: The veranda is held up by tall wooden pillars and built without a single nail. The Japanese saying 'to jump off the stage at Kiyomizu' means to take a bold leap.

blurb: New Zealand's adventure capital on Lake Wakatipu under the Remarkables: bungy, jet boats, skiing, wineries and great walks.
fun_fact: Bungy jumping went commercial here: the world's first commercial bungy site opened at the Kawarau Bridge near Queenstown in 1988.

blurb: A modern beach city in central Vietnam, with long sandy beaches, the Marble Mountains and a dragon bridge over the river.
fun_fact: Its Dragon Bridge, shaped like a golden dragon, breathes real fire and water on weekend nights.

blurb: A windy town on the Altiplano that is the base for tours of the Salar de Uyuni and the lagoons of the far southwest.
fun_fact: It was founded in 1890 as a trading post, and British engineers who came to build the railway formed a large community here.

blurb: A giant bronze Buddha sitting in the open air at Kotoku-in temple in Kamakura, about 13 m tall. You can even step inside it.
fun_fact: It once sat inside a hall, but storms and a tsunami in 1498 washed the building away, and it has stood outside ever since.

blurb: The blue town of the Rif mountains: alleys, stairs and houses painted in every shade of blue.
fun_fact: It was founded in 1471, and its population grew fast with Muslim and Jewish refugees from Spain.

blurb: The grey marble mausoleum in Hanoi where Ho Chi Minh's body lies on display, on the square where he declared independence.
fun_fact: Ho Chi Minh asked to be cremated, but the leadership embalmed him instead. Each autumn the mausoleum closes while the body is maintained.

blurb: A narrow covered street of food stalls in central Kyoto: pickles, tofu, sweets, fresh fish and knives.
fun_fact: Locals call it 'Kyoto's kitchen', and there has been a market on this street for centuries.

blurb: A green farming town in the highlands between Lake Manyara and Ngorongoro, with coffee farms and lodges for the night before the crater.
fun_fact: It is home to the Iraqw, a people whose language is unrelated to the Bantu and Maasai languages around them.

blurb: A breezy whitewashed port on the Atlantic with blue fishing boats, sea walls, galleries and wind for surfers.
fun_fact: Until the 1960s it was called Mogador, and its sea walls appear as Astapor in Game of Thrones.

blurb: A small red wooden bridge with a temple on it, the symbol of Hoi An's old town.
fun_fact: Legend says it was built to pin down a giant monster, Namazu, whose movements caused earthquakes.

blurb: The city of artisans across the river from Kathmandu, with a superb Durbar Square, metalworkers' courtyards and a fine museum.
fun_fact: Its old name is Lalitpur, the 'city of beauty', and locals still call it Yala, after a legendary king.

blurb: A headland near Vík with a huge natural rock arch, a lighthouse, puffins in summer and views along the black beaches.
fun_fact: Its name means 'door hill island': it was once an island, and the arch is big enough for a boat to sail through.

blurb: A quiet island on Lake Titicaca with Inca terraces, a few villages and no cars. Islanders still wear traditional dress.
fun_fact: Here the men do the knitting, from childhood. UNESCO listed Taquile's textile art as intangible heritage in 2005.

blurb: Japan's highest mountain, an almost perfect volcanic cone at 3,776 m, best seen on clear winter mornings or climbed in July and August.
fun_fact: It is still an active volcano: its last eruption was in 1707.

blurb: A path through a forest of tall bamboo on the edge of Kyoto, creaking and swaying in the wind. Go at sunrise to avoid the crowds.
fun_fact: Japan's Ministry of the Environment lists the sound of the wind in this bamboo as one of the country's protected soundscapes.

blurb: A 19th-century palace in Marrakech with painted cedar ceilings, tiled courtyards and gardens of orange trees.
fun_fact: Its name means 'brilliance'. It was built by a grand vizier who was descended from a family of slaves.

blurb: Hanoi's maze of narrow streets north of Hoan Kiem Lake, with motorbikes, street food, tube houses and old temples.
fun_fact: Many streets are still named after the trade once done there, like Hàng Bạc, silver street, and Hàng Mã, paper offerings street.

blurb: New Zealand's biggest city, spread over volcanoes between two harbours, with islands and beaches a ferry ride away.
fun_fact: It is built on a field of about 50 volcanoes, and it is one of the few cities with harbours on two different seas.

blurb: An oasis town of palm groves in the Ziz valley, on the way to the Erg Chebbi dunes, famous for its fossils and dates.
fun_fact: The black stone around Erfoud is full of fossils hundreds of millions of years old, and the town's workshops polish them into tables and sinks.

blurb: The winding road over the High Atlas between Marrakech and Ouarzazate, with Berber villages and views at every bend.
fun_fact: At 2,260 m it is the highest major mountain pass in North Africa.

blurb: A vermilion shrine in the forest of Nara Park, lined with thousands of stone and bronze lanterns.
fun_fact: Its lanterns are lit all together only twice a year, at the lantern festivals in February and August.

blurb: Chile's capital between the snowy Andes and the coastal hills, with hilltop viewpoints, lively markets and wineries on its doorstep.
fun_fact: It was founded in 1541 by Pedro de Valdivia and named after Saint James, the patron saint of Spain.

blurb: A red lake at 4,278 m in Bolivia's far southwest, coloured by algae and dotted with thousands of pink flamingos.
fun_fact: The red comes from algae and sediments in the water, and the lake is a key breeding ground for the rare James's flamingo.

blurb: The Habsburgs' summer palace in Vienna: gilded rooms, huge baroque gardens, a hilltop Gloriette and the world's oldest zoo.
fun_fact: Its name means 'beautiful spring', after a well whose water was drunk at the court.

blurb: A romantic royal tomb in pine woods outside Hue, with lotus ponds, pavilions and a lakeside house the emperor used as a retreat.
fun_fact: Its stone stele is the largest in Vietnam, and bringing it from the quarry took four years.

blurb: The quieter neighbour of Ha Long Bay off Cat Ba Island: limestone islets, small beaches and calm water for kayaking.
fun_fact: Lan Ha holds hundreds of limestone islands, and is home to the golden-headed langur, one of the rarest monkeys in the world.

blurb: The South Island's biggest city, rebuilt after the 2011 earthquake, with a big botanic garden, punts on the Avon and street art.
fun_fact: It became a city by Royal Charter in 1856, which makes it officially the oldest city in New Zealand.

blurb: A huge mosque on the Atlantic in Casablanca, with a minaret of 210 m. It is one of the few mosques in Morocco open to non-Muslims on guided tours.
fun_fact: Part of it stands over the ocean, and its roof can open to the sky.

blurb: One of the highest cities in the world, at about 4,000 m, below the silver mountain of Cerro Rico that made Spain rich.
fun_fact: In the 1500s Potosí was one of the richest and biggest cities in the world, and 'worth a Potosí' became a Spanish saying for great wealth.

blurb: Giant drawings scratched into the desert of southern Peru: a monkey, a hummingbird, a spider and dead-straight lines, best seen from a small plane.
fun_fact: They have lasted some 2,000 years because the area is one of the driest places on Earth, with almost no rain or wind.

blurb: A river town in the Amazon, the gateway to jungle lodges on the Tambopata and Madre de Dios rivers.
fun_fact: The rainforest of Tambopata nearby has some of the richest wildlife on Earth, with famous clay licks where hundreds of macaws gather.

blurb: The biggest town in the Sacred Valley, by the river under the snowy peak of Chicón, with a local market and many valley hotels nearby.
fun_fact: In the first week of June the town fills with dancers from the surrounding villages, who perform in the streets.

blurb: A big Tokyo park full of museums, a zoo, temples and a pond of lotus, and one of the city's best spots for cherry blossom.
fun_fact: It was one of Japan's first public parks, opened in 1873 on the grounds of a temple that guarded Edo Castle's unlucky northeast 'demon gate'.

blurb: A peninsula in west Iceland nicknamed 'Iceland in miniature': a glacier-capped volcano, black beaches, fishing villages and lava fields.
fun_fact: Jules Verne chose the Snæfellsjökull volcano here as the entrance in Journey to the Centre of the Earth.

blurb: Bolivia's white colonial capital, with whitewashed churches, quiet plazas and mild weather, where the country's independence was signed.
fun_fact: At 2,790 m it is the second highest capital city in the world after Quito.

blurb: A palm oasis near Ouarzazate scattered with old earthen kasbahs, a quiet stop on the road of a thousand kasbahs.
fun_fact: Its Kasbah Amridil is so famous it was printed on Morocco's old 50-dirham banknote.

blurb: A walled city within Arequipa: a convent of bright red and blue lanes, cloisters and fountains, open to visitors.
fun_fact: It was founded in 1579 and was closed to the outside world for almost four centuries, until it opened to the public in 1970.

blurb: The Sun Gate: a stone gateway on the ridge above Machu Picchu where the Inca Trail ends, with the first view of the whole citadel.
fun_fact: It was a checkpoint for people entering and leaving the sanctuary, and at the June solstice the sun rises right through it.

blurb: A green Mekong Delta province of coconut palms, canals and orchards, explored by sampan and bicycle.
fun_fact: It is known as the 'land of coconuts', and coconut candy is made here by hand in small family workshops.

blurb: A lake in north Iceland's volcanic zone, ringed by lava pillars, craters, bubbling mud pots and warm nature baths.
fun_fact: Its name means 'midge lake', after the swarms of tiny flies in summer. It was formed by a lava eruption 2,300 years ago.

blurb: The 'waterfall of the gods', a wide horseshoe of falling water in north Iceland, right next to the Ring Road.
fun_fact: The story says pagan idols were thrown into it when Iceland became Christian around the year 1000, but the tale seems to be a 19th-century invention.

blurb: Lima's seaside district on the cliffs, with parks, the Larcomar mall, surfers below and paragliders above.
fun_fact: In the middle of the district stands Huaca Pucllana, a big adobe pyramid built by a pre-Inca culture some 1,500 years ago.

blurb: A rocky 'island' in the middle of the Salar de Uyuni, covered in giant cactuses, with a view over endless white salt.
fun_fact: It is the top of an ancient volcano that once stood in a prehistoric lake, which is why it has fossil coral.

blurb: A city of marble tombs and statues in Buenos Aires where presidents, writers and Eva Perón are buried.
fun_fact: It was the city's first public cemetery, made in 1822 from the garden of a monks' convent. The BBC named it one of the world's best cemeteries.

blurb: A hot-spring town in the mountains near Mount Fuji, with a lake, pirate-ship cruises, a ropeway over volcanic vents and art museums.
fun_fact: Eggs boiled in the hot springs of Owakudani turn black, and legend says each one adds seven years to your life.

blurb: Thousands of salt pans terraced down a canyon in the Sacred Valley, worked by local families since Inca times.
fun_fact: The salt comes from a single salty spring, and the ponds are shared among local families who each harvest their own.

blurb: Africa's highest mountain, a snow-capped volcano rising from the plains, climbed in 6 to 8 days without ropes.
fun_fact: At 5,895 m it is the highest free-standing mountain in the world: it stands alone, not part of a range.

blurb: The main town of the Lofoten islands, with fishing boats, cod-drying racks and steep peaks right behind the harbour.
fun_fact: The rock pinnacle above town, the 'Svolvær Goat', has two horns, and climbers jump the gap between them.

blurb: Vienna's Gothic cathedral with a colourful tiled roof and a tall spire, in the middle of the old town.
fun_fact: Its roof is covered with about 230,000 glazed tiles that form the double-headed eagle of the Habsburgs.

blurb: A yellow baroque church and convent in central Lima, with a huge old library and catacombs beneath.
fun_fact: The catacombs were Lima's first cemetery, and the bones of thousands of people are laid out in patterns underground.

blurb: Jungle and grassland in Nepal's lowlands with one-horned rhinos, crocodiles, elephants and the chance of a tiger.
fun_fact: It was Nepal's first national park, in 1973. By the late 1960s only 95 rhinos were left here; today there are hundreds.

blurb: The shoguns' Kyoto residence, with painted screens, gardens and wide moats.
fun_fact: Its corridors have 'nightingale floors' that chirp when you walk on them, so nobody could sneak in unheard.

blurb: A huge park of lawns and forest in Nara, home to great temples and more than 1,200 roaming deer.
fun_fact: Legend says a god arrived here riding a white deer, which is why the deer are treated as sacred messengers.

blurb: A highland village above the Sacred Valley with Inca walls, a colonial church and women weaving in the traditional way.
fun_fact: Legend says Chinchero was the birthplace of the rainbow, and its Sunday market still runs partly by barter.

blurb: Tanzania's biggest city on the Indian Ocean, a busy port with fish markets, beaches and ferries to Zanzibar.
fun_fact: Its name means 'house of peace' in Arabic, and it is one of the fastest-growing cities in Africa.

blurb: A geothermal town on a lake, with geysers, boiling mud, Māori culture, hot pools and mountain-bike trails in the redwoods.
fun_fact: The town smells of rotten eggs because of the hydrogen sulphide from its hot springs. Locals stop noticing it.

blurb: The gateway to Sossusvlei: a fuel stop and campsite at the park gate, next to a small canyon carved by the Tsauchab River.
fun_fact: Its name means 'six belts' in Afrikaans: early settlers needed six leather straps tied together to lower a bucket to the water in the canyon.

blurb: Lima's bohemian seaside barrio, with colourful old mansions, street art, bars and peñas with live Afro-Peruvian music.
fun_fact: Its wooden Bridge of Sighs has a legend: if you cross it holding your breath on the first try, your wish comes true.

blurb: Inca ruins on a ridge facing Machu Picchu, reached on the Salkantay trek, with a rare side view of the citadel.
fun_fact: It is lined up with Machu Picchu and with the sunrise of the June solstice, which suggests it had a ceremonial role.

blurb: A 16th-century Koranic school in Marrakech with a courtyard of carved stucco, cedar and tiles around a pool.
fun_fact: Once finished it was the largest Islamic college in North Africa, and up to some 900 students lived in its small rooms.

blurb: A port town on the Atlantic where you can kayak with seals, watch flamingos on the lagoon and drive into the dunes at Sandwich Harbour.
fun_fact: It was a South African enclave until 1994, four years after Namibia's independence.

blurb: A rocky valley in Damaraland with thousands of ancient rock engravings of giraffes, rhinos and lions.
fun_fact: It was Namibia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site, in 2007. Its Afrikaans name means 'doubtful spring'.

blurb: Europe's most powerful waterfall after the Rhine Falls: a thundering wall of grey glacier water in a canyon in northeast Iceland.
fun_fact: It appears in the opening scene of the film Prometheus.

blurb: Rowing boats glide down a river through rice fields and caves between limestone cliffs in Ninh Binh. Rowers often use their feet.
fun_fact: Tam Cốc means 'three caves', and the boat ride passes through all three.

blurb: A small bronze dog outside Shibuya Station, Tokyo's most famous meeting point.
fun_fact: Hachikō waited at this station every day for nearly ten years after his owner died, and became a symbol of loyalty.

blurb: The capital of north Iceland at the head of a long fjord, with a botanical garden, cafés, whale watching and a ski hill.
fun_fact: Its traffic lights show red hearts instead of round red lights, a gesture of positivity after the 2008 financial crash.

blurb: A cone-shaped mountain by the sea on the Snæfellsnes peninsula, with a small waterfall in front, especially striking under the northern lights.
fun_fact: It is said to be the most photographed mountain in Iceland, and it appears as the 'arrowhead mountain' in Game of Thrones.

blurb: A small park between the Rift Valley wall and a soda lake, with forest, flamingos and lions that climb trees.
fun_fact: More than 350 kinds of birds have been seen on the lake.

blurb: An adobe village in the Atacama Desert under the Licancabur volcano, the base for geysers, salt lakes and stargazing.
fun_fact: The desert around it is one of the driest places on Earth, which is why many of the world's big telescopes are built nearby.

blurb: Norway's second city between seven mountains and the fjords, with the colourful wooden houses of Bryggen and a fish market on the harbour.
fun_fact: It is one of the rainiest cities in Europe. It was founded in 1070 and was Norway's largest city until the 1830s.

blurb: The main town of the Colca Valley at 3,600 m, with a busy market, hot springs and terraced fields all around.
fun_fact: Its hot springs at La Calera are fed by volcanic heat, a welcome soak after the cold Andean nights.

blurb: A fiord in Fiordland where sheer cliffs and waterfalls drop into dark water under Mitre Peak. Cruise it or kayak it, rain or shine.
fun_fact: Rudyard Kipling called it the eighth wonder of the world. Its Māori name, Piopiotahi, comes from a now extinct bird.

blurb: A desert town in southern Peru, the base for flights over the Nazca Lines and visits to ancient aqueducts and cemeteries.
fun_fact: It gets about 4 mm of rain a year, one of the driest places on Earth, and the Nazca people built spiral wells, puquios, that still carry water.

blurb: Forests, lakes and peat bogs running down to the Beagle Channel just outside Ushuaia, with easy coastal walks.
fun_fact: The Pan-American Highway, which starts in Alaska, ends inside this park, and the 'End of the World Train' stops here.

blurb: A great Zen temple in Arashiyama with a famous 14th-century pond garden that 'borrows' the hills behind as its backdrop.
fun_fact: It was founded in 1339 by the shogun Ashikaga Takauji, and its name means 'Temple of the Heavenly Dragon', after a dream of a dragon rising from the river.

blurb: Richly carved royal tombs of the Saadian sultans in Marrakech, with marble columns and painted cedar domes.
fun_fact: A later sultan walled them up, and they were forgotten until they were rediscovered from the air in 1917.

blurb: Arctic islands of sharp peaks rising straight from the sea, red fishing cabins, white beaches and northern lights in winter.
fun_fact: Near Borg stands a reconstructed Viking chief's longhouse, the largest ever found, 83 m long.

blurb: Inca terraces and houses built into a steep slope above the Urubamba, the last ruin on the Inca Trail before Machu Picchu.
fun_fact: Its name means 'forever young' in Quechua, after an orchid that grows here.

blurb: The great cathedral on Cusco's main square, full of colonial paintings and gold, built on the site of an Inca palace.
fun_fact: A famous painting here shows the Last Supper with a roasted guinea pig, cuy, on the table.

blurb: A turquoise glacial lake at about 4,200 m under the ice of Humantay peak, a steep day hike from Soraypampa on the Salkantay route.
fun_fact: Local communities consider the lake and the mountain above it sacred, and hikers sometimes leave small stone stacks as offerings.

blurb: A snowy 5,680 m peak over the Sacred Valley, seen from Ollantaytambo and along the train line to Machu Picchu.
fun_fact: Its Quechua name is Waqay Willka, often translated as 'tears of the sun'.

blurb: Pokhara's lake, with colourful rowing boats, a temple on an island and the Annapurnas reflected on calm mornings.
fun_fact: The two-storey Tal Barahi temple stands on a small island in the middle of the lake.

blurb: Rowing-boat trips through flooded caves and between limestone peaks in Ninh Binh, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
fun_fact: The film Kong: Skull Island was partly shot here.

blurb: A huge wall of blue ice, about 70 m high, that cracks and calves into Lago Argentino in front of the walkways.
fun_fact: Unlike most glaciers it is not shrinking much, and every few years it dams the lake until the water bursts through the ice.

blurb: Morocco's calm, green capital on the Atlantic, with a clifftop kasbah, an unfinished minaret and a tidy medina.
fun_fact: In the 17th century Rabat and Salé were a pirate republic, home to the Barbary corsairs who raided ships as far as Iceland.

blurb: A green salt lake at the foot of the Licancabur volcano on the Chilean border, the far end of the Uyuni jeep tour.
fun_fact: Its colour comes from minerals in the water and turns brightest green when the wind stirs it up.

blurb: The ruins of a great city near Lake Titicaca, older than the Incas, with carved stone gateways and giant statues.
fun_fact: Its Gateway of the Sun was cut from a single block of stone. The Aymara name of the site may mean 'stone in the centre', the centre of the world.

blurb: Kyoto's western edge: the Togetsukyo bridge, the bamboo grove, temples, monkeys on the hill and boat rides on the river.
fun_fact: Kyoto's nobles came here for boating parties a thousand years ago, and its mountain is a protected place of scenic beauty.

blurb: Marrakech's great mosque, whose 77 m minaret is the landmark you see from all over the medina.
fun_fact: It was built in the 12th century and inspired the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat.

blurb: A quieter imperial city with giant gates, stables and granaries built by Sultan Moulay Ismail.
fun_fact: Moulay Ismail's stables were built for some 12,000 horses.

blurb: A carved limestone outcrop near Cusco, with tunnels, zigzag channels and an altar inside a cave.
fun_fact: It was one of the largest holy places of the Inca region, where offerings and perhaps mummification took place.

blurb: The temples of Vietnam's first capital, set among rice fields and limestone peaks in Ninh Binh.
fun_fact: It was the capital of Vietnam from 968 to 1009, before the court moved to what is now Hanoi.

blurb: A maze of clay spires and canyons on the edge of La Paz, eroded by wind and rain into a lunar landscape.
fun_fact: Its Spanish name, Valle de la Luna, is said to come from Neil Armstrong, who visited in 1969 and found it looked like the Moon.

blurb: Five marble hills south of Da Nang riddled with caves, shrines and pagodas, with steps up to sea views.
fun_fact: Each hill is named after one of the five elements: metal, water, wood, fire and earth.

blurb: A tiny fishing village at the very end of the road in Lofoten, with red cabins, cod racks and a stockfish museum.
fun_fact: Its name is a single letter, Å, Norse for 'small river'.

blurb: A green valley of rice fields and stilt houses of the White Thai people, a few hours west of Hanoi. Stay overnight in a homestay.
fun_fact: The White Thai women of the valley are known for their weaving, and many homes have a loom under the house.

blurb: A small garden in Marrakech of cactuses, bamboo and palms around a villa painted an intense cobalt blue.
fun_fact: That colour is called Majorelle blue, after the painter who made the garden. Yves Saint Laurent later bought and saved it.

blurb: A red-brick cathedral built by the French in central Saigon, with two bell towers, next to the old post office.
fun_fact: All its bricks were shipped from Marseille.

blurb: A tiny wooden pagoda standing on a single stone pillar in a lotus pond in Hanoi.
fun_fact: Emperor Lý Thái Tông built it in 1049 after dreaming of a goddess seated on a lotus flower.

blurb: A tree-lined avenue in Tokyo with striking designer stores by famous architects, leading up to Meiji Shrine.
fun_fact: Omotesandō means 'front approach': it was laid out as the main road to the shrine.

blurb: 'Salta la linda', a colonial city in the northwest with pink churches, folk music in the peñas and the road to colourful valleys.
fun_fact: Its museum keeps three Inca child mummies found on the summit of the Llullaillaco volcano, among the best preserved in the world.

blurb: A mountain striped red, yellow and turquoise by minerals, at about 5,000 m south of Cusco. A tough but short hike.
fun_fact: Its colours were hidden under ice until recently: it only became a tourist site in the 2010s, after the snow cover melted.

blurb: The volcanic peninsula by the airport, with lava fields, steaming vents, the Blue Lagoon and recent eruptions.
fun_fact: A bridge here crosses the gap between the North American and Eurasian plates, so you can walk between two continents.

blurb: A relaxed lake town at the gate of Mount Aspiring National Park, with ski fields, hikes like Roys Peak and the famous lone willow in the water.
fun_fact: The 'Wanaka Tree', a willow growing in the lake, may be the most photographed tree in New Zealand.

blurb: New Zealand's small, windy capital on a harbour, with cafés, the national museum Te Papa and a cable car up the hill.
fun_fact: It is the southernmost capital city of a sovereign state in the world.

blurb: A beach village at the northern tip of Zanzibar with white sand, swimming at any tide and dhows built on the beach.
fun_fact: It is a traditional centre of dhow building, and you can watch wooden boats being made by hand on the shore.

blurb: Lima's main square, framed by the cathedral, the Government Palace with its changing of the guard and yellow colonial balconies.
fun_fact: Francisco Pizarro laid it out when he founded Lima on 18 January 1535.

blurb: Reykjavik's giant concrete church, whose tower gives the best view over the colourful roofs of the city.
fun_fact: Its shape is inspired by basalt columns like those of Svartifoss, and at 74.5 m it is the largest church in Iceland.

blurb: A viewpoint on the rim of the Colca Canyon where Andean condors glide on the morning air, often just metres away.
fun_fact: Andean condors have wingspans of over 3 m and can live for more than 50 years.

blurb: Cusco's main square, with two great churches, wooden balconies and hills all around. It was the heart of the Inca capital.
fun_fact: In Inca times the square was much bigger, and it was built over a swamp that the Incas drained.

blurb: A quieter alternative to Rainbow Mountain, with three striped mountains and an easier, shorter walk.
fun_fact: The colours come from layers of minerals, iron for red and copper sulphate for green and blue.

blurb: Saigon's big covered market under a clock tower: clothes, coffee, dried fruit and food stalls, with a night market outside.
fun_fact: The building dates from 1914 and is one of the oldest surviving structures in the city. The market itself began by the Saigon River in the 1600s.

blurb: A small Inca hillfort above the start of the Inca Trail, looking down on the ruins of Patallacta and the Cusichaca valley.
fun_fact: It sits on a rocky spur where the Cusichaca stream meets the Urubamba, a strategic lookout over the valley entrance.

blurb: A savannah park a few hours from Dar es Salaam, with elephants, giraffes, zebras and lions on the open Mkata floodplain.
fun_fact: It borders the vast Selous (Nyerere) reserve to the south, and together they form one huge ecosystem.

blurb: A rocky headland on the Skeleton Coast with one of the biggest Cape fur seal colonies in the world: tens of thousands of seals, and a strong smell.
fun_fact: The Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão landed here in 1486 and put up a stone cross, which gave the cape its name.

blurb: A narrow canyon cut by the Tsauchab River near the Sossusvlei gate, cool and shady for a short walk between its walls.
fun_fact: In places it is only 2 m wide, and one stretch holds water all year, where animals come to drink.

blurb: The skeleton of a domed hall that survived the atomic bomb of 1945, kept as it was beside the river in Hiroshima.
fun_fact: It was designed by a Czech architect, Jan Letzel, in 1915, and was one of the few buildings left standing near where the bomb exploded.

blurb: The largest island of the Ha Long area, with a national park of jungle hills, beaches and boat trips into Lan Ha Bay.
fun_fact: Legend says the island's name, 'women's island', comes from three women whose bodies washed ashore here and were honoured with temples.

blurb: The steaming valley of Haukadalur, where the geyser Strokkur erupts every few minutes, a few steps from the old Great Geysir.
fun_fact: Great Geysir gave its name to all the geysers in the world, but today it rarely erupts. Strokkur does the show for it.

blurb: A tiny salt-making village on the edge of the Salar de Uyuni, where families dry and pack salt by hand and build with salt blocks.
fun_fact: Most of the people of Colchani live from salt: they cut it from the flat, dry it in cones and pack it for all of Bolivia.

blurb: A glacier that runs from the Southern Alps almost down to rainforest on the West Coast, best seen on a heli-hike.
fun_fact: It was named in 1865 after the Austrian emperor Franz Joseph I by the geologist Julius von Haast.

blurb: Vienna's huge park of meadows and chestnut avenues, with an old amusement park and the famous giant Ferris wheel.
fun_fact: The Riesenrad Ferris wheel dates from 1897 and starred in the film The Third Man.

blurb: The wooden 'Moon Crossing Bridge' over the river in Arashiyama, with forested hills behind, lovely in cherry and maple season.
fun_fact: An emperor named it in the 13th century after watching the moon seem to cross over it.

blurb: The highest and hardest point of the Inca Trail, at 4,200 m, reached on day two after a long climb.
fun_fact: Its Quechua name, Warmi Wañusqa, means 'dead woman': seen from below, the ridge looks like a woman lying on her back.

blurb: An Inca site on a steep rock spur along the Inca Trail, reached by a narrow stone stairway, with mountain views all around.
fun_fact: Its name is usually translated as 'inaccessible town', because cliffs protect it on three sides.

blurb: Inca ruins with ceremonial baths on a ridge of the Inca Trail at 3,600 m, often wrapped in cloud.
fun_fact: It is called 'the town above the clouds', and its five stone baths still fill with water in the rainy season.

blurb: The historic square of Buenos Aires, facing the pink presidential palace, the Casa Rosada, and the scene of Argentina's great moments.
fun_fact: Since 1977 the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo have walked here every Thursday to ask about their children who disappeared under the dictatorship.

blurb: The vast winter palace of the Habsburgs in central Vienna, with the imperial apartments, the Sisi Museum and the Spanish Riding School.
fun_fact: It was the seat of power for more than 600 years, and today it is the office of the Austrian president.

blurb: A cool highland town on a hill in southern Tanzania, the base for safaris in Ruaha National Park.
fun_fact: Its name comes from the Hehe word lilinga, 'fort'. The Hehe chief Mkwawa defeated a German column nearby in 1891.

blurb: Wild desert mountains in northwest Namibia, with ancient rock art and desert-adapted elephants and rhinos.
fun_fact: Its elephants have adapted to the desert: they can go days without drinking and walk long distances between waterholes.

blurb: Kyoto's Silver Pavilion, a simple Zen temple with a raked sand garden, a cone of sand and a mossy hillside walk.
fun_fact: Despite its name, it was never covered in silver. The nickname only appeared centuries later.

blurb: An old merchant town in the Japanese Alps with dark wooden streets, sake breweries, morning markets and Hida beef.
fun_fact: Its float festival, held in spring and autumn, is considered one of the three most beautiful festivals in Japan.

blurb: Huge circular Inca terraces sunk into the ground on the plateau above the Sacred Valley, like a giant amphitheatre.
fun_fact: It may have been an agricultural lab: the temperature changes by several degrees between the top and bottom terraces.

blurb: A fishing village on small islands in Lofoten, with galleries, cafés and racks of drying cod.
fun_fact: Its football pitch, squeezed onto a rocky islet surrounded by sea, is famous as one of the most beautiful in the world.

blurb: Tokyo's 634 m broadcasting tower, with observation decks that on clear days show Mount Fuji.
fun_fact: It is the tallest tower in the world, and the height 634 can be read as 'Musashi', the old name of the Tokyo region.

blurb: A quiet valley of rice terraces, bamboo forest and stilt-house villages southwest of Hanoi, for hikes and homestays.
fun_fact: Its waterwheels made of bamboo still lift water into the rice fields.

blurb: A baroque old town on the Salzach under a hilltop fortress, the birthplace of Mozart and the setting of The Sound of Music.
fun_fact: Its name means 'salt castle': the city grew rich on salt from mines nearby.

blurb: An island on Lake Titicaca with no cars and no hotels, where visitors sleep with local families and climb to two hilltop temples.
fun_fact: It is called the 'Island of the Kantuta', after the red flower that is the national flower of Peru and Bolivia.

blurb: A grand French colonial post office next to Saigon's cathedral, still in use, with a vaulted hall and old maps on the walls.
fun_fact: It was built at the end of the 19th century, and a giant portrait of Ho Chi Minh hangs over the counters.

blurb: One of the few corners of Tokyo where the old town survives: temples, a big cemetery, craft shops and lots of cats.
fun_fact: It escaped both the 1923 earthquake fires and the wartime bombing, which is why its old wooden streets are still there.

blurb: A white-and-gold castle on giant stone walls in a big park in Osaka, with a museum inside and moats around.
fun_fact: The keep is a 1931 concrete copy, but its walls of interlocking granite boulders from the 1620s still stand.

blurb: A twisting moss-green canyon in south Iceland, about 100 m deep, with a path along its edge.
fun_fact: It became so popular after a Justin Bieber music video was filmed here in 2015 that it had to be closed to protect the moss.

blurb: A mountain village at 2,860 m where almost every Everest trek begins, after a short, steep flight from Kathmandu.
fun_fact: Its tiny sloping runway, named after Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, has been called the most dangerous airport in the world.

blurb: A milky-blue geothermal spa in a black lava field near the airport, with silica mud masks and a swim-up bar.
fun_fact: The water is runoff from the geothermal power plant next door, rich in silica and algae, which give it its colour.

blurb: Tokyo's young, loud shopping and nightlife hub around the famous scramble crossing, with rooftop views from Shibuya Sky.
fun_fact: The statue of the loyal dog Hachikō outside the station is the most popular meeting point in the area.

blurb: A row of colourful wooden merchant houses on Bergen's harbour, with narrow alleys, craft shops and a Hanseatic museum.
fun_fact: German Hanseatic merchants ran it as a trading post for about 400 years. The houses have burned many times and were always rebuilt the old way.

blurb: The 'rich mountain' above Potosí, still mined by cooperatives; visitors can go into the tunnels with a former miner.
fun_fact: Between the 16th and 18th centuries, 80% of the world's silver came from this one mountain.

blurb: A long ribbon of palm groves, kasbahs and earthen villages following the Draa River south from Ouarzazate towards the Sahara.
fun_fact: The Draa is Morocco's longest river, but it rarely reaches the Atlantic: most of its water is used up or lost in the desert.

blurb: A crater lake in Hakone with a red torii gate in the water, pirate-ship cruises and, on clear days, Mount Fuji behind.
fun_fact: It sits in the caldera of the Hakone volcano, which last erupted around the year 1170.

blurb: The snow-capped volcano that rises over Arequipa, a perfect cone of 5,822 m that can be climbed in two days.
fun_fact: It is an active volcano, and in 1998 archaeologists found Inca mummies of children who had been sacrificed on its summit.

blurb: A star-shaped red dune over 170 m high on the road to Sossusvlei, the classic dune to climb at sunrise.
fun_fact: It takes its name from its position: kilometre 45 of the road from the Sesriem gate. Its sand is about 5 million years old.

blurb: A mountain village in the High Atlas below walnut trees and terraced fields, the starting point for climbing Toubkal.
fun_fact: Mount Toubkal above it is the highest mountain in North Africa, at 4,167 m.

blurb: An Inca site of stone fountains and channels near Cusco, where water still flows as it did 500 years ago.
fun_fact: Its Spanish nickname is El Baño del Inca, 'the bath of the Inca'.

blurb: Tall stone burial towers on a peninsula above Lake Umayo near Puno, built by the Colla people before and under the Incas.
fun_fact: The towers, called chullpas, only have openings facing east, where the sun was believed to be reborn each day.

blurb: The pink presidential palace on Plaza de Mayo, with the balcony from which Eva Perón addressed the crowds.
fun_fact: One story says the pink colour came from mixing white paint with cow's blood, a common technique of the time.

blurb: A white marble and glass opera house rising from the Oslo fjord, with a sloping roof you can walk up for city views.
fun_fact: Its roof is meant to be walked on: the architects designed it like a glacier sliding into the sea.

blurb: A Mekong Delta river town with a floating market, fruit orchards, a French-style church and boats loaded with produce.
fun_fact: At the floating market, boats hang a sample of what they sell, a pineapple or a cabbage, from a tall pole so buyers can see it from afar.

blurb: The Argentine town near Iguazu Falls, at the point where Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay meet.
fun_fact: From the Hito Tres Fronteras viewpoint in town you can see three countries at once, across the rivers.

blurb: Japan's finest original castle, a white fortress of layered roofs on a hill, nicknamed the White Heron.
fun_fact: It has survived for almost 700 years, including the bombing of the city in the Second World War and the 1995 Kobe earthquake.

blurb: A glacier-capped volcano at the tip of the Snæfellsnes peninsula, visible from Reykjavik on clear days.
fun_fact: In Jules Verne's Journey to the Centre of the Earth, the heroes climb down into its crater to begin their journey.

blurb: The twin-towered city hall in Shinjuku with free observation decks 202 m up and views to Mount Fuji on clear days.
fun_fact: Its architect, Kenzo Tange, designed the twin towers with a hint of a Gothic cathedral.

blurb: A mountain town north of Tokyo with richly decorated shrines in a cedar forest, lakes and waterfalls.
fun_fact: The famous carving of the 'three wise monkeys', see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil, is on a stable at Tōshō-gū shrine here.

blurb: A milky turquoise lake in the Mackenzie Basin, with a small stone church and lupins in early summer.
fun_fact: It sits in a dark sky reserve, one of the best places on Earth for stargazing.

blurb: A narrow fjord of sheer cliffs and waterfalls, like the Seven Sisters, with farms perched high above the water.
fun_fact: Some farms on its cliffs were so steep that legend says the farmers pulled up their ladders when the tax collector came.

blurb: A small village at the end of the Aurlandsfjord, where the steep Flåm Railway climbs to the mountains.
fun_fact: The Flåm Railway is one of the steepest standard-gauge railways in the world: a gradient of 5.5% for most of the line.

blurb: The vast ruined palace of a 16th-century sultan in Marrakech, with sunken gardens and storks nesting on the walls.
fun_fact: It was paid for with a ransom from Portugal, and its name means 'the incomparable'. A later sultan stripped it to build Meknes.

blurb: A beach village on Zanzibar's northwest coast with soft white sand, calm water at all tides and sunset parties.
fun_fact: Unlike much of Zanzibar's coast, the sea at Kendwa barely pulls back at low tide, so you can swim all day.

blurb: A smoky Taoist temple in Saigon full of carved wooden statues of gods and heroes, and a pond of turtles.
fun_fact: It was built in 1909 by the Cantonese community, and US president Barack Obama visited it in 2016.

blurb: A French colonial theatre from 1900 in central Saigon, where you can see the acrobatic bamboo show 'À Ố'.
fun_fact: It was built in the style of the Petit Palais in Paris, and after 1956 it was used for a time as the parliament of South Vietnam.

blurb: A small island off Stone Town with a sandy beach, snorkelling and giant tortoises that you can feed.
fun_fact: Its prison was never used for prisoners: it became a quarantine station for yellow fever instead.

blurb: The river that winds through Hue past pagodas and royal tombs, best seen on a slow dragon-boat trip.
fun_fact: It is said to get its name from flowers of orchards upstream that fall into the water in autumn and give it a scent.

blurb: An adobe village in the Quebrada de Humahuaca at the foot of the Hill of Seven Colours, with a craft market on its square.
fun_fact: Its Hill of Seven Colours owes its stripes to rock layers of different ages, from purple to green and yellow.

blurb: A man-made island in Tokyo Bay with a beach, malls, a giant Gundam robot statue and views of the Rainbow Bridge.
fun_fact: It began as small fortress islands built in the 1850s to defend Tokyo against foreign ships. 'Daiba' means 'cannon battery'.

blurb: The Sherpa capital, a horseshoe of houses on a mountainside at 3,440 m, where Everest trekkers stop to get used to the altitude.
fun_fact: Its Saturday market draws traders who walk for days from lower valleys, and even from Tibet in the past.

blurb: Fez's oldest tannery, a honeycomb of stone vats of dye seen from leather-shop terraces. Take the sprig of mint they offer.
fun_fact: It has been working since around the 11th century, and the hides are still softened with pigeon droppings.

blurb: A mountain town in the Middle Atlas with pitched roofs, gardens and cedar forests where Barbary macaques live.
fun_fact: Its Alpine look has earned it the nickname 'the Switzerland of Morocco', and it holds one of Africa's lowest recorded temperatures, -23.9 °C.

blurb: An oasis town on the edge of the Sahara near the Erg Chebbi dunes, with a big traditional market and old ksars.
fun_fact: Nearby lie the ruins of Sijilmasa, once a great caravan city on the gold trade route across the Sahara.

blurb: A tiny desert stop of a fuel station, rusting car wrecks and a famous bakery on the road to Sossusvlei.
fun_fact: Its bakery is famous all over Namibia for its apple pie, a must for every road trip.

blurb: A red, very salty lake in the Rift Valley under the Ol Doinyo Lengai volcano, where most of East Africa's lesser flamingos breed.
fun_fact: Its water is so alkaline it can calcify animals that die in it, leaving them looking like stone statues.

blurb: Peru's share of the Amazon covers more than half the country: river lodges, canopy walks, monkeys, macaws and giant otters.
fun_fact: The Amazon is the largest rainforest on Earth, and its river carries more water than the next seven largest rivers combined.

blurb: Green mountains in northeast Tanzania with forest, villages and viewpoints over the plains, for walks from Lushoto.
fun_fact: The African violet, a popular houseplant all over the world, was first found in these mountains.

blurb: A cool hill town in the Usambara Mountains, with a colonial past, a busy market and walks to viewpoints and villages.
fun_fact: The Germans called it Wilhelmstal and used it as a summer retreat from the heat of the coast.

blurb: The cathedral on Lima's main square, rebuilt after several earthquakes, with carved choir stalls and Pizarro's tomb.
fun_fact: Francisco Pizarro, who founded Lima, is buried inside, in a chapel decorated with mosaics.

blurb: A 307 m cliff on the island of Magerøya, at the top of Europe, under the midnight sun in summer.
fun_fact: It is often called Europe's northernmost point, but a nearby headland, Knivskjellodden, actually reaches about 1.5 km further north.

blurb: A mountain village in the Quebrada de Humahuaca with a rebuilt pre-Inca hill fort, the Pucará, and colourful hills all around.
fun_fact: Its Pucará was a fortified town of the Omaguaca people, built about 900 years ago on a hill above the river.

blurb: A well-preserved castle town on the Sea of Japan, with geisha and samurai districts, gold leaf crafts and fresh seafood.
fun_fact: Almost all of Japan's gold leaf, about 99%, is made in Kanazawa. You can even eat it on ice cream.

blurb: One of the three finest gardens in Japan, with ponds, stone lanterns, bridges and old pines held up by ropes in winter.
fun_fact: Its name means 'garden of the six qualities': space, seclusion, artifice, antiquity, water and views.

blurb: A fishing village in Lofoten of red cabins on small islands, under steep granite peaks. The Reinebringen hike gives the classic view.
fun_fact: It has often been called the most beautiful village in Norway.

blurb: A Mekong river town near the Cambodian border with floating fish farms, a Cham village and the sacred Sam Mountain.
fun_fact: Families live in floating houses with fish farms in cages under the floor.

blurb: A field of geysers and steaming vents at 4,320 m above San Pedro de Atacama, best at sunrise when the steam is thickest.
fun_fact: It is one of the highest geyser fields in the world and the largest in the southern hemisphere.

blurb: A car-free island on Lake Titicaca with Inca ruins, terraced hills and walking trails, reached by boat from Copacabana.
fun_fact: The Incas believed the sun god was born here, and that the first Inca came out of the lake nearby.

blurb: A small rainforest village at the foot of the Franz Josef Glacier, the base for glacier heli-hikes and hot pools.
fun_fact: The glacier is named after the Austrian emperor Franz Joseph I, and its Māori name, Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere, means 'the tears of the avalanche girl'.

blurb: A former gold-rush town near Queenstown, with a tree-lined main street of old cottages and golden colours in autumn.
fun_fact: It was founded after gold was found in the Arrow River in 1862, and you can still see the huts of its Chinese gold miners.

blurb: One of the largest canyons in the world, a vast gorge in southern Namibia with a famous five-day hiking trail.
fun_fact: It is about 160 km long and up to 550 m deep, often called the second largest canyon on Earth.

blurb: A medieval castle and fortress on Oslo's harbour, with ramparts to walk and views over the fjord.
fun_fact: It has never been taken by an enemy in battle, although it was handed over to the Germans in 1940.

blurb: One of the narrowest fjords in the world, only about 250 m wide in places, with cliffs and waterfalls on both sides.
fun_fact: It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the Geirangerfjord.

blurb: Argentina's biggest lake, milky turquoise from glacier water, with boat trips to the Upsala and Spegazzini glaciers.
fun_fact: Its colour comes from 'glacial flour', rock ground so fine by the ice that it floats in the water.

blurb: A lagoon where giant dunes meet the Atlantic south of Walvis Bay, reached by 4x4 along the beach at low tide.
fun_fact: The dunes here drop straight into the ocean, so the route depends on the tide.

blurb: A hidden waterfall inside a narrow canyon near Seljalandsfoss. Wade in along the stream to see it fall into a rocky chamber.
fun_fact: Its name means 'canyon dweller', because the falls are almost completely hidden by the rock.

blurb: A colourful village at the end of a deep fjord in east Iceland, with a rainbow street, art galleries and the ferry to Europe.
fun_fact: It is where the ferry from Denmark arrives, after almost three days at sea via the Faroe Islands.

blurb: A Buddhist monastery at 3,867 m on the Everest trail, with one of the best views of Everest and Ama Dablam.
fun_fact: It is the largest monastery of the Khumbu, and every autumn its monks hold the masked dance festival of Mani Rimdu.

blurb: A cave at the foot of a mountain in Ninh Binh, with about 500 steps up to a dragon on the summit and a view over the rice fields.
fun_fact: The stone dragon winding along the summit ridge is the reward for the climb, with Tam Coc's river below.

blurb: A port city of colourful houses on steep hills, street art, old funiculars and poets' houses.
fun_fact: Its old funicular lifts, the ascensores, have carried people up its hills since 1883.

blurb: A desert peninsula of red beaches, cliffs and sea lions, south of Lima, where the desert meets the Pacific.
fun_fact: It is named after the Paracas culture, which buried its dead wrapped in fine woven textiles more than 2,000 years ago.

blurb: The biggest barrio of Buenos Aires: parks, rose gardens, cafés, bars and the trendy streets of Palermo Soho.
fun_fact: Its park, Bosques de Palermo, was once the private estate of the 19th-century ruler Juan Manuel de Rosas.

blurb: A small harbour town at the head of Queen Charlotte Sound, where the ferry from Wellington docks.
fun_fact: The museum on its waterfront keeps the Edwin Fox, one of the oldest surviving merchant ships in the world, built in 1853.

blurb: A coastal town between snowy mountains and the sea, famous for whale watching, dolphins, seals and crayfish.
fun_fact: Sperm whales feed here all year because a deep undersea canyon comes very close to the shore.

blurb: A maze of drowned valleys and green islands at the top of the South Island, for boating, kayaking and the Queen Charlotte Track.
fun_fact: The Sounds are river valleys that were flooded by the sea, and they make up about a fifth of New Zealand's coastline.

blurb: A lakeside town on Lake Taupō, with Huka Falls, hot springs, skydiving and trout fishing.
