fun_fact: Lake Taupō fills the crater of a supervolcano whose eruption about 1,800 years ago was one of the most violent of the last 5,000 years.

blurb: A needle of granite topped by ice near El Chaltén, one of the hardest mountains in the world to climb. Hikers see it from Laguna Torre.
fun_fact: Its first ascent is still disputed: Cesare Maestri claimed it in 1959, but many climbers do not believe him.

blurb: Namibia's highest mountain, a granite massif rising from the desert, home to thousands of ancient rock paintings.
fun_fact: Its most famous painting, the 'White Lady', is thousands of years old.

blurb: A small village at the head of the Nærøyfjord where fjord cruises from Flåm arrive, under steep cliffs and waterfalls.
fun_fact: It has a reconstructed Viking village, Njardarheimr, where people live and work as in the Viking age.

blurb: A small red-stone Inca site on the road above Cusco, once a checkpoint and resting place on the royal road.
fun_fact: Its name means 'red fortress', after the colour its stones take at sunset.

blurb: The Moroccan edge of the world's largest hot desert: dunes, camel rides, starry nights in a camp and Berber music.
fun_fact: The Sahara is about as large as the United States, but only around a quarter of it is sand dunes.

blurb: The 67 m white obelisk in the middle of Avenida 9 de Julio, the symbol of Buenos Aires and the place to celebrate football wins.
fun_fact: It was built in just 31 days in 1936, for the 400th anniversary of the city's first founding.

blurb: A mountain village at 2,870 m in rhododendron forest, the base for the sunrise climb to Poon Hill.
fun_fact: From Poon Hill above it you can see both Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, two of the world's ten highest peaks.

blurb: A long valley in Argentina's far north with hills striped in every colour, adobe villages and old churches.
fun_fact: It has been a route of people and trade for about 10,000 years, and part of the Inca road ran through it.

blurb: A riverside village at 2,610 m, the first night's stop on the Everest trek from Lukla, with suspension bridges and prayer wheels.
fun_fact: It sits on the Dudh Kosi, the 'milk river', named after its white glacial water.

blurb: A tongue of the Mýrdalsjökull glacier in south Iceland, easy to reach for a guided glacier walk with crampons.
fun_fact: It lies over the Katla volcano, one of the most dangerous in Iceland, and the ice is streaked with black volcanic ash.

blurb: Reykjavik's concert hall on the harbour, with a glass facade of honeycomb panels that glitter in the light.
fun_fact: The facade was designed with the artist Olafur Eliasson, inspired by Iceland's basalt columns.

blurb: A fishing village at the north tip of the Vesterålen islands, the best place in Norway to go whale watching for sperm whales.
fun_fact: The sea floor drops to more than 1,000 m just off Andenes, so sperm whales feed close to shore.

blurb: A small village in south Iceland among lava fields and waterfalls, a good stop on the Ring Road towards Skaftafell.
fun_fact: In 1783 its priest gave a famous 'fire sermon' and, it is said, the lava flow stopped just before the church.

blurb: A high-plateau town between the Middle and High Atlas, a stop on the road from Fez to the Sahara, known for apples and fossils.
fun_fact: It is called Morocco's apple capital and holds an apple festival every autumn.

blurb: Three volcanoes in the middle of the North Island, crossed by the Tongariro Alpine Crossing, past emerald crater lakes.
fun_fact: It was New Zealand's first national park, gifted by the Ngāti Tūwharetoa chief in 1887, and Mount Ngauruhoe played Mount Doom in The Lord of the Rings.

blurb: A glacial lake right under the granite towers of Fitz Roy, the reward for the steep last hour of El Chaltén's classic hike.
fun_fact: It is named after three members of a French expedition, the team that made the first ascent of Fitz Roy in 1952.

blurb: The Waikato River squeezes through a narrow gorge just outside Taupō and shoots out in a roaring rush of icy-blue water.
fun_fact: So much water passes through that it could fill an Olympic swimming pool in about 11 seconds.

blurb: A small stone church on the shore of Lake Tekapo, with a window framing the lake and mountains behind the altar.
fun_fact: It was built in 1935 for the farming families of the Mackenzie Basin, and it is one of the most photographed buildings in New Zealand.

blurb: Limestone cliffs at Punakaiki on the West Coast layered like stacks of pancakes, with blowholes that spout at high tide.
fun_fact: Nobody fully knows how the layers formed: they started as sea-floor sediment some 30 million years ago.

blurb: A Berber village of stone houses stacked on a slope above Imlil, on the trail to Toubkal.
fun_fact: Mules still carry trekkers' bags up the paths, as there is no road to the top of the village.

blurb: A vegetable village just outside Hoi An where farmers grow herbs organically. Join them for a morning of farming and cooking.
fun_fact: Farmers here fertilise the herbs with a special seaweed from the nearby river, which is said to give them their aroma.

blurb: A French colonial prison in central Hanoi, now a museum of Vietnam's prisoners and, later, American pilots.
fun_fact: American prisoners of war ironically nicknamed it the 'Hanoi Hilton'. Senator John McCain was held here.

blurb: Osaka's retro 'New World' district under the Tsutenkaku tower: neon, cheap kushikatsu skewers and old-school arcades.
fun_fact: It was designed in 1912 with its north half modelled on Paris and its south on New York's Coney Island.

blurb: Hanoi's oldest pagoda, a tall red tower on a small island in West Lake, beautiful at sunset.
fun_fact: It is around 1,500 years old: it was first built in the 6th century on the banks of the Red River and later moved to the lake.

blurb: The green valley of the Urubamba River below Cusco, with Inca terraces, maize fields and the train to Machu Picchu.
fun_fact: The Incas called the river Willkamayu, the 'sacred river', and saw it as the earthly mirror of the Milky Way.

blurb: Fossil tree trunks lying in the open in the desert near Khorixas, with strange welwitschia plants around them.
fun_fact: The trunks are about 280 million years old and were washed here by a flood, then turned to stone.

blurb: The red-brick city hall on Oslo's harbour, with huge murals inside. Visits are free.
fun_fact: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in its main hall every 10 December.

blurb: A hill at 3,210 m above Ghorepani, climbed before dawn for sunrise over Dhaulagiri and the Annapurnas.
fun_fact: It is one of the most famous viewpoints of the Himalaya, reached by a short trek, with no permit for climbing needed.

blurb: A sacred mountain of more than a hundred temples where you can sleep in a monastery and eat Buddhist vegetarian food.
fun_fact: Its Okunoin cemetery, with over 200,000 graves in a cedar forest, is the largest in Japan.

blurb: A huge new Buddhist temple complex on a hill in Ninh Binh, with long corridors of stone arhats and giant bronze statues.
fun_fact: It holds several Vietnamese records, including the largest bronze Buddha and the longest corridor of arhat statues, about 500 of them.

blurb: The camp on the Khumbu Glacier at about 5,364 m where Everest expeditions start, reached on a 12-day trek.
fun_fact: You cannot actually see the summit of Everest from base camp: trekkers climb nearby Kala Patthar for the view.

blurb: A valley of salt-crusted ridges, dunes and canyons near San Pedro de Atacama that turns red and gold at sunset.
fun_fact: NASA has tested Mars rovers in the Atacama because its soil is so dry and lifeless.

blurb: A lakeside town at the gate of Fiordland, the base for Milford and Doubtful Sound and the Kepler Track.
fun_fact: Across the lake, the Te Anau caves are lit by thousands of glowworms, seen from a small boat in the dark.

blurb: A field of boiling mud pools and steam vents at nearly 5,000 m in Bolivia's far southwest, eerie at dawn.
fun_fact: Its name means 'morning sun', because the steam is most spectacular in the cold of early morning.

blurb: A huge, deep-blue lake high in the Andes, shared by Peru and Bolivia, with reed islands, island villages and Inca legends.
fun_fact: At about 3,800 m it is often called the highest navigable lake in the world, and it is the largest lake in South America.

blurb: A blue-and-white walled village on a cliff at the mouth of the river in Rabat, with an Andalusian garden and sea views.
fun_fact: It was built in the 12th century, and later housed pirates of the Republic of Salé.

blurb: The summit of Kilimanjaro at 5,895 m, the roof of Africa, reached at sunrise after a night climb.
fun_fact: 'Uhuru' means 'freedom' in Swahili: the summit got the name in 1964, when Tanzania was formed.

blurb: A park in Oslo filled with more than 200 sculptures of the human body, all by one artist, Gustav Vigeland.
fun_fact: It is the world's largest sculpture park made by a single artist, and its granite Monolith is carved from one block.

blurb: Norway's longest and deepest fjord, with branches like the Nærøyfjord, stave churches and orchards on its shores.
fun_fact: It is more than 200 km long and over 1,300 m deep, the longest fjord in Norway.

blurb: One of the largest caves in Ha Long Bay, with huge chambers of stalactites, reached by steps from the water.
fun_fact: Its name means 'surprise cave', after the reaction of the first visitors to its giant hall.

blurb: A quiet beach city on the central coast with seafood, long bays and old Cham towers.
fun_fact: Its Twin Towers, Tháp Đôi, are Cham temples built about 800 years ago, now in the middle of the city.

blurb: A 14th-century Marinid college with carved cedar, stucco and tiles around a courtyard. Fez and Meknes each have one by this name.
fun_fact: The one in Fez, built 1350–55, is the only madrasa in Morocco that also served as a Friday mosque.

blurb: Limestone caves where a silent boat drifts under a ceiling of thousands of glowworms, like a sky full of stars.
fun_fact: The 'glowworms' are fly larvae that glow to lure insects into sticky threads they hang from the ceiling.

blurb: Osaka's big theme park with rides from film and games, including Super Nintendo World and the Wizarding World of Harry Potter.
fun_fact: It opened in 2001 and was the first Universal theme park in Asia.

blurb: A large earthen kasbah in Ouarzazate with a maze of rooms and painted ceilings, once home of the powerful Glaoui family.
fun_fact: At its height it housed hundreds of people, from the family and servants to craftsmen, and it appears in several films.

blurb: The long inlet south of Oslo, dotted with islands, beaches and summer houses, reached by local ferries.
fun_fact: It is not a real fjord, geologically speaking: it was not carved by a glacier the way fjords are.

blurb: A peninsula on Lake Titicaca where Quechua families welcome visitors to stay in their homes and work the fields.
fun_fact: Its community runs one of the oldest home-stay programmes on the lake, started so that tourism money stays with the families.

blurb: A small 14th-century college in the Fez medina, by the spice market, with some of the finest tile and wood carving in Morocco.
fun_fact: It is named after the attarin, the spice and perfume sellers, whose market is right outside.

blurb: A protected coral reef around a tiny private island off Zanzibar, the best place on the island for snorkelling with dolphins and turtles.
fun_fact: The island itself is privately owned and off limits, but the reef around it is open to snorkellers and divers.

blurb: A hilltop above Pokhara for sunrise over the Annapurnas and the take-off point for paragliding over Phewa Lake.
fun_fact: It is one of the most popular paragliding sites in the world, thanks to reliable thermals above the lake.

blurb: A busy beach city with a long bay, islands for snorkelling, mud baths and the old Po Nagar Cham towers.
fun_fact: The Po Nagar towers have been a place of worship for more than a thousand years, used by Cham and Vietnamese alike.

blurb: Rainbow-coloured mountains, lava fields and a natural hot pool in the Icelandic Highlands, the start of the Laugavegur trek.
fun_fact: Its hills owe their pinks, yellows and greens to rhyolite, a volcanic rock rare in Iceland.

blurb: The biggest of the Iguazu Falls, a U-shaped chasm where half the river pours in. Reach it on a catwalk over the river.
fun_fact: It is about 80 m high and 150 m wide, and the spray rises so high you can see it from kilometres away.

blurb: A mountain village of steep thatched farmhouses in the Japanese Alps, magical under snow.
fun_fact: The roofs are built like hands joined in prayer, gasshō-zukuri, so heavy snow slides off.

blurb: A rocky hill at about 5,645 m above Gorak Shep, the highest point of the Everest trek and the best view of Everest itself.
fun_fact: Its name means 'black rock'. It is often higher than Everest base camp by about 300 m.

blurb: A funicular that climbs from central Bergen to Mount Fløyen in 6 minutes, for views over the city and forest walks.
fun_fact: It opened in 1918 and carries over a million passengers a year.

blurb: A shallow salt lake below the Rift Valley wall, where you can spend a morning with the Hadzabe hunter-gatherers.
fun_fact: The Hadzabe are among the last people in Africa who live mainly by hunting and gathering, and their language uses clicks.

blurb: A mountain pass and village in the Southern Alps, crossed by the TranzAlpine train, with alpine walks and cheeky kea parrots.
fun_fact: Kea, the world's only alpine parrot, live here and are famous for pulling rubber off cars.

blurb: A white stupa on a ridge above Phewa Lake in Pokhara, reached by boat and a forest climb, with views of the Annapurnas.
fun_fact: It was built by Japanese Buddhist monks, one of several peace pagodas they have raised around the world.

blurb: A rock shaped like a tree in the Siloli Desert, sculpted by wind and sand, on the jeep route across Bolivia's southwest.
fun_fact: It is about 7 m tall, and the wind carrying sand has worn its 'trunk' thinner than its 'crown'.

blurb: A street of stalls in La Paz selling herbs, potions, amulets and dried llama foetuses for offerings to Mother Earth.
fun_fact: Dried llama foetuses are buried under the foundations of new houses as an offering to Pachamama for good luck.

blurb: A small lakeside town on Lake Titicaca with a white Moorish-style basilica, boats to Isla del Sol and great sunsets.
fun_fact: Its basilica holds the Virgin of Copacabana, and the famous beach in Rio de Janeiro was named after her.

blurb: New Zealand's highest mountain at 3,724 m, with easy walks like the Hooker Valley Track to a lake full of icebergs.
fun_fact: Edmund Hillary trained on its slopes before climbing Everest. A huge rockfall in 1991 knocked about 10 m off its summit.

blurb: A pagoda built into a mountain in three levels near Tam Coc, with caves and views over the rice fields.
fun_fact: It dates from 1428, and its name means 'Jade Cave'.

blurb: An Arctic port town between mountains and fjord, with a ski slope above town and a scenic railway into Sweden.
fun_fact: Fierce naval battles were fought in its fjord in 1940, and German and British wrecks still lie on the bottom.

blurb: The mountain town of the Cordillera Blanca, the base for treks and climbs among Peru's highest snowy peaks and turquoise lakes.
fun_fact: Almost the whole town was destroyed by the 1970 earthquake, one of the deadliest in the history of the Americas.

blurb: A hill village on the rim of the Kathmandu Valley, known for sunrise views over a long stretch of the Himalaya.
fun_fact: On a clear day you can see Everest from here, far to the east.

blurb: A tiny village on the wild West Coast next to the Pancake Rocks and blowholes, with walks into Paparoa National Park.
fun_fact: The rocks at Punakaiki look like stacked pancakes, and at high tide seawater blasts up through the blowholes.

blurb: A maze of twisted lava pillars, caves and arches near Lake Mývatn, with short marked trails.
fun_fact: Its name means 'dark castles'. Icelandic folklore says the 13 Yule Lads, troll-like Christmas figures, live here.

blurb: A Zen temple in Kyoto famous for its rock garden: 15 stones on raked white gravel, made for silent contemplation.
fun_fact: From any point on the viewing platform you can see only 14 of the 15 stones at once.

blurb: A white holy town on two hills near Volubilis, built around the tomb of the founder of Morocco's first Islamic dynasty.
fun_fact: It has Morocco's only cylindrical minaret, covered in green tiles with Quranic verses.

blurb: A modern Arctic port, the gateway to Lofoten by ferry, with sea eagles and the world's strongest tidal current nearby.
fun_fact: Near the city, the Saltstraumen strait has one of the strongest tidal currents in the world, with whirlpools up to 10 m across.

blurb: A long sandy beach and lagoon between Hue and Da Nang, at the foot of the Hai Van Pass, with oyster farms and seafood stalls.
fun_fact: Its bay belongs to the 'Club of the Most Beautiful Bays in the World'.

blurb: A long sandy beach about 5 km from Hoi An's old town, easy to reach by bicycle through the rice fields.
fun_fact: Storms have eaten away much of the beach in recent years, and it has been rebuilt with sandbags and new sand.

blurb: A stony desert of bare hills an hour from Marrakech, with camps for sunset camel rides and dinner under the stars.
fun_fact: It has no sand dunes: it is a desert of rocks and pale hills, with the snowy Atlas on the horizon in winter.

blurb: Huge walled orchards of olives, oranges and pomegranates next to the royal palace in Marrakech, watered by old channels from the Atlas.
fun_fact: The gardens were laid out in the 12th century and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site with the medina.

blurb: Two baroque palaces with formal gardens in Vienna, home to Klimt's The Kiss and other great Austrian art.
fun_fact: It was built as a summer home for Prince Eugene of Savoy, the general who beat the Ottomans, and the name means 'beautiful view'.

blurb: One of the world's great opera houses, with performances almost every night and cheap standing places sold on the day.
fun_fact: Its orchestra's musicians form the Vienna Philharmonic, which plays the famous New Year's Concert.

blurb: A windswept desert at about 4,500 m in Bolivia's southwest, with strange rock formations and volcanoes on the horizon.
fun_fact: It is one of the driest places in Bolivia, and the wind has carved its rocks into shapes like the Árbol de Piedra.

blurb: A small town among red canyons and cactus country in southern Bolivia, for horse rides and the back way into Uyuni.
fun_fact: The outlaws Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid robbed a mining payroll near here in 1908 and died days later in nearby San Vicente.

blurb: The massive unfinished minaret of a 12th-century mosque in Rabat, among rows of broken columns, facing the royal mausoleum.
fun_fact: It was meant to be the largest mosque in the world, but work stopped when the sultan died in 1199.

blurb: The royal square of Bhaktapur with the 55-window palace, the golden gate and pagoda temples.
fun_fact: The Golden Gate of its palace is considered one of the finest pieces of metalwork in the Kathmandu Valley.

blurb: The king's yellow palace at the top of Oslo's main street, in a public park, with a daily changing of the guard.
fun_fact: Unlike many palaces, its park is open to everyone and has no fence.

blurb: A small Newari town at the meeting of two rivers outside Kathmandu, with medieval temples and homestays.
fun_fact: Legend says a third, invisible river joins the two here, which makes the meeting point holy.

blurb: A hill town east of Kathmandu with old Newari houses and views of the Himalaya, a good first stop on the road to Tibet.
fun_fact: On a clear day its viewpoints show a sweep of peaks from Langtang to Everest.

blurb: A Mekong Delta town of rivers and orchards, with homestays on Binh Hoa Phuoc island among fruit trees.
fun_fact: It sits between two branches of the Mekong, the Tiền and the Hậu, and the islands in between are covered in fruit orchards.

blurb: A series of waterfalls on the Kunene River on the Angolan border, lined with baobabs and palms, in Himba country.
fun_fact: Epupa means 'falling water' in the Herero language.

blurb: A fishing town on a lagoon in southeast Iceland with views of Vatnajökull's glaciers, famous for its langoustines.
fun_fact: It is called Iceland's lobster capital and holds a lobster festival every summer.

blurb: A quiet coast of long fjords, fishing villages, reindeer and mountains in east Iceland.
fun_fact: They are the only place in Iceland with wild reindeer, brought from Norway in the 18th century.

blurb: A small town at the end of a fjord in north Iceland, once the herring capital, with a lively herring museum.
fun_fact: In the 1940s and 50s thousands of workers came here each summer to salt herring, and it was nicknamed the 'Atlantic Klondike'.

blurb: A Sherpa village at 3,985 m under Ama Dablam on the Everest trail, with the oldest monastery in the Khumbu.
fun_fact: For years its monastery claimed to keep a yeti scalp and hand, until tests showed they came from other animals.

blurb: A cluster of lodges at about 4,940 m on the Everest trail, by the Khumbu Glacier, the last stop before Gorak Shep.
fun_fact: Nearby stands a pyramid-shaped research station run by Italian scientists, one of the highest laboratories in the world.

blurb: A frozen lakebed at 5,164 m with a few lodges, the last stop before Everest Base Camp and Kala Patthar.
fun_fact: It was the base camp for the 1953 expedition that made the first ascent of Everest.

blurb: A narrow side fjord in Lofoten, only about 100 m wide at its entrance, between cliffs over 1,000 m high, seen by boat.
fun_fact: In 1890 fishermen fought a battle here over the right to fish its cod, the 'Battle of Trollfjord'.

blurb: The capital of Hokkaido, famous for its snow festival, miso ramen, beer and ski slopes close to town.
fun_fact: It hosted the 1972 Winter Olympics, the first Winter Olympics held in Asia.

blurb: A 19.4 km day hike across a volcanic landscape, past the Red Crater and the Emerald Lakes, often called New Zealand's best day walk.
fun_fact: The trail passes Mount Ngauruhoe, which played Mount Doom in The Lord of the Rings.

blurb: The hobbit village built for The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit, on a farm in the green hills of Matamata.
fun_fact: It is on a working sheep farm, and the film crew chose it because it had no power lines or roads in view.

blurb: Europe's largest mountain plateau, bare and full of lakes, crossed by hiking trails and the Oslo–Bergen railway.
fun_fact: It is home to Europe's largest herd of wild reindeer.

blurb: Chile's neoclassical presidential palace in central Santiago, with a changing of the guard and an underground cultural centre.
fun_fact: It was built as the colonial mint, which is why it is called La Moneda, 'the coin'. It was bombed during the 1973 coup.

blurb: The main town of east Iceland on a lake and river, with forest walks and a good base for the East Fjords.
fun_fact: Its lake, Lagarfljót, is said to hide a giant serpent, the Lagarfljót Worm, Iceland's own Loch Ness monster.

blurb: A 17th-century earthen kasbah in the Skoura palm grove, with towers, courtyards and an old olive press.
fun_fact: It was printed on Morocco's old 50-dirham banknote.

blurb: A port city on the Strait of Gibraltar, with a kasbah on the hill, cafés and views of Spain across the water.
fun_fact: From 1923 to 1956 it was an international zone run by several countries, a haven for spies, writers and smugglers.

blurb: A large Gurung village of stone houses on a hillside facing Annapurna South and Machapuchare, on the Annapurna treks.
fun_fact: Many men from Gurung villages like this have served as Gurkha soldiers in the British and Indian armies.

blurb: A seaside town on the Patagonian coast, the base for the Valdés Peninsula, whales and penguins.
fun_fact: It was founded in 1865 by Welsh settlers, and Welsh tea houses still survive in the region.

blurb: A wild peninsula of Patagonian steppe and beaches, with southern right whales, sea elephants, sea lions and penguins.
fun_fact: Its orcas are famous for beaching themselves on purpose to grab sea lion pups at the water's edge.

blurb: A retro steel tower in Osaka's Shinsekai district, with a lucky god, Billiken, on the observation deck.
fun_fact: Visitors rub the soles of Billiken's feet for luck. The figure is an American lucky charm that became a symbol of Osaka.

blurb: A border town on the Red River facing China, where the night train from Hanoi arrives for the road up to Sapa.
fun_fact: A bridge over the river here links Vietnam to China's Yunnan province, and you can walk across.

blurb: A city west of Kobe dominated by Himeji Castle, the finest original castle in Japan, with a garden next to it.
fun_fact: Himeji Castle survived the bombing of the city in 1945: legend says a bomb that hit the top floor failed to explode.

blurb: An 18th-century merchants' inn in the Fez medina, now a woodworking museum with a rooftop café.
fun_fact: Traders once kept their goods and animals on the ground floor and slept in the rooms above.

blurb: The river on Namibia's southern border with South Africa, for multi-day canoe trips through desert canyons.
fun_fact: It is the longest river in South Africa, and its mouth is a protected wetland for birds.

blurb: A farming town in northern Namibia near the Hoba meteorite, the largest known meteorite on Earth.
fun_fact: The Hoba meteorite weighs about 60 tonnes and has never been moved since it fell some 80,000 years ago.

blurb: Nepal's oldest temple, on a hilltop above the Kathmandu Valley, covered in carvings of Vishnu.
fun_fact: It holds the oldest known stone inscription in Nepal, from the year 464.

blurb: Namibia's foggy desert coast of shipwrecks, whale bones, seal colonies and dunes running into the Atlantic.
fun_fact: The San called it 'the land God made in anger', and Portuguese sailors 'the gates of hell'.

blurb: A long beach village on Zanzibar's east coast with seaweed farms in the lagoon and the sea retreating far at low tide.
fun_fact: Local women farm seaweed in the shallow lagoon, which is sold for cosmetics and food.

blurb: A small island with a white beach and coral reefs off Stone Town, for snorkelling and a quiet day.
fun_fact: The first telegraph cable linking Zanzibar to the world came ashore here in 1879.

blurb: The jewel of the Westfjords: a waterfall fanning out like a bridal veil down a 100 m rock slope, with smaller falls below.
fun_fact: Its name means 'thunderous', after the noise it makes.

blurb: Europe's westernmost point, a 14 km line of sea cliffs in the Westfjords where puffins come close in summer.
fun_fact: Millions of seabirds nest on its cliffs, which rise to about 440 m.

blurb: A narrow, lantern-lit alley in Kyoto between the Kamo River and Kiyamachi, lined with restaurants and teahouses.
fun_fact: In summer, restaurants build wooden platforms over the river, kawayuka, for dining in the evening breeze.

blurb: An Arctic town in Finnmark known as the 'town of the northern lights', with prehistoric rock carvings and an ice hotel.
fun_fact: Its rock carvings are up to 7,000 years old and form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

blurb: A blinding white salt flat at 3,450 m in the Jujuy highlands, on the road over the mountains from Purmamarca.
fun_fact: Workers cut rectangular pools in the crust to harvest salt, and the pools fill with turquoise water.

blurb: A lonely little black church standing in a lava field by the sea on the Snæfellsnes peninsula.
fun_fact: It was rebuilt in 1987 on the foundations of a 19th-century church, and it is one of the most photographed churches in Iceland.

blurb: A steep climb of almost 2,000 stone steps above Reine to the most famous view in Lofoten.
fun_fact: Sherpas from Nepal built the stone staircase, finished in 2019, to make the slippery old path safer.

blurb: An archipelago north of Lofoten, wilder and quieter, with whale safaris from Andenes and fjords among the islands.
fun_fact: Its waters are one of the best places in the world to see sperm whales, which feed in a deep underwater canyon close to shore.

blurb: A Sherpa village of stone-walled fields at 4,410 m on the Everest trek, where trekkers rest a day to get used to the altitude.
fun_fact: Its stone walls protect the barley and potato fields from the strong winds of the valley.

blurb: Tokyo's upscale shopping district of flagship stores, department store food halls and the Kabuki-za theatre.
fun_fact: Its name means 'silver mint': a silver coin mint stood here in the Edo period.

blurb: A lavishly carved and gilded shrine in a cedar forest, the tomb of the shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu.
fun_fact: It is where you find the famous three wise monkeys and a carving of a 'sleeping cat' that guards the way to the tomb.

blurb: A salt lake in the Atacama near San Pedro where you float like in the Dead Sea, with volcanoes all around.
fun_fact: The water is saltier than the ocean, so swimmers float without any effort.

blurb: A port town between Lofoten and Tromsø, with Viking history, a medieval stone church and whale-watching in winter.
fun_fact: Its Trondenes church is the northernmost medieval stone church in the world.

blurb: A port town near Sapporo with a lamp-lit canal, old stone warehouses, glass workshops and fresh sushi.
fun_fact: Its canal was nearly filled in to build a road in the 1980s; local protests saved half of it.

blurb: A glacier tumbling from the Southern Alps towards the rainforest on the West Coast, seen on walks and heli-hikes.
fun_fact: Nearby Lake Matheson reflects Aoraki/Mount Cook and Mount Tasman like a mirror on calm mornings.

blurb: A temple at 3,710 m above Jomsom, sacred to Hindus and Buddhists, where pilgrims bathe under 108 water spouts.
fun_fact: A natural gas flame burns on water inside one of its shrines, a wonder pilgrims have revered for centuries.

blurb: A white marble mausoleum with a green-tiled roof in Rabat, guarded by horsemen, opposite the Hassan Tower.
fun_fact: It holds the tombs of King Mohammed V, who led Morocco to independence, and of his sons.

blurb: An adventure town between Bergen and the fjords, with rafting, skydiving, ski slopes and a lake.
fun_fact: It hosts 'Ekstremsportveko', one of the biggest extreme-sports festivals in the world, every June.

blurb: A harbour town in north Iceland with colourful houses and a wooden church, Iceland's whale-watching capital.
fun_fact: It is the setting of the 2020 film Eurovision Song Contest: The Story of Fire Saga, and the song 'Husavik' was nominated for an Oscar.

blurb: Kanazawa's old geisha quarter of wooden teahouses with lattice windows, some open to visitors.
fun_fact: One teahouse, Shima, has been kept as it was in 1820 and is a nationally important cultural property.

blurb: Africa's largest national park, covering the red dunes of Sossusvlei, canyons and the Naukluft mountains.
fun_fact: The Namib is often called the oldest desert in the world: it has been dry for at least 55 million years.

names: Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve
blurb: A high-altitude reserve in Bolivia's far southwest with coloured lagoons, flamingos, geysers and volcanoes.
fun_fact: Three species of flamingo live here, including the rare James's flamingo, once thought extinct.

blurb: A port town on islands on Norway's west coast, rebuilt in Art Nouveau style, with a viewpoint up 418 steps.
fun_fact: It burned down in 1904 and was rebuilt in only three years, all in the Art Nouveau style.

blurb: A small hill in central Santiago with stairs, fountains and terraces up to a fortress and a city view.
fun_fact: It is where Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago in 1541.

blurb: A small town in south Iceland with the Lava Centre, a museum on Iceland's volcanoes and earthquakes.
fun_fact: It is in the heart of Njáls saga country, one of the most famous Icelandic sagas.

blurb: A green highland town in the south of Tanzania, among tea fields, crater lakes and waterfalls.
fun_fact: The region gets some of the highest rainfall in Tanzania, which keeps it green all year.

blurb: A Coromandel beach where you dig your own hot pool in the sand at low tide.
fun_fact: Hot water from underground springs, up to about 64 °C, seeps up through the sand.

blurb: A huge rock arch on a white sand beach on the Coromandel Peninsula, reached by a coastal walk or kayak.
fun_fact: It appears in the film The Chronicles of Narnia: Prince Caspian.

blurb: A town on Peru's south coast near Paracas, which gave its name to the grape brandy.
fun_fact: Pisco brandy is named after the port, from where it was shipped in colonial times.

blurb: A temple on a small island in Hoan Kiem Lake, reached by the red Huc Bridge.
fun_fact: It displays a giant preserved turtle from the lake, linked to the legend of the returned sword.

blurb: A jagged granite massif of 3,405 m above El Chaltén, glowing pink at sunrise, seen best from Laguna de los Tres.
fun_fact: It is the mountain on the Patagonia clothing logo, and the Tehuelche called it Chaltén, the 'smoking mountain'.

blurb: A windy mountain town in the Kali Gandaki valley, with an airstrip, apple orchards and the road to Muktinath.
fun_fact: The Kali Gandaki valley here is one of the deepest gorges in the world, between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna.

blurb: A Magar village on the Poon Hill trek, reached by a long stairway of thousands of stone steps.
fun_fact: The climb from Tikhedhunga to Ulleri is famous among trekkers for its 3,000-odd stone steps.

blurb: Iceland's remote northwest: deep fjords, steep mountains, bird cliffs and few people.
fun_fact: Only about 7,000 people live there, and arctic foxes have a protected reserve at Hornstrandir.

blurb: A wine town in the Calchaquí Valleys, famous for its Torrontés white wine and the red rocks of the Quebrada de las Conchas.
fun_fact: Its vineyards are among the highest in the world, at about 1,700 m and above.

blurb: A tiny fishing village on the Snæfellsnes coast with basalt cliffs, sea arches and a stone troll statue.
fun_fact: The stone giant statue in the village is Bárður Snæfellsás, a half-troll from a saga who is said to guard the glacier.

blurb: Norway's second largest island, with sharp peaks, white beaches and fishing villages, less crowded than Lofoten.
fun_fact: It is often called 'Norway in miniature', for having mountains, fjords, forests and beaches on one island.

blurb: A Gurung village on a ridge facing Annapurna South, the gateway to the Annapurna Sanctuary.
fun_fact: It is the last permanent village before the Annapurna Sanctuary, a high basin ringed by peaks of 7,000 to 8,000 m.

blurb: A glacier lake under Cerro Torre, the goal of an easy day hike from El Chaltén, with icebergs floating in front of the glacier.
fun_fact: Cerro Torre above it is so often hidden by cloud that many hikers never see its summit.

blurb: A desert city on Peru's south coast surrounded by vineyards and pisco bodegas, next to the oasis of Huacachina.
fun_fact: It is one of the main producers of pisco, and its bodegas offer tastings.

blurb: New Zealand's largest lake in the heart of the North Island, with trout fishing, sailing and Māori rock carvings.
fun_fact: It fills the crater of a supervolcano, and one of its eruptions, about 1,800 years ago, was among the most violent of the last 5,000 years.

blurb: La Paz's main square, with the cathedral, the presidential palace, parliament and plenty of pigeons.
fun_fact: Its clock on the parliament building runs backwards, a 2014 symbol of looking at the world from the south.

blurb: A busy market street under the railway tracks near Ueno, with cheap snacks, seafood, sweets and clothes.
fun_fact: It began as a black market after the Second World War. 'Ame' may come from the candy sold there, or from 'America'.

blurb: A big leafy park next to Harajuku and Meiji Shrine, where Tokyo goes to picnic, jog and play music on Sundays.
fun_fact: It was the athletes' village for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.

blurb: The towering adobe walls of an Inca temple to the god Viracocha, on the road between Cusco and Puno.
fun_fact: Its central wall stands about 15 m high, on stone foundations, the remains of one of the largest Inca roofed buildings.

blurb: Golden beaches, clear water and coastal forest at the top of the South Island, explored by kayak, water taxi and the coast track.
fun_fact: It is New Zealand's smallest national park, named after the Dutch explorer Abel Tasman, who anchored nearby in 1642.

blurb: A lake town at the foot of Mount Fuji with classic views across the water, onsen hotels and cherry and maple trees.
fun_fact: It is one of the Fuji Five Lakes, formed when lava flows from Fuji dammed the valleys.

blurb: A stone path along a canal lined with cherry trees in eastern Kyoto, between Ginkaku-ji and Nanzen-ji.
fun_fact: It is named after the philosopher Nishida Kitarō, who walked here every day to meditate.

blurb: A palm-oasis town in the Draa Valley, the gateway to camel treks in the desert.
fun_fact: A famous painted sign in town says 'Tombouctou 52 jours', the time it took caravans to cross the Sahara by camel.

blurb: The highest peak in North Africa at 4,167 m, climbed in two days from Imlil via a mountain refuge.
fun_fact: It is the highest mountain in North Africa and the Arab world.

blurb: A modern beach resort on the Atlantic, with a long sandy bay, a seafront promenade and a hilltop kasbah.
fun_fact: It was rebuilt almost from scratch after an earthquake destroyed it in 1960.

blurb: A riverside village near Nayapul, the starting point of many Annapurna treks, with a permit checkpoint.
fun_fact: It stands where the Modi Khola and Bhurungdi rivers meet, among terraced fields.

blurb: The largest town on the West Coast, a former gold and coal town where the TranzAlpine train ends.
fun_fact: It is named after Sir George Grey, a 19th-century governor of New Zealand.

blurb: A deep gorge near Queenstown with vineyards on its slopes and the historic bridge of the first commercial bungy jump.
fun_fact: The world's first commercial bungy jump opened on the Kawarau Gorge Suspension Bridge in 1988.

blurb: One of the best preserved fishing villages in Norway, in a narrow Lofoten inlet, now a living museum.
fun_fact: It was among the first places in Norway chosen for a UNESCO project to protect traditional architecture, in 1975.

blurb: The only village on the Valdés Peninsula, where whale-watching boats leave from the beach.
fun_fact: From June to December southern right whales come so close to shore here that you can see them from the beach.

blurb: A protected beach on the Patagonian coast where you walk among hundreds of thousands of Magellanic penguins.
fun_fact: It is the largest colony of Magellanic penguins in South America.

blurb: A mountain town near the Chinese border, famous for its Sunday market where Flower Hmong people come to trade.
fun_fact: Flower Hmong women wear some of the most colourful clothes in Vietnam, with embroidery in bright pinks and greens.

blurb: Argentina's wine capital at the foot of the Andes, with tree-lined streets, Malbec vineyards and Aconcagua close by.
fun_fact: Its streets are lined with irrigation channels, acequias, first dug by the Huarpe people and still used to water the trees.

blurb: Rows of food stalls and shops around Tokyo's old fish market, for sushi breakfasts, tamago and kitchen knives.
fun_fact: The famous wholesale fish market moved to Toyosu in 2018, but the outer market stayed.

blurb: A long, deep, Z-shaped lake in the mountains around Queenstown, with steamboat cruises and mountain views.
fun_fact: The lake's surface rises and falls about 10 cm every few minutes. Māori legend says it is the heartbeat of a sleeping giant.

blurb: A clifftop park in Miraflores with a giant sculpture of a kissing couple and mosaic walls, made for sunsets over the Pacific.
fun_fact: It opened on Valentine's Day 1993, and its walls carry lines of love poems by Peruvian poets.

blurb: A cool, misty mountain park between Hue and Da Nang, with jungle trails, waterfalls and the ruins of French colonial villas.
fun_fact: The French built a hill station on its summit in the 1930s to escape the coastal heat; only ruins of the villas remain.

blurb: Buenos Aires' grand opera house, with a golden horseshoe hall, painted dome and guided tours by day.
fun_fact: Its acoustics are ranked among the best in the world, alongside Vienna's Musikverein and Boston's Symphony Hall.

blurb: A geothermal field near Mývatn of boiling mud pots, hissing steam vents and orange sulphur ground.
fun_fact: It sits on top of the Krafla volcanic system, one of the most active in Iceland, and the ground is too hot to leave the paths.

blurb: A winding gorge in the High Atlas with red cliffs, kasbahs and a famous hairpin road climbing out of the valley.
fun_fact: The rock formations along the valley are nicknamed 'monkey fingers' and 'the brain of the mountain' for their strange shapes.

blurb: The tiled and carved tomb of Sultan Moulay Ismail in Meknes, one of the few holy places in Morocco open to non-Muslims.
fun_fact: Moulay Ismail ruled Morocco for 55 years, from 1672 to 1727, one of the longest reigns in history.

blurb: A small village on the Okavango River in the Caprivi strip, near Popa Falls and the Bwabwata and Mahango wildlife areas.
fun_fact: The Okavango River here never reaches the sea: it ends in the Okavango Delta in Botswana's Kalahari.

blurb: An old coastal trading town north of Dar es Salaam with crumbling Swahili and German buildings and ancient ruins.
fun_fact: It was a major port for the caravan trade, and its name is often read as 'lay down your heart' in Swahili.

blurb: Thick, misty forest on the outer slopes of the Ngorongoro crater rim, with elephants, buffalo and guided walks.
fun_fact: The forest catches moisture from the clouds, and its rain feeds the springs and lakes of the crater floor below.

blurb: A viewpoint on the edge of the Usambara Mountains near Lushoto, looking straight down 1,000 m to the Maasai plains.
fun_fact: A farm near the viewpoint makes its own cheese and bread, a famous picnic stop for walkers.

blurb: A narrow wine valley near Queenstown known for its Pinot Noir, with cellar doors and a cycle trail between them.
fun_fact: It is one of the southernmost wine regions in the world, and its wine caves are dug into the hillside.

blurb: An old suspension bridge over a turquoise gorge near Queenstown, home of the world's first commercial bungy jump.
fun_fact: AJ Hackett opened the world's first commercial bungy here in 1988, with a 43 m jump over the river.

blurb: A white triangular church in Tromsø shaped like an iceberg, with a huge glass mosaic and midnight-sun concerts.
fun_fact: Its eastern window is one of the largest glass mosaics in Europe.

blurb: A medieval village of mud houses and a red monastery at the gateway to Upper Mustang, along the Kali Gandaki river.
fun_fact: Beyond Kagbeni lies Upper Mustang, a former kingdom that foreigners need a special, costly permit to enter.

blurb: A grand royal tomb outside Hue, with pavilions, gates and lakes laid out in harmony with the hills.
fun_fact: It was built from 1840 to 1843 for Emperor Minh Mạng, who died before it was finished.

blurb: A vast cemetery in a forest of giant cedars on Mount Koya, with mossy tombs, stone lanterns and the mausoleum of Kōbō Daishi.
fun_fact: With more than 200,000 graves it is the largest cemetery in Japan, and believers say Kōbō Daishi is still meditating there.

blurb: A fishing town on Magerøya island, the nearest town to the North Cape.
fun_fact: It calls itself the northernmost city in the world, though it is very small.

blurb: Highlands around the Ngorongoro crater where Maasai herders live side by side with wildlife, including Olduvai Gorge.
fun_fact: It is one of the few places in Africa where people and wildlife share a protected area. Early humans lived here millions of years ago.

blurb: The old docks of Buenos Aires turned into a district of red-brick warehouses, restaurants and modern towers.
fun_fact: All its streets are named after women, and its white Puente de la Mujer is shaped to suggest a couple dancing tango.

blurb: A remote mining town at 3,775 m on the Puna plateau, on the route of the Train to the Clouds.
fun_fact: The Tren a las Nubes reaches the La Polvorilla viaduct, about 4,200 m high, near the town.

blurb: A white colonial village in the Calchaquí Valleys under the snowy Nevado de Cachi, with an adobe church and archaeology museum.
fun_fact: Its church has a ceiling and altar made of cactus wood, a building material of the high valleys.

blurb: A horseshoe-shaped canyon with 100 m cliffs and birch woods in north Iceland, part of Vatnajökull National Park.
fun_fact: Norse legend says it is the hoofprint of Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse of the god Odin.

blurb: A windy village at 4,371 m on the Everest trail, home to a volunteer clinic for altitude sickness.
fun_fact: The Himalayan Rescue Association clinic here has treated trekkers for altitude sickness since 1975.

blurb: A glacial basin at 4,130 m ringed by Annapurna I, Machapuchare and other giants, the goal of a 7 to 12-day trek.
fun_fact: Annapurna I was the first 8,000 m peak ever climbed, by a French team in 1950.

blurb: A village below Chhomrong with natural hot springs by the river, a favourite soak after the Annapurna Sanctuary trek.
fun_fact: Its hot springs bubble up right on the bank of the Modi Khola, about 20 minutes' walk below the village.

blurb: Santiago's main square, with the cathedral, palm trees, chess players and the national history museum.
fun_fact: Pedro de Valdivia laid out the square in 1541 when he founded the city.

blurb: A cool wine valley between Santiago and Valparaíso, famous for crisp white wines like Sauvignon Blanc.
fun_fact: It had no vineyards until the 1980s: the cool ocean fog that winemakers now love was thought too cold for grapes.

blurb: A waterfall in Skaftafell falling over a cliff of dark hanging basalt columns, like organ pipes.
fun_fact: Its basalt columns inspired the design of Hallgrímskirkja church in Reykjavik.

blurb: A geothermal lagoon by the sea in Reykjavik, with an infinity edge over the ocean and a seven-step sauna ritual.
fun_fact: Its walls are built from turf blocks, the traditional building method of old Icelandic farmhouses.

blurb: The main town of the Westfjords on a spit in a deep fjord, with old wooden houses and boats to Hornstrandir.
fun_fact: Its airport is one of the trickiest in Europe: planes have to fly down the narrow fjord and turn at the end to land.

blurb: A crack in Þingvellir filled with crystal-clear glacier water, where you can snorkel or dive between two continents.
fun_fact: The water is so clear you can see more than 100 m, and it is about 2 °C all year round.

blurb: A remote Polynesian island in the Pacific with nearly a thousand giant stone moai, volcanic craters and empty beaches.
fun_fact: It is one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth: the nearest inhabited land is about 2,000 km away.

blurb: A mining village in the Lípez region on the Uyuni jeep route, with a 17th-century church.
fun_fact: The whole village was moved, church and all, stone by stone, to make way for a huge silver mine.

blurb: A small, quiet island on Lake Titicaca near Isla del Sol, with the ruins of an Inca temple of the moon.
fun_fact: The Incas believed the moon rose from here, and its temple housed women chosen to serve the sun.

blurb: The emperor's residence in central Tokyo, behind moats and stone walls, with the public East Gardens.
fun_fact: In the 1980s, the palace grounds were said to be worth more than all the land in California.

blurb: A friendly town at the foot of Kilimanjaro, with coffee farms and the starting point for most climbs.
fun_fact: On clear mornings the snowy top of Kilimanjaro appears above the town, about 30 km away.

blurb: Turquoise pools and waterfalls in the Rif mountains near Chefchaouen, with a walk to a natural rock bridge.
fun_fact: The 'God's Bridge' near the falls is a natural rock arch high above the river.

blurb: A West Coast town of driftwood beaches and gorges, known for pounamu, New Zealand greenstone carving.
fun_fact: The Hokitika Gorge has milky turquoise water coloured by glacial flour.

blurb: A huge white fortress on the hill above Salzburg, reached by funicular, with views over the old town and the Alps.
fun_fact: It is one of the largest medieval castles in Europe, and it has never been taken by force.

blurb: A national park of jungle and limestone mountains hiding some of the largest caves in the world.
fun_fact: Its Sơn Đoòng cave is the largest known cave passage in the world: a 40-storey building would fit inside.

blurb: Cusco's artisans' quarter: steep cobbled lanes, whitewashed houses, workshops, cafés and a small church with a famous pulpit.
fun_fact: The pulpit of its church is carved from a single tree trunk, considered one of the finest wood carvings of the Americas.

blurb: A wide wall of blue ice ending in Lago Grey in Torres del Paine, with icebergs floating on the lake.
fun_fact: It is part of the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, the third largest ice field in the world after Antarctica and Greenland.

blurb: Oslo's famous ski jump on the hill above the city, with a ski museum and a view over the fjord from the top.
fun_fact: There has been ski jumping here since 1892, and the current jump was rebuilt in steel for the 2011 World Championships.

blurb: A shallow soda lake at the foot of the Rift Valley wall, shimmering pink with flamingos at some times of year.
fun_fact: Hemingway called it 'the loveliest lake in Africa'.

blurb: The highest mountain on Earth, at 8,849 m, seen up close from Kala Patthar or on a scenic flight from Kathmandu.
fun_fact: It still grows a few millimetres every year as the Indian plate pushes into Asia.

blurb: A small village at the head of the Geirangerfjord, with waterfalls and hairpin roads climbing to famous viewpoints.
fun_fact: The Eagle Road above it climbs with 11 hairpin bends to a viewpoint over the whole fjord.

blurb: A mountain town in Romsdalen, with the Rampestreken viewpoint, the Trollstigen road and the Rauma railway.
fun_fact: The nearby Troll Wall is the tallest vertical rock face in Europe, about 1,100 m from top to bottom.

blurb: A village south of Cusco whose plain church hides a dazzling interior of murals and gold leaf.
fun_fact: Its church is called the 'Sistine Chapel of the Americas' for its painted ceilings and walls.

blurb: The highest point on the road and railway between Cusco and Puno, at about 4,335 m, with snowy peaks and grazing alpacas.
fun_fact: It marks the watershed where streams turn either to the Amazon or to Lake Titicaca.

blurb: The simple wooden house on stilts by a pond where Ho Chi Minh lived and worked, behind the Presidential Palace in Hanoi.
fun_fact: He chose this small house over the grand French Presidential Palace next door, which he found too luxurious.

blurb: Auckland's 328 m tower, with a revolving restaurant, a glass floor and a SkyJump off the top.
fun_fact: It is the tallest free-standing structure in the Southern Hemisphere.

blurb: An active volcano above Lake Natron, sacred to the Maasai, climbed overnight to see sunrise from the crater rim.
fun_fact: It is the only active volcano on Earth that erupts natrocarbonatite lava, which flows black and cools white.

blurb: A temple to Vietnam's first emperor in the old capital of Hoa Lư, with carved stone dragons and wooden halls.
fun_fact: Đinh Tiên Hoàng united the country and founded the first Vietnamese empire in 968.

blurb: An ornate Chinese assembly hall in Hoi An, with a dragon fountain, incense coils and a temple to the sea goddess.
fun_fact: It was built by Chinese merchants from Fujian around 1690, and sailors prayed here to Thiên Hậu for safe voyages.

blurb: The wide brown river that loops through Ho Chi Minh City, with ferries, dinner cruises and the speedboat to the Cu Chi tunnels.
fun_fact: It carries some of Vietnam's busiest shipping, and its port made Saigon the economic heart of the south.

blurb: A province near Saigon, home to the colourful Cao Đài Holy See and the sacred mountain Bà Đen.
fun_fact: Cao Đài is a Vietnamese religion founded in 1926 that honours Buddha, Jesus, Confucius and even Victor Hugo as saints.

blurb: Dozens of small waterfalls streaming out of a lava field into the turquoise Hvítá river in west Iceland.
fun_fact: The water flows out from under the lava itself, so the falls appear to come from nowhere along a 900 m stretch.

blurb: The sacred peak of Miyajima, reached by ropeway and a short climb, with views over the Seto Inland Sea.
fun_fact: A flame in its temple hall is said to have been burning for 1,200 years, since the monk Kōbō Daishi lit it.

blurb: The former government house of the shoguns in Takayama, with tatami rooms, rice storehouses and a morning market outside.
fun_fact: It is the only such provincial government office from the Edo period that survives in Japan.

blurb: A tiny village in green hills above a world of caves, famous for glowworm boat rides and black-water rafting.
fun_fact: Its name comes from the Māori wai, water, and tomo, hole: water flowing into holes in the ground.

blurb: A fenced valley in Wellington where native forest and birds like the kākā and takahē have been brought back.
fun_fact: It was the world's first fully fenced urban ecosanctuary, with a fence designed to keep out every mammal pest.

blurb: A peninsula of beaches, bush and gold-mining towns east of Auckland, with Cathedral Cove and Hot Water Beach.
fun_fact: Gold was found here in 1852, the first major gold strike in New Zealand.

blurb: A lone willow growing in the water of Lake Wānaka, with mountains behind. Come at sunrise for the classic photo.
fun_fact: It began as a fence post for a farm around 1939, and grew into a tree. It is said to be the most photographed tree in New Zealand.

blurb: One of the oldest and best preserved castles in Norway, on Bergen's harbour, with a medieval royal hall.
fun_fact: Its Haakon's Hall was built in the 13th century as the largest building of the royal residence when Bergen was Norway's capital.

blurb: Saigon's backpacker district, with cheap hostels, street food and the noisy bars of Bui Vien walking street.
fun_fact: The street is named after Phạm Ngũ Lão, a general who helped defeat the Mongol invasions of the 13th century.

blurb: The river that flows past Hoi An, with lantern boats at night and boat trips to craft villages.
fun_fact: Every month at full moon, people float paper lanterns on the river for good luck.

blurb: Two turquoise lakes in a deep glacial valley under Huascarán, Peru's highest peak, an easy day trip from Huaraz.
fun_fact: The lakes sit at the foot of Huascarán, at 6,768 m the highest mountain in Peru and in the tropics.

blurb: A remote beach at the tip of the Valdés Peninsula with sea lions, elephant seals and, in autumn, hunting orcas.
fun_fact: Its orcas are famous for charging onto the beach to catch sea lion pups, a hunting trick seen in very few places.

blurb: A whitewashed village of flat-roofed houses and stone lanes in the Kali Gandaki valley, famous for its apples.
fun_fact: Its orchards make apple brandy, cider and pie, sold to trekkers along the Annapurna Circuit.

blurb: A hilltop Newari town of old brick houses on a car-free bazaar street, halfway between Kathmandu and Pokhara.
fun_fact: It was a rich stop on the old trade route between India and Tibet, until the new highway bypassed it in the 1970s.

blurb: The biggest city of the Mekong Delta, the base for boat trips to the Cai Rang floating market at dawn.
fun_fact: Its Cái Răng floating market is the largest in the delta, with boats selling fruit and vegetables at sunrise.

blurb: An extravagant royal tomb on a hillside near Hue, blending Vietnamese and European styles, with glass and porcelain mosaics.
fun_fact: Its interior is covered in mosaics made of broken porcelain and glass, some imported from China and Japan.

blurb: A dusty frontier town in the far northwest, the capital of Kaokoland, where Himba, Herero and other peoples come to trade.
fun_fact: Himba women cover their skin and hair with otjize, a paste of butterfat and red ochre, which gives them their red colour.

blurb: Iceland's longest fjord in the north, with Akureyri at its head and whale-watching boats crossing its waters.
fun_fact: It is about 60 km long, the longest fjord in Iceland.

blurb: Boca Juniors' steep, yellow-and-blue stadium in La Boca, with a museum and one of the loudest crowds in football.
fun_fact: Its nickname means 'the chocolate box', because of its shape. Fans say the stands literally shake during matches.

blurb: A hill above Salta reached by cable car or a stairway, with gardens and a view over the whole city.
fun_fact: Over 1,000 steps lead from the city to the top, a popular workout for locals.

blurb: A hill behind Purmamarca striped in red, purple, green and yellow, best seen in the morning light.
fun_fact: Each colour is a different rock layer, laid down over millions of years and then tilted by the rise of the Andes.

blurb: The coastal desert that runs along all of Namibia, with the highest dunes on Earth, fog-fed beetles and desert elephants.
fun_fact: It is thought to be the oldest desert in the world, dry for at least 55 million years.

blurb: A house in Stone Town with a small museum on Freddie Mercury, the Queen singer born in Zanzibar in 1946.
fun_fact: Freddie Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara in Zanzibar and spent his early years here.

blurb: A white suspension bridge across Tokyo Bay to Odaiba, with a walkway and city views, lit up at night.
fun_fact: Its lights are powered by solar panels on the bridge, and on special occasions it glows in rainbow colours.

blurb: Kathmandu's lively tourist district, a tangle of lanes full of gear shops, guesthouses, bars and momo restaurants.
fun_fact: It has been the hub of Himalayan trekking since the 1970s, when it was a stop on the hippie trail.

blurb: A ridge-top village in rhododendron forest on the Annapurna treks, with sunrise views of Annapurna South and Machapuchare.
fun_fact: Its name means 'far water': villagers once had to walk far down the hill to fetch water.

blurb: Japan's hot-spring capital on Kyushu, with steaming vents across town, sand baths and colourful 'hell' pools.
fun_fact: It has more hot springs and more hot water than any other spa town in Japan.

blurb: Chile's largest salt flat, a crusty white plain with lagoons full of flamingos, near San Pedro de Atacama.
fun_fact: Its brine holds about a quarter of the world's known lithium reserves.

blurb: Kamakura's most important shrine, at the end of a long avenue from the sea, with lotus ponds and a grand staircase.
fun_fact: It was founded in 1063 and moved here by Minamoto no Yoritomo, the first shogun.

blurb: A flat-topped cliff jutting out 604 m above the Lysefjord, the reward of a 2 to 3-hour hike.
fun_fact: It appears in Mission: Impossible – Fallout, in the final fight scene.

blurb: A waterfall tumbling over the rift wall at Þingvellir, a short walk from the old parliament site.
fun_fact: The river was diverted over the cliff by early Icelanders, perhaps to bring water to the parliament grounds.

blurb: A rushing waterfall in a narrow lava canyon right next to Hraunfossar in west Iceland.
fun_fact: Its name means 'children's waterfall': legend says two children fell from a stone arch here, and their mother had it destroyed.

blurb: A red five-storey pagoda on a hillside above Fujiyoshida, with Mount Fuji behind it, the classic view at cherry time.
fun_fact: It is a peace memorial built in 1963, and about 400 steps lead up to it.

blurb: The volcano quarry on Easter Island where the moai were carved, with hundreds still standing on its slopes.
fun_fact: Almost all of the island's moai were carved from its volcanic tuff, and about 400 remain here, some half buried.

blurb: A ceremonial stone village on the crater rim of Rano Kau on Easter Island, with petroglyphs and sea views.
fun_fact: It was the centre of the Birdman cult: each year men swam to an islet to fetch the first sooty tern egg of the season.

blurb: A narrow gravel road clinging to cliffs from the high Andes down to the jungle, now ridden downhill by mountain bike.
fun_fact: It was once called the world's most dangerous road. A new highway opened in 2006, leaving it mostly to cyclists.

blurb: A huge, fast-growing city on the Altiplano above La Paz, with a giant Sunday market and colourful 'cholet' buildings.
fun_fact: At about 4,150 m it is one of the highest large cities in the world.

blurb: A lakeside city ringed by mountains, with a covered wooden bridge, an old town of painted facades and boats to Mount Rigi and Pilatus.
fun_fact: Its Chapel Bridge is the oldest covered wooden bridge in Europe, from the 14th century.

blurb: An international city on Lake Geneva, home of the Red Cross and the UN, with a giant lake fountain and the Alps on the horizon.
fun_fact: Its Jet d'Eau fountain shoots water 140 m into the air at 200 km/h.

blurb: The highest volcano on the North Island, with two ski fields and a hot crater lake at the top.
fun_fact: It is one of the most active volcanoes in the world, and its crater lake is warm.

blurb: A port city in southern Hokkaido with a famous night view from Mount Hakodate, a morning fish market and a star-shaped fort.
fun_fact: Its fort Goryōkaku is shaped like a five-pointed star, built in Western style in the 1860s.

blurb: Iceland's biggest national park, around the Vatnajökull ice cap, with glaciers, Skaftafell, Jökulsárlón and Dettifoss.
fun_fact: It covers about 14% of Iceland and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its mix of fire and ice.

blurb: A Tyrolean village with a baroque church, at the edge of the SkiWelt, one of Austria's biggest ski areas.
fun_fact: Its twin-towered church is so big for a village that locals call it the 'cathedral of the Brixental'.

blurb: One of Japan's finest original castles, a black wooden keep beside a moat with the Japanese Alps behind.
fun_fact: Its black walls earned it the nickname 'Crow Castle', and it is one of Japan's oldest surviving keeps.

blurb: A quiet turquoise lake in the Mackenzie Basin, with mountain views and the Alps 2 Ocean cycle trail.
fun_fact: It is part of a dark sky area where the Milky Way is so bright it casts shadows.

blurb: A huge, silent fiord in Fiordland, wilder and less visited than Milford, reached by boat and bus across a lake and pass.
fun_fact: Captain Cook named it in 1770 because he doubted he could sail back out, so he never went in.

blurb: A fishing town on the Snæfellsnes peninsula, right next to Kirkjufell mountain.
fun_fact: Kirkjufell, its neighbour, is said to be the most photographed mountain in Iceland.

blurb: A cluster of grassy pseudo-craters on the shore of Lake Mývatn, with a short walk around them.
fun_fact: They are not real volcanoes: they formed when hot lava flowed over wet ground and steam blasted through it.

blurb: The only inhabited island of the Westman Islands, with puffin cliffs and a volcano that nearly buried the town in 1973.
fun_fact: In 1973 islanders sprayed seawater on the advancing lava to save their harbour, and it worked.

blurb: Basalt sea stacks rising from the waves off Vík, seen from Reynisfjara beach or the village.
fun_fact: Legend says they are two trolls who tried to drag a ship ashore and were turned to stone by the rising sun.

blurb: A mountain city in the Japanese Alps with a black castle, old merchant streets and the gateway to Kamikōchi.
fun_fact: Its castle is one of only five in Japan listed as a National Treasure.

blurb: The grand gateway of Meknes' imperial city, covered in green and white tiles and carved stone.
fun_fact: It was finished in 1732 and is named after its architect, El-Mansour, a Christian convert to Islam.

blurb: A busy roadside town in the Marsyangdi valley, the usual starting point of the Annapurna Circuit.
fun_fact: From here the circuit climbs more than 4,500 m to the Thorong La pass at 5,416 m.

blurb: A stone village at 3,540 m on the Annapurna Circuit, where trekkers stop for a day to acclimatise before Thorong La.
fun_fact: Its people were once famous long-distance traders, with special trading rights granted by the king of Nepal.

blurb: A Sherpa village above Namche Bazaar with a school founded by Edmund Hillary and a monastery.
fun_fact: Its monastery keeps what it says is a yeti scalp.

blurb: A windswept headland on the West Coast with a walkway to a busy fur seal colony.
fun_fact: Captain Cook named it in 1770 after a storm blew his ship back out to sea.

blurb: Norway's third city and its first capital, with Nidaros Cathedral, colourful wharf houses and a student buzz.
fun_fact: Nidaros Cathedral is the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world and was built over the grave of Saint Olav.

blurb: A mountain station at 866 m where the Flåm Railway begins its steep descent to the fjord.
fun_fact: Myrdal has no road access: you can only reach it by train, bike or on foot.

blurb: A steaming volcanic valley in Hakone, reached by ropeway, with sulphur vents and eggs cooked black in the hot springs.
fun_fact: Legend says eating one of its black eggs adds seven years to your life.

blurb: A geothermal valley in Rotorua with the Pōhutu geyser, mud pools, a kiwi house and a Māori arts and crafts institute.
fun_fact: Pōhutu, its biggest geyser, erupts up to 20 times a day, sometimes 30 m high.

blurb: A river town north of Buenos Aires at the gateway to the Paraná Delta, with a fruit market and boats through the islands.
fun_fact: In the delta, houses stand on stilts along hundreds of channels, and boats deliver the post and groceries.

blurb: The riding school in Vienna's Hofburg where white Lipizzaner horses perform classical dressage in a baroque hall.
fun_fact: It is the oldest riding school of its kind in the world, and the Lipizzaners are born dark and turn white with age.

blurb: A quarry wall near Sucre covered in thousands of dinosaur footprints, with a park of life-size dinosaur models.
fun_fact: It has more than 5,000 dinosaur tracks on a near-vertical wall, the largest collection in the world.

blurb: A turf-roofed farmhouse in north Iceland, now a museum showing how Icelanders lived for centuries.
fun_fact: Its rooms are linked by a central corridor so people could move around in winter without going outside.

blurb: Africa's largest lake, shared by Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya, with fishing villages and islands near Mwanza.
fun_fact: It is the largest tropical lake in the world and the main source of the White Nile.

blurb: Morocco's wildest dunes, 60 km of sand beyond the end of the road at M'Hamid, reached by 4x4 or camel.
fun_fact: Some of its dunes reach about 300 m high, and there is no paved road to reach them.

blurb: A predator-free island in Lake Wānaka with a lake inside it and an island inside that lake.
fun_fact: Arethusa Pool on the island is a lake on an island in a lake on an island in a lake on an island, as it were.

blurb: The Gothic cathedral on Christchurch's main square, heavily damaged in the 2011 earthquake and being restored.
fun_fact: While it is rebuilt, the city uses a 'Cardboard Cathedral' made from cardboard tubes, designed by Shigeru Ban.

blurb: A deep blue lake near Wānaka, quieter than its neighbour, for fishing, swimming and hiking.
fun_fact: It lies just a few hundred metres from Lake Wānaka at a place called 'The Neck'.

blurb: A high plain of tussock in the South Island with turquoise lakes, lupins and the darkest skies for stargazing.
fun_fact: It is part of the Aoraki Mackenzie Dark Sky Reserve, one of the largest in the world.

blurb: A tiny fishing village in Lofoten whose red cabins on a rocky islet form one of Norway's most famous views.
fun_fact: It is one of the oldest fishing villages in Lofoten, and its rorbuer cabins were built for visiting cod fishermen.

blurb: A lakeside town with an open-air museum of old farms and the ski jumps of the 1994 Winter Olympics.
fun_fact: Its Maihaugen museum gathered nearly 200 old buildings from across the valley, including a stave church.

blurb: An oxbow lake in the jungle near Puerto Maldonado, explored by canoe, with giant otters, caimans and macaws.
fun_fact: It is one of the few places where you can see giant river otters, up to 1.7 m long.

blurb: An 18th-century tiled-roof wooden bridge in a farming village near Hue, where locals rest on its benches.
fun_fact: It was built in 1776 by a woman of the village so that farmers could cross the canal.

blurb: A great temple in Nara Park with a five-storey pagoda reflected in a pond, and a museum of Buddhist statues.
fun_fact: Its five-storey pagoda is the second tallest wooden pagoda in Japan.

blurb: A huge glacier at the north end of Lago Argentino, reached by boat among icebergs.
fun_fact: It is one of the fastest-retreating glaciers in South America.

blurb: A remote mountain desert in Namibia's far northwest, home to the Himba people and desert-adapted elephants.
fun_fact: It is one of the least populated places in Africa, with fewer than one person per square kilometre.

blurb: The sea passage between the Atlantic and Pacific at the tip of South America, crossed by ferry from Punta Arenas.
fun_fact: Ferdinand Magellan sailed through it in 1520, the first European to do so, during the first voyage around the world.

blurb: A green valley hidden between three glaciers in south Iceland, reached by 4x4 bus across rivers, with great hiking.
fun_fact: Its name means 'Thor's forest', after the Norse god of thunder.

blurb: A canyon in east Iceland lined with thousands of hexagonal basalt columns around a blue-green river.
fun_fact: It was hidden under a glacial river until a dam upstream lowered the water in 2009 and revealed the columns.

blurb: A remote beach of red-gold sand in the Westfjords, stretching about 10 km under green cliffs.
fun_fact: Its colour comes from crushed scallop shells mixed into the sand.

blurb: A port city in the Chilean Lake District, the gateway to Chiloé, Patagonian fjords and the Carretera Austral.
fun_fact: Its Angelmó market and fishing harbour serve curanto, a dish of seafood and meat cooked over hot stones.

blurb: A white castle with lead-tiled roofs in a big park next to Kenroku-en garden, rebuilt in traditional wooden style.
fun_fact: Its roof tiles are made of lead, which turns white over time. Legend says they could be melted into bullets in a siege.

blurb: A small village on the Everest trail at 2,835 m, at the entrance to Sagarmatha National Park.
fun_fact: Sagarmatha, the park you enter at Monjo, is the Nepali name for Everest, meaning 'forehead of the sky'.

blurb: A roadside village where many Annapurna treks start, after a short drive from Pokhara.
fun_fact: Nayapul means 'new bridge' in Nepali, after the bridge over the Modi Khola.

blurb: A hilly port city on Kyushu with a history of foreign trade, a Peace Park and a famous night view.
fun_fact: For over 200 years it was Japan's only window to Europe: Dutch traders were allowed on the tiny artificial island of Dejima.

blurb: A big hill in Santiago reached by funicular or cable car, with a statue of the Virgin and views to the Andes.
fun_fact: Its funicular opened in 1925 and is a national monument.

blurb: A port city of white wooden houses on the west coast, the base for Preikestolen and the Lysefjord.
fun_fact: It grew rich from North Sea oil and is called Norway's oil capital, with a Petroleum Museum on the harbour.

blurb: One of Tokyo's best parks, with Japanese, English and French gardens, a greenhouse and over 1,000 cherry trees.
fun_fact: It was once the private garden of a feudal lord, then of the imperial family, and opened to the public in 1949.

blurb: A gorge of milky turquoise water and white granite near Hokitika, with a swing bridge and a short bush walk.
fun_fact: The colour comes from 'rock flour', fine powder ground by glaciers upstream.

blurb: Bolivia's biggest city, in the tropical lowlands, with a laid-back main square and access to Jesuit missions and Amboró park.
fun_fact: It has grown from about 40,000 people in 1950 to well over a million, one of the fastest-growing cities in South America.

blurb: A natural hot pool at 4,400 m on the Uyuni jeep route, where you soak at dawn surrounded by mountains.
fun_fact: The water comes out at about 30 °C, while the air at dawn is often below freezing.

blurb: A small town in the Draa Valley among palm groves and old kasbahs, below a jagged mountain.
fun_fact: Its Kasbah of Caid Ali has been in the same family for more than 300 years.

blurb: New Zealand's largest national park: fiords, rainforest, waterfalls and famous tracks like the Milford and Kepler.
fun_fact: It is one of the wettest places on Earth, with up to 7 m of rain a year in some spots.

blurb: A sacred red lacquered bridge over a river gorge at the entrance to Nikkō's shrines.
fun_fact: Legend says a god threw two snakes across the river to help a monk cross, and they became the first bridge.

blurb: A fishing village in Lofoten with a ferry quay, hiking trails and a famous theatre festival.
fun_fact: It is a stop on the Hurtigruten coastal ship, which has sailed the Norwegian coast since 1893.

blurb: A huge park of glaciers, lakes and granite spires, home to Perito Moreno, Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre.
fun_fact: Almost half of it is covered by ice, part of the largest ice field outside Antarctica and Greenland.

blurb: Austria's mountain heartland: ski resorts, alpine villages, summer hiking and the city of Innsbruck.
fun_fact: Ötzi the Iceman, the 5,300-year-old mummy found in the Alps in 1991, was discovered on the old Tyrolean border.

blurb: A village on the north edge of the Kathmandu Valley, the start of hikes into Shivapuri park and the Helambu trek.
fun_fact: A reservoir here has supplied Kathmandu with drinking water since the early 20th century.

blurb: A hilltop village on the first day of the Helambu trek, with wide views of the Langtang and Ganesh Himal ranges.
fun_fact: From here, on a clear day, you can see a chain of Himalayan peaks stretching for more than 100 km.

blurb: A hilltop Buddhist monastery and stupa southeast of Kathmandu, one of the holiest pilgrimage sites in Nepal.
fun_fact: Legend says a prince gave his body here to feed a starving tigress and her cubs.

blurb: A jagged mountain range that rises behind Queenstown, with a ski field in winter and alpine lakes in summer.
fun_fact: It is one of only two mountain ranges in the world that run almost exactly north to south.

blurb: A quiet bay in Tierra del Fuego National Park where the Pan-American Highway ends, by forests and peat bogs.
fun_fact: A sign here marks the end of Route 3, about 3,000 km from Buenos Aires and 17,800 km from Alaska.

blurb: A cool hill town in the Central Highlands with pine forests, lakes, flower farms and French villas.
fun_fact: The French founded it as a hill station, and today it grows much of Vietnam's flowers, coffee and strawberries.

blurb: A mining city in the Atacama, the airport for San Pedro, next to one of the biggest copper mines in the world.
fun_fact: The Chuquicamata mine nearby is one of the largest open-pit mines on Earth, more than 4 km long.

blurb: A park of giant cardón cactuses on the road from Salta to Cachi, with mountains in every shade of brown.
fun_fact: The cactuses grow only a few centimetres a year, so the tallest are hundreds of years old.

blurb: A white coral-sand beach with palm trees on Easter Island, watched over by a row of restored moai.
fun_fact: Legend says the first king of the island, Hotu Matu'a, landed here.

blurb: The birthplace of the Buddha in southern Nepal, with the Maya Devi temple and monasteries built by many countries.
fun_fact: A stone pillar put up by the Indian emperor Ashoka in 249 BC still marks the spot.

blurb: An oasis town with a long palm grove and kasbahs, at the entrance to the Todra Gorge.
fun_fact: Its palm grove stretches for about 30 km along the Todra river.

blurb: A village in a valley of pink granite boulders in the Anti-Atlas, with almond blossom in February.
fun_fact: A Belgian artist painted some of the nearby boulders blue in 1984, and the 'Painted Rocks' became an attraction.

blurb: A market town in the Souss valley inside high ochre walls, nicknamed 'little Marrakech', but calmer.
fun_fact: Its walls run about 7 km around the town and are among the best preserved in Morocco.

blurb: The tallest dune around Sossusvlei, a long climb rewarded with a view over Deadvlei's white pan and black trees.
fun_fact: It is about 325 m high, and running down its steep face to Deadvlei takes just a few minutes.

blurb: A tiny coastal village on a lagoon in South Westland, for kayaking and spotting the rare kiwi.
fun_fact: It is home to the rowi, the rarest kind of kiwi, with only a few hundred birds left.

blurb: A wild park of glaciers, beech forest and river valleys near Wānaka, with the Rob Roy Glacier walk.
fun_fact: Mount Aspiring is nicknamed the 'Matterhorn of the South' for its pyramid shape.

blurb: A mountain road with 11 hairpin bends climbing a steep wall in Romsdalen, with waterfalls and viewing platforms.
fun_fact: It is only open in summer, and it took eight years to build, opening in 1936.

blurb: A Patagonian town founded by Welsh settlers, with a dinosaur museum and Welsh tea houses nearby.
fun_fact: Its museum displays bones of Patagotitan, one of the largest dinosaurs ever found.

blurb: A village of banana and coffee farms on the slopes of Kilimanjaro, the start of the Marangu route to the summit.
fun_fact: The Marangu route is nicknamed the 'Coca-Cola route', as it is the only one with huts to sleep in.

blurb: A river cave in Phong Nha national park, explored by boat past stalactites deep into the mountain.
fun_fact: Its underground river is about 14 km long.

blurb: A dormant volcano on the north shore of the Salar de Uyuni, with red and yellow slopes and a cave of mummies.
fun_fact: Aymara legend says the Salar was formed from the tears and milk of Tunupa, crying over her lost child.

blurb: A small town in the Mackenzie Basin, a base for Aoraki/Mount Cook and the Alps 2 Ocean trail.
fun_fact: It was built in 1968 as a temporary town for hydro dam workers, but residents fought to keep it.

blurb: A mountain railway from Myrdal down to the Aurlandsfjord at Flåm, past waterfalls and hairpin tunnels.
fun_fact: Its gradient of up to 5.5% makes it one of the steepest standard-gauge railways in the world.

blurb: The highest mountain in the Americas at 6,961 m, seen from a park near the road from Mendoza to Chile.
fun_fact: It is the highest mountain outside Asia, and the highest in both the western and southern hemispheres.

blurb: Vienna's giant Ferris wheel in the Prater, with old wooden cabins that turn slowly over the city.
fun_fact: It was built in 1897 and starred in the film The Third Man.

blurb: The colonial building in Sucre where Bolivia's declaration of independence was signed, now a museum.
fun_fact: Bolivia declared independence here in 1825, and the country was named after Simón Bolívar.

blurb: A warm hill town in the Yungas, at the bottom of the Death Road, with coffee and citrus farms.
fun_fact: The Yungas are home to the Afro-Bolivian community, with their own music, saya.
