blurb: A riverside trading port of yellow houses, wooden shophouses, temples and lanterns, kept almost unchanged since the 1800s.
fun_fact: Its old town was saved from modern building partly because the river silted up and trade moved to Da Nang.

blurb: The most powerful hot spring in Europe, boiling out of the ground in west Iceland.
fun_fact: It pours out about 180 litres of boiling water a second, which heats nearby towns through pipelines.

blurb: A natural hot pool in the village of Flúðir, with steaming vents and a little geyser nearby.
fun_fact: It is said to be the oldest swimming pool in Iceland, built in 1891.

blurb: A river along the road between Kathmandu and Pokhara, popular for easy one-day white-water rafting.
fun_fact: It starts in Tibet and is named after Shiva's trident: legend says he struck the ground with it to make the river.

blurb: A restored palace garden in the Marrakech medina, with fountains, orange trees and a tower view.
fun_fact: Its water still flows through khettara, old underground channels bringing water from the Atlas mountains.

blurb: A surf village on the Atlantic north of Agadir, with good breaks, yoga retreats and seafood.
fun_fact: Its famous wave, Anchor Point, is one of the best right-hand breaks in Africa.

blurb: The last village at the end of the road in the Draa valley, the starting point for trips to Erg Chigaga.
fun_fact: It was once a key caravan stop on the route to Timbuktu.

blurb: An alpine village with thermal pools, forest walks, mountain biking and jet boats on the Waiau river.
fun_fact: Its hot springs have drawn bathers since the 1880s.

blurb: A West Coast town by the Buller River, with beaches, a seal colony and the Old Ghost Road trail.
fun_fact: It was once the coal capital of New Zealand.

blurb: A wild beach near Westport with a seal colony on the rocks and a cliff walk to Cape Foulwind.
fun_fact: New Zealand fur seals breed here, and in summer you can watch pups on the rocks.

blurb: A long lake surrounded by mountains, with beaches, islands and the famous lone willow tree near the shore.
fun_fact: It is New Zealand's fourth-largest lake, carved by glaciers.

blurb: A wild coast in the far south of the South Island, with waterfalls, forest, sea lions and rare yellow-eyed penguins.
fun_fact: At Curio Bay you can see a petrified forest, 180 million years old, at low tide.

blurb: The largest active geyser in the Southern Hemisphere, in Rotorua's Whakarewarewa valley.
fun_fact: It erupts up to 20 times a day, sometimes reaching 30 m.

blurb: A small town in the King Country at the meeting of two rivers, the start of the Whanganui River canoe trip.
fun_fact: The railway nearby climbs through the Raurimu Spiral, a famous loop of tunnels and bends built in 1908.

blurb: An arm of the Jostedalsbreen glacier ending in a small lake, reached by a walk past waterfalls.
fun_fact: Jostedalsbreen is the largest glacier in mainland Europe.

blurb: A Lofoten village with a long white sand beach and turquoise water facing open sea.
fun_fact: The water may look Caribbean, but its temperature rarely tops 14 °C even in summer.

blurb: A neighbourhood of Arequipa with white stone arches framing the view of El Misti.
fun_fact: Its arches are carved with lines from Arequipa's poets.

blurb: A seafront park in Stone Town that turns into a night food market with grilled seafood and Zanzibar pizza.
fun_fact: 'Zanzibar pizza', sold at the stalls, is really a stuffed pancake fried on a griddle.

blurb: White sand and turquoise water at Nungwi and Kendwa, where the sea stays deep enough to swim at all tides.
fun_fact: Unlike the east coast, the northern beaches barely feel the tide, so you can swim all day.

blurb: An elegant barrio of French-style mansions, cafés and museums around the famous cemetery.
fun_fact: Many of its grand houses were built after a yellow fever epidemic in 1871 drove rich families north from San Telmo.

blurb: A small town on a peninsula in west Iceland with a Settlement Centre telling the story of the first Icelanders.
fun_fact: It is the setting of Egil's saga, about the Viking poet Egill Skallagrímsson.

blurb: A white sand beach in Lofoten between steep green mountains, one of the most beautiful in Norway.
fun_fact: In summer the midnight sun never sets here, so you can lie on the beach at 2 a.m.

blurb: A beach of sand and rounded stones in Lofoten, famous for photos of the northern lights and the midnight sun.
fun_fact: Lofoten lies above the Arctic Circle, so from late May to mid July the sun never sets over this beach.

blurb: The northernmost island of Vesterålen, with whale safaris, white beaches and a space launch site.
fun_fact: Its rocket range has launched research rockets since 1962.

blurb: The river in the northern Serengeti where the herds of the great migration make their dramatic crossings.
fun_fact: Thousands of wildebeest cross at once, and crocodiles wait for them in the water.

blurb: A Buddhist village south of Kathmandu with cave shrines and monasteries.
fun_fact: Guru Rinpoche, who brought Buddhism to Tibet, is said to have meditated in its caves.

blurb: A complex of temples and cave shrines in limestone mountains southwest of Hanoi, reached by a rowing-boat ride.
fun_fact: Each spring hundreds of thousands of pilgrims come for its festival, one of the biggest in Vietnam.

blurb: An old-style Tokyo district around a big park, with museums, a zoo, the Ameyoko market and cheap izakayas.
fun_fact: The Tokyo National Museum in Ueno Park is the oldest and largest art museum in Japan, founded in 1872.

blurb: A remote village at 3,500 m on the Puna plateau, among salt flats, coloured hills and the 'Eyes of the Sea' pools.
fun_fact: Its 'Ojos de Mar' pools contain stromatolites, layered rocks built by some of the oldest forms of life on Earth.

blurb: A tiny fishing village on the Varanger peninsula in the far northeast, with Arctic birds and wild coast.
fun_fact: The Varanger peninsula is one of the few places in Europe with true Arctic tundra by the sea.

blurb: A small Arctic fishing village on the Barents Sea, famous for its men's choir and its storm-battered harbour.
fun_fact: Its men's choir starred in the documentary Heftig og begeistret (Cool and Crazy), a hit in Norway in 2001.

blurb: A white hilltop temple to the goddess Durga in Pokhara's old bazaar, with views of the Annapurnas.
fun_fact: Its goddess is said to have been brought from India in the 18th century by a king of Kaski.

blurb: The biggest floating market of the Mekong Delta near Can Tho, best at dawn when boats trade fruit and vegetables.
fun_fact: Sellers hang their goods from tall bamboo poles on their boats so buyers can see from a distance what they offer.

blurb: An adobe town in the Quebrada de Humahuaca with cobbled lanes, a big independence monument and the road to Hornocal.
fun_fact: Nearby, the Hornocal hills show 14 colours of rock, the 'Serranía de Hornocal'.

blurb: A red-rock canyon on the road from Salta to Cafayate, with the Devil's Throat and the Amphitheatre formations.
fun_fact: Its rocks hold fossils of the sea shells that gave it its name, 'Shells Gorge'.

blurb: Kanazawa's lively covered fish and produce market, for crab, seafood rice bowls and sushi at counters.
fun_fact: It has been the city's kitchen for about 300 years.

blurb: Osaka's buzzing entertainment hub around the station, with shops, theatres, food streets and Dotonbori nearby.
fun_fact: The Namba Grand Kagetsu theatre is the home of Yoshimoto, Japan's most famous comedy company.

blurb: A valley of deep red hills near Rainbow Mountain, seen on a short walk from the ridge.
fun_fact: Its colour comes from iron oxide in the rock, the same mineral that makes rust red.

blurb: A big Tokyo hub with department stores, the Sunshine City complex, an aquarium and anime shops for women fans.
fun_fact: Its station is one of the busiest in the world, used by over two million people a day.

blurb: A maze of moving ice towers and crevasses above Everest base camp, the first and most dangerous obstacle for climbers.
fun_fact: The ice moves about a metre a day, so ladders and ropes must be repaired every season.

blurb: A small island in Ha Long Bay with a beach and a summit viewpoint over the karsts.
fun_fact: It was named after the Soviet cosmonaut Gherman Titov, who visited with Ho Chi Minh in 1962.

blurb: A Black Hmong village in the Muong Hoa valley below Sapa, among terraced rice fields.
fun_fact: Black Hmong women dye their clothes deep blue with indigo, which often stains their hands.

blurb: A huge lava field covered in thick green moss beside the Ring Road in south Iceland.
fun_fact: It was created by the Laki eruption of 1783, whose poisonous gases killed about a fifth of Iceland's people.

blurb: A quiet glacier lagoon near Jökulsárlón, with icebergs and a glacier face close to the shore.
fun_fact: Its glacier, Fjallsjökull, drops from Iceland's highest peak, Hvannadalshnúkur.

blurb: An active volcano on Kyushu with one of the largest calderas in the world, grassy plains and a smoking crater.
fun_fact: Its caldera is about 25 km long, and around 50,000 people live inside it.

blurb: A shallow lagoon in the Salar de Atacama with three species of flamingo and the Andes behind.
fun_fact: The flamingos feed on tiny brine shrimp, which give them their pink colour.

blurb: Shinjuku's neon red-light and nightlife district, with bars, karaoke, host clubs and a giant Godzilla head.
fun_fact: It was meant to host a kabuki theatre after the war, which gave it its name, but the theatre was never built.

blurb: A small lava cave near Mývatn with a hot water pool inside, where light falls through a crack.
fun_fact: It appears in Game of Thrones, in the cave scene between Jon Snow and Ygritte.

blurb: A huge black volcanic crater near Mývatn, about 1 km wide, with a path up to walk around its rim.
fun_fact: It formed in an eruption about 2,500 years ago.

blurb: A waterfall dropping 182 m into a canyon on the edge of the Hardangervidda plateau, seen from viewing bridges.
fun_fact: It is one of the most visited natural attractions in Norway, with a new stair bridge over the gorge.

blurb: A narrow fjord near Stavanger with sheer granite walls, home to Preikestolen and Kjeragbolten.
fun_fact: Kjeragbolten is a boulder wedged in a crack 1,000 m above the fjord, and brave hikers stand on it.

blurb: The main shopping town of the Lofoten islands, with the airport and the Viking Museum nearby.
fun_fact: The Lofotr Viking Museum near Leknes has a reconstruction of the largest Viking longhouse ever found.

blurb: A lava rock pool on the Reykjanes coast where big Atlantic waves crash in.
fun_fact: Legend says it was the bathing pool of a troll woman named Oddný.

blurb: Blue ice caves that form each winter under the Vatnajökull glacier, visited only with a guide from November to March.
fun_fact: The caves are new every winter: summer meltwater carves them and they collapse or change by the next year.

blurb: A volcano on the Reykjanes peninsula that erupted in 2021, 2022 and 2023 after 800 years asleep.
fun_fact: Its 2021 eruption was one of the most visited in history: thousands hiked out to watch lava flow near Reykjavik.

blurb: Reykjavik's harbour of whale-watching boats, fish restaurants, museums and colourful warehouses.
fun_fact: Whale-watching boats leave here to see minke whales and humpbacks in Faxaflói bay.

blurb: A steaming valley near Hveragerði where you can bathe in a warm river after an hour's walk.
fun_fact: Its name means 'Steam Valley', after the hot springs that bubble up all over it.

blurb: The only town on Easter Island, with a harbour, a few moai, small museums and Polynesian dance shows.
fun_fact: Almost all of the island's people live in Hanga Roa.

blurb: A row of 15 giant moai on a stone platform facing inland on Easter Island, famous at sunrise.
fun_fact: A tsunami in 1960 scattered its statues, and they were put back up with a Japanese crane in the 1990s.

blurb: An extinct volcano at the tip of Easter Island with a huge crater lake of reeds and the Orongo village on its rim.
fun_fact: Its crater lake is covered in totora reeds, the same plant used on Lake Titicaca.

blurb: Sucre's palm-lined main square, with the cathedral and the house where Bolivia's independence was declared.
fun_fact: It is named after 25 May 1809, when an uprising in Sucre began the fight for independence.

blurb: A near-perfect volcanic cone in Tongariro National Park, seen all along the Alpine Crossing.
fun_fact: It played Mount Doom in The Lord of the Rings films.

blurb: Hanoi's largest lake, with cafés, pagodas, a lakeside cycling loop and sunsets over the water.
fun_fact: Tran Quoc, the oldest pagoda in Hanoi, stands on a small island in the lake.

blurb: The place in the Bay of Islands where Māori chiefs and the British Crown signed New Zealand's founding treaty in 1840.
fun_fact: Its giant ceremonial war canoe, Ngātokimatawhaorua, is about 35 m long and needs at least 76 paddlers.

blurb: A seaside town in the Bay of Islands, with boat trips to the Hole in the Rock and dolphins.
fun_fact: The Bay of Islands has about 144 islands in its sheltered waters.

blurb: A glacier arm tumbling down a valley in Fjærland, with a lake below and a road almost to its foot.
fun_fact: It is an arm of Jostedalsbreen, the largest glacier in mainland Europe.

blurb: The capital of Tyrol, an old town with a golden roof right under the mountains, with a cable car to alpine views.
fun_fact: Its Golden Roof is covered with 2,657 fire-gilded copper tiles, made for Emperor Maximilian I around 1500.

blurb: Three levels of tunnels near the old demilitarised zone where a whole village lived during the war.
fun_fact: Seventeen babies were born underground in the tunnels during the bombing.

blurb: A forested river gorge on the road to the West Coast, with New Zealand's longest swing bridge.
fun_fact: Its swing bridge is 110 m long, the longest in New Zealand.

blurb: A mountain pass through the Southern Alps between Wānaka and the West Coast, with waterfalls and blue pools.
fun_fact: It was the last main road across the Alps to be built, opening in 1965.

blurb: A lake of many islands in Fiordland, crossed by boat on the way to Doubtful Sound.
fun_fact: A 1970 petition to stop it being raised for hydropower became New Zealand's first big environmental campaign.

blurb: A charming harbour town on Snæfellsnes, with old wooden houses and boats out to the islands of Breiðafjörður.
fun_fact: Its Library of Water, an art installation, holds columns of water from Iceland's glaciers.

blurb: A fishing village in the East Fjords with a row of giant stone eggs and views of a pyramid-shaped mountain.
fun_fact: Its 34 granite eggs, one for each local bird species, are a sculpture by Sigurður Guðmundsson.

blurb: A wine town on the Danube at the start of the Wachau valley, with old lanes, galleries and apricot orchards.
fun_fact: The Wachau is famous for its apricots and its white wines, especially Grüner Veltliner.

blurb: A sacred hill near Chau Doc covered in temples and pagodas, with views over the rice fields into Cambodia.
fun_fact: Its Bà Chúa Xứ temple is one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in southern Vietnam.

blurb: A huge cave near Puerto Natales where remains of a giant ground sloth were found.
fun_fact: The mylodon was a ground sloth as big as a bear, and bits of its skin were found here in 1895.

blurb: A canyon of tilted rock blades like arrows on Ruta 40 between Cafayate and Cachi.
fun_fact: Its name means 'Gorge of the Arrows', after the sharp rock slabs tilted by the rise of the Andes.

blurb: Seven moai standing in a row inland on Easter Island, unusually facing the sea.
fun_fact: Legend says they represent seven explorers sent ahead by the island's first king.

blurb: A black pebble beach on Snæfellsnes with rusted shipwreck pieces and old lifting stones.
fun_fact: Fishermen once had to lift its heavy stones to prove they were strong enough to work on the boats.

blurb: A post town on the old Nakasendō road, with stone-paved slopes and wooden inns, the start of a hike to Tsumago.
fun_fact: The Nakasendō connected Edo and Kyoto through the mountains, and Magome was one of its 69 stations.

blurb: A Zen temple in eastern Kyoto with a massive gate, rock gardens and a brick aqueduct in its grounds.
fun_fact: A 19th-century brick aqueduct runs through its grounds, bringing water from Lake Biwa to Kyoto.

blurb: The largest city on Shikoku, with a hilltop castle and the ancient Dōgo Onsen bathhouse.
fun_fact: Dōgo Onsen is said to be one of Japan's oldest hot springs, and it inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away.

blurb: A small town on the road to Etosha, a stop for fuel and supplies, known for its bakery.
fun_fact: Its water tower, the Naulila monument and the old German post station recall its past as a colonial outpost.

blurb: A famous rock painting in a gorge of the Brandberg, reached by a guided walk of about 40 minutes.
fun_fact: It is at least 2,000 years old, and despite its name the figure is now thought to be a man.

blurb: A tall red sandstone plateau rising from the bush, a refuge for rare animals like the black rhino.
fun_fact: It was used to breed rare species, such as rhinos and sable antelope, safe from predators on its top.

blurb: A Gurung village on a ridge facing Annapurna South, on the trail between Dhampus and Ghandruk.
fun_fact: Its slate-roofed houses look across the Modi Khola valley at Ghandruk, on the other side.

blurb: A village on the Annapurna Circuit where the Manaslu trek joins it, in the Marsyangdi valley.
fun_fact: It is where two famous treks meet: the Manaslu Circuit comes down here to join the Annapurna Circuit.

blurb: The highest point of the Annapurna Circuit at 5,416 m, crossed before dawn to beat the afternoon wind.
fun_fact: It is one of the highest trekking passes in the world.

blurb: A riverside village on the Annapurna Circuit with natural hot springs, a favourite rest stop.
fun_fact: Its name means 'hot water' in Nepali.

blurb: A Gurung village on a ridge near Pokhara, with sunrise views of the Annapurnas and Machapuchare.
fun_fact: It sits at about 1,650 m, low enough for a short trek with high-mountain views.

blurb: A village on the shore of turquoise lakes at 4,750 m, a quieter alternative to the Everest base camp trek.
fun_fact: The Gokyo lakes are among the highest freshwater lake systems in the world.

blurb: A peak of 5,357 m above Gokyo, with one of the finest panoramas of Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Cho Oyu.
fun_fact: From the top you can see four of the world's six highest mountains.

blurb: A dark lake near Fox Glacier that mirrors Aoraki/Mount Cook and Mount Tasman on calm mornings.
fun_fact: Its water is dark brown from natural tannins leaching from the forest floor, which makes the reflections sharp.

blurb: A reconstructed Viking chieftain's longhouse on Vestvågøy, with feasts, crafts and a Viking ship.
fun_fact: The original longhouse found here was 83 m long, the largest Viking building ever discovered.

blurb: A green valley town between Cusco and Ayacucho, a stop for travellers heading to Choquequirao.
fun_fact: Its valley is known as the 'Valley of Eternal Spring' for its mild climate.

blurb: The last village on the Inca Trail, a camp at the end of day one before the climb to Dead Woman's Pass.
fun_fact: Its fields are planted with maize and potatoes, as they were in Inca times.

blurb: A small round Inca ruin on the Inca Trail, below a second pass, perhaps an old watchpost.
fun_fact: It is one of the few circular Inca buildings, and it may have served as a tambo, a rest stop for messengers.

blurb: A long lagoon on the Valdés Peninsula with elephant seals on the beach and Magellanic penguins nearby.
fun_fact: Southern elephant seal males can weigh up to 4 tonnes.

blurb: A high plateau at about 3,800 m on Kilimanjaro's western side, with views of the summit cone.
fun_fact: It is the remains of Shira, one of Kilimanjaro's three volcanoes, which collapsed long ago.

blurb: A Mekong Delta town where boat trips to the islands, coconut candy workshops and fruit orchards begin.
fun_fact: It is the closest Mekong town to Saigon, about 70 km away.

blurb: Vietnam's oldest national park, a jungle of ancient trees and caves, with a primate rescue centre.
fun_fact: It was the first national park in Vietnam, opened in 1962 by Ho Chi Minh.

blurb: A UNESCO park of jungle and limestone mountains near the Laos border, with hundreds of caves to explore.
fun_fact: Its karst formed about 400 million years ago, making it the oldest major karst area in Asia.

blurb: A dry cave in Phong Nha with a long wooden walkway through huge chambers of stalactites.
fun_fact: It is about 31 km long and was only discovered in 2005.

blurb: A canyon road through the High Atlas between Midelt and Errachidia, with palm groves along the river.
fun_fact: The French Foreign Legion built the tunnel here in the 1920s, called the Legionnaires' Tunnel.

blurb: A mountain viewpoint 1,500 m above the Geirangerfjord, reached by a toll road with hairpin bends.
fun_fact: It is the highest fjord view in Europe reachable by road.

blurb: A tiny fishing village in Eyjafjörður, with whale-watching boats and hot tubs on the beach.
fun_fact: It was the starting point of Iceland's first whale-watching tours, in 1993.

blurb: Tanzania's second city on Lake Victoria, with granite boulders along the shore and access to the western Serengeti.
fun_fact: Its 'Bismarck Rock' is a giant boulder balanced on the lake shore.

blurb: A clifftop promenade above the Pacific in Lima, with parks, cycle paths and paragliders taking off.
fun_fact: Paragliders take off from the cliffs here and fly along the coast above the surfers.

blurb: A park of illuminated fountains in central Lima, with a laser and music show every evening.
fun_fact: It holds the Guinness record for the largest fountain complex in a public park.

blurb: A twin-spired Roman Catholic cathedral in Stone Town's alleys, built by French missionaries.
fun_fact: It was designed by the architect of the Notre-Dame de la Garde basilica in Marseille.

blurb: Vast marshes and lagoons in northeast Argentina, with capybaras, caimans, marsh deer and birds by the hundred.
fun_fact: Jaguars, which had vanished here for 70 years, were reintroduced in 2021.

blurb: A small island in the Beagle Channel where you can walk among Magellanic and gentoo penguins.
fun_fact: It is one of the few places in Argentina where gentoo penguins breed.

blurb: Salzburg's baroque cathedral with a huge dome and five organs, where Mozart was baptised.
fun_fact: Mozart was baptised in its font the day after he was born, in 1756.

blurb: The highest peak in southern Vietnam, near Tay Ninh, with a cable car to temples and a giant Buddha.
fun_fact: Its Vietnamese name, Núi Bà Đen, comes from the legend of a woman who died on the mountain.

blurb: A leafy riverside suburb north of Buenos Aires with a cathedral, colonial houses and the Tren de la Costa.
fun_fact: Its racecourse is one of the largest grass horse-racing tracks in the world.

blurb: A maze of river islands near Buenos Aires, with stilt houses, boat buses and quiet channels.
fun_fact: It is one of the few deltas in the world that is not at the sea, but at a river, the Río de la Plata.

blurb: A fjord and valley region in west Iceland with hot springs, lava caves, waterfalls and saga sites.
fun_fact: It is home to Deildartunguhver, the most powerful hot spring in Europe.

blurb: The Annapurna massif in central Nepal, crossed by some of the world's most popular treks: the Circuit, the Sanctuary and Poon Hill.
fun_fact: Annapurna I was the first 8,000 m peak ever climbed, by Maurice Herzog's French team in 1950.

blurb: A deep, clear caldera lake near Sapporo surrounded by volcanoes and forest, with hot springs on its shore.
fun_fact: It is the second deepest lake in Japan and almost never freezes, even in Hokkaido's winter.

blurb: Casablanca's 'new medina', built by the French in the 1930s in Moroccan style, with olive and pastry markets.
fun_fact: It was designed as a model neighbourhood that blended traditional Moroccan design with modern town planning.

blurb: A small oasis village in the pre-Saharan south of Morocco, with a waterfall and palm grove.
fun_fact: A meteorite from Mars fell near here in 2011 and was named after the village.

blurb: A former tin-mining village at the foot of the Brandberg, the base for walks to its rock paintings.
fun_fact: Its name means 'brackish water' in the Damara language.

blurb: A hilltop Newari town southwest of Kathmandu, with old temples, brick lanes and valley views.
fun_fact: It resisted the army of Prithvi Narayan Shah for years before falling in 1767, during the unification of Nepal.

blurb: A mountain pass through beech forest on the northern route across the Southern Alps, with hot springs nearby.
fun_fact: It is named after Henry Lewis, a surveyor who crossed it in 1860.

blurb: A quiet beach village on the Coromandel Peninsula, with white sand and a relaxed holiday feel.
fun_fact: Like much of the Coromandel, it began as a gold-mining settlement in the 1890s.

blurb: A small historic town on the west side of the Coromandel Peninsula, with old gold-rush buildings and a narrow-gauge railway.
fun_fact: Its Driving Creek Railway was built by a potter to bring clay down from the hills.

blurb: A rust-red volcanic crater at the highest point of the Tongariro Alpine Crossing, still steaming.
fun_fact: Its colour comes from iron in the rock, oxidised by the heat of the volcano.

blurb: The highest of Bergen's seven mountains, reached by cable car, with views and hikes along the ridge.
fun_fact: A popular hike along the ridge, the Vidden trail, links it to Mount Fløyen.

blurb: A river in the Peruvian Amazon lined with jungle lodges, leading to some of the richest wildlife on Earth.
fun_fact: Its clay licks attract hundreds of macaws and parrots that eat the clay every morning.

blurb: A huge white cathedral of volcanic stone filling one side of Arequipa's main square.
fun_fact: It is one of the few churches in Peru that runs the whole length of its square.

blurb: A high mountain pass on the Lares trek in the Andes, with lakes, llamas and snow peaks.
fun_fact: Lares treks cross passes over 4,000 m, among villages where people still weave in traditional style.

blurb: One of Valparaíso's prettiest hills, with colourful houses, viewpoints and cafés, reached by funicular.
fun_fact: It was settled by British and German immigrants in the 19th century, who left an Anglican church and Victorian houses.

blurb: The old walled medina of Fez, with about 9,000 alleys, souks, tanneries and mosques.
fun_fact: It is thought to be the largest car-free urban area in the world.

blurb: Four Cham towers on a hill near Quy Nhon, overlooking rice fields.
fun_fact: They were built in the 11th and 12th centuries by the Champa kingdom.

blurb: A small turquoise bay with white sand near Quy Nhon, reached by boat or a coastal road.
fun_fact: Its clear water and coral make it a good spot for snorkelling.

blurb: A small island near Quy Nhon with coral reefs and fishing villages.
fun_fact: Its coral reefs are among the best snorkelling spots on the central coast.

blurb: A sloping stone-paved lane of old wooden shops and teahouses below Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto.
fun_fact: Local legend says that if you trip and fall on it, you will have bad luck for three years.

blurb: A tiny village in south Iceland by Skógafoss, with a folk museum of turf houses and old fishing boats.
fun_fact: Its museum keeps a ring said to come from a chest of gold hidden behind Skógafoss.

blurb: A baroque church with a green dome and two giant columns in Vienna, with a lift up to see the frescoes.
fun_fact: It was promised by the emperor during the plague of 1713, to thank God for the end of the epidemic.

blurb: A huge snowy mountain of 6,438 m that rises over La Paz, visible from almost everywhere in the city.
fun_fact: It is the second highest mountain in Bolivia and the symbol of La Paz.

blurb: The world's northernmost zoo, near Bardu, with wolves, bears, lynx and musk oxen in large enclosures.
fun_fact: You can book a visit inside the wolf enclosure and meet socialised wolves.

blurb: Zanzibar's quieter northern island, green and hilly, with clove farms, mangroves and some of the best diving in East Africa.
fun_fact: Pemba grows most of Zanzibar's cloves.

blurb: One of Tanzania's biggest and wildest parks, with huge elephant herds, lions and baobabs along the Great Ruaha River.
fun_fact: It holds about one tenth of all the lions in Africa.

blurb: A highland city in southwest Tanzania, a base for the green Southern Highlands and crater lakes.
fun_fact: It is on the TAZARA railway, built by China in the 1970s to link Tanzania with Zambia.

blurb: A small gorge of tall basalt columns near Twyfelfontein, like the pipes of an organ.
fun_fact: The columns formed about 150 million years ago, when lava cooled slowly and cracked into regular shapes.

blurb: A Hindu temple to the goddess Kali in a forest gorge south of Kathmandu, busy with offerings on Tuesdays and Saturdays.
fun_fact: Animal sacrifices are offered to the goddess here, mostly roosters and goats.

blurb: A colonial city on Peru's north coast, with pastel mansions, the adobe city of Chan Chan and the beach of Huanchaco.
fun_fact: Chan Chan, next to Trujillo, was the largest city of the Americas before the Spanish, all built of mud.

blurb: A glacier with walls up to 135 m high on an arm of Lago Argentino, reached by boat.
fun_fact: It has the highest ice walls of the glaciers in Los Glaciares National Park.

blurb: The island at the end of South America, shared by Argentina and Chile, with mountains, lakes and penguins.
fun_fact: Magellan named it 'Land of Fire' after seeing the campfires of its native people from his ship.

blurb: Norway's easternmost town, on an island in the Barents Sea, with a star fortress and a witch trial memorial.
fun_fact: It lies further east than Istanbul and St Petersburg.

blurb: A small town on the edge of Chitwan National Park, the base for jungle walks, canoe trips and safaris.
fun_fact: One-horned rhinos sometimes wander into the town from the park.

blurb: A waterfall in Pokhara that disappears into a narrow underground tunnel.
fun_fact: It is named after a Swiss woman, Mrs Davis, who was swept into the hole in 1961.

blurb: A deep valley between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, followed by the Annapurna Circuit and the Jomsom road.
fun_fact: By some measures it is the deepest gorge in the world, with peaks over 8,000 m on both sides.

blurb: A valley below Sapa with terraced rice fields, a river and Hmong and Dao villages, for walks and homestays.
fun_fact: It has ancient carved stones with mysterious patterns, thought to be hundreds of years old.

blurb: A floodlit waterhole at Okaukuejo camp in Etosha, where rhinos, elephants and lions come to drink at night.
fun_fact: It is one of the best places in Africa to see black rhinos, which come to drink after dark.

blurb: A vast white salt pan at the heart of Etosha, shimmering with mirages, flooded briefly after good rains.
fun_fact: Its name is often translated as 'great white place'.

blurb: A cluster of volcanic islands off south Iceland, with the town of Heimaey and huge puffin colonies.
fun_fact: The island of Surtsey rose from the sea in an eruption that began in 1963.

blurb: A mountain range in the Highlands with colourful rhyolite slopes, hot springs and steaming valleys.
fun_fact: It was a summer ski area until 2000, the only one in Iceland's Highlands.

blurb: A German-style lake town in the Chilean Lake District, facing the Osorno volcano across Lake Llanquihue.
fun_fact: It was settled by German immigrants in the 1850s, and kuchen cakes are still a local tradition.

blurb: A perfect snowy cone over Lake Llanquihue, with a ski area and summer hikes on its slopes.
fun_fact: Charles Darwin saw it erupting in 1835 from the deck of the Beagle.

blurb: A small town on the Carretera Austral at the foot of a volcano that erupted in 2008.
fun_fact: The 2008 eruption was a surprise: the volcano was thought to have been quiet for over 9,000 years.

blurb: A volcanic crater lake on the Golden Circle, with red slopes and green water.
fun_fact: Its crater is about 6,500 years old, young for the area, and concerts were once held on a raft on the lake.

blurb: A waterfall in east Iceland dropping 128 m down a cliff striped with red clay layers.
fun_fact: The red layers are ancient soil, baked between layers of lava millions of years ago.

blurb: A quiet botanical garden and waterfall near Aguas Calientes, full of orchids, birds and butterflies.
fun_fact: The cloud forest around Machu Picchu has hundreds of orchid species.

blurb: An old fishing village in Lofoten with a huge wooden church and museums about Lofoten fishing.
fun_fact: Its church is called the 'Lofoten Cathedral', and it seats about 1,200 people.

blurb: A headland near the North Cape that is the real northernmost point of mainland Europe, reached on a hike.
fun_fact: It reaches about 1.5 km further north than the North Cape.

blurb: A small island near Kamakura with shrines, caves, a lighthouse and seafood, linked by a bridge.
fun_fact: Its shrine honours Benzaiten, goddess of music and fortune, who is said to have raised the island from the sea.

blurb: An Arctic island village north of Tromsø, a winter base for whale watching with orcas and humpbacks.
fun_fact: In winter, humpbacks and orcas follow herring into the fjords here.

blurb: The park around Everest, with Sherpa villages, monasteries and rhododendron forest below the giants.
fun_fact: It holds three of the world's highest peaks, Everest, Lhotse and Cho Oyu, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

blurb: A tiny stop at about 4,600 m on the Everest trail, at the foot of a climb lined with climbers' memorials.
fun_fact: The memorial cairns above it honour climbers and Sherpas who died on Everest.

blurb: A Giay village in the Muong Hoa valley below Sapa, among rice terraces, with homestays.
fun_fact: The Giay people here live in houses on the ground, unlike the stilt houses of other groups.

blurb: A Red Dao village near Sapa with rice terraces, waterfalls and a bamboo forest.
fun_fact: Red Dao women wear bright red headscarves and are known for their herbal baths.

blurb: The emperors' palace in a large park in the middle of Kyoto, with gates, halls and gardens open to visitors.
fun_fact: It was the residence of Japan's emperors until 1869, when the capital moved to Tokyo.

blurb: A carved wooden palace on Durbar Square, home of the Kumari, a young girl worshipped as a living goddess.
fun_fact: The Kumari is chosen as a small child and stays a goddess until puberty.

blurb: The quieter northern neighbour of Ha Long Bay, with similar limestone islands and far fewer boats.
fun_fact: Its name is often linked to the legend of a dragon's children, the 'dragon's tail'.

blurb: A lively city on Kyushu, famous for tonkotsu ramen eaten at open-air yatai food stalls by the river.
fun_fact: It has about 100 yatai stalls, more than anywhere else in Japan.

blurb: A deep blue lake at about 4,100 m in the Atacama, framed by volcanoes and golden grass.
fun_fact: It and its twin, Miñiques, formed when a lava flow blocked a valley.

blurb: A perfect volcanic cone of 5,916 m on the Chile-Bolivia border above San Pedro de Atacama.
fun_fact: Its summit crater holds one of the highest lakes in the world.

blurb: A 250 m shopping street leading to Senso-ji in Asakusa, lined with stalls selling snacks and souvenirs.
fun_fact: It is one of the oldest shopping streets in Japan, dating from the early 1700s.

blurb: A mountain resort on the Oslo–Bergen railway, with skiing in winter and hiking on Hardangervidda in summer.
fun_fact: It lies halfway between Oslo and Bergen.

blurb: A beach village on Zanzibar's east coast, one of the best kitesurfing spots in Africa.
fun_fact: Its shallow lagoon and steady trade winds make it ideal for kitesurfing.

blurb: A pond in Ueno Park covered in giant lotus leaves in summer, with a temple on an island.
fun_fact: Its temple honours Benten, goddess of music and the arts.

blurb: The great river on Namibia's northeast border, with hippos, crocodiles and sunset cruises.
fun_fact: It flows over Victoria Falls, the largest curtain of falling water in the world.

blurb: Six narrow alleys of tiny bars in Shinjuku, many seating only five or six people.
fun_fact: About 200 tiny bars are squeezed into this small area.

blurb: The town by Iceland's international airport, with a Viking ship museum and the Blue Lagoon nearby.
fun_fact: Its airport was built by the US Army during the Second World War.

blurb: An active volcano of 5,868 m on the Bolivia-Chile border, with a steaming summit seen on the Uyuni tour.
fun_fact: Steam still rises from a vent near its summit.

blurb: The narrow strait on Lake Titicaca where buses cross on wooden barges between La Paz and Copacabana.
fun_fact: Passengers cross in small boats while their bus floats across separately on a wooden raft.

blurb: A floating fishing village in Bai Tu Long Bay, with homes on rafts among the limestone islands.
fun_fact: Families here have lived on the water for generations, farming fish and pearls.

blurb: A star-shaped Western-style fort in Hakodate, with a moat lined with cherry trees and a tower view.
fun_fact: It saw the last battle of the Boshin War in 1869, where the short-lived Republic of Ezo fell.

blurb: A giant figure like a candelabra carved into a sandy hillside on the Paracas peninsula, seen from the boat to the Ballestas.
fun_fact: It is about 180 m tall, and nobody knows for sure who made it, or when.

blurb: A car-free mountain village on a cliff above the Lauterbrunnen valley, facing the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.
fun_fact: It can only be reached by cable car or mountain railway, and its cable car goes on to the Schilthorn of the Bond film.

blurb: A 32 km alpine trek of 2 to 4 days between Mount Aspiring and Fiordland, past lakes and waterfalls.
fun_fact: It is one of New Zealand's Great Walks, and huts must be booked months ahead.

blurb: A temple complex of underground galleries and stone heads in the Andes, 3,000 years old.
fun_fact: Deep in its galleries stands the Lanzón, a carved stone idol over 4 m tall.

blurb: A colonial pampas town outside Buenos Aires, home of gaucho culture, silverwork and estancias.
fun_fact: Every November it hosts the Fiesta de la Tradición, Argentina's biggest gaucho festival.

blurb: The mountains that cover most of Switzerland, with glaciers, lakes, mountain railways and famous peaks like the Matterhorn.
fun_fact: The Alps cover about 60% of Switzerland.

blurb: A small island in the Westfjords with eider ducks, puffins and Iceland's only windmill.
fun_fact: Its windmill, from 1840, is the only one left in Iceland.

blurb: A valley in the middle of the W trek in Torres del Paine, with glaciers cracking above and granite towers around.
fun_fact: You can hear ice breaking from the French Glacier echo through the valley.

blurb: Chile's second largest lake, with German towns on its shore and Osorno volcano rising across the water.
fun_fact: It is the second largest lake entirely in Chile.

blurb: An emerald lake surrounded by volcanoes in Chile's oldest national park, crossed by boat towards Argentina.
fun_fact: It is part of the Cruce Andino, a boat-and-bus crossing of the Andes to Bariloche.

blurb: A huge golden baroque abbey on a cliff above the Danube, with a magnificent library and church.
fun_fact: Benedictine monks have lived here without a break since 1089.

blurb: A white mineral lake next to Laguna Verde at the foot of Licancabur, near the Chilean border.
fun_fact: It is linked to Laguna Verde by a narrow channel, but the two lakes have different colours.

blurb: The Argentine park around Iguazu Falls, with jungle trails, catwalks over the falls and toucans and coatis.
fun_fact: About 275 separate waterfalls make up the Iguazu Falls.

blurb: The jagged 'horns' of Torres del Paine, pale granite towers capped with dark rock, rising over lakes Pehoé and Nordenskjöld.
fun_fact: Their two colours come from granite that pushed up under dark shale about 12 million years ago; glaciers then carved the rest away.

blurb: An ice cap over a volcano in south Iceland, seen from the Ring Road near Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss.
fun_fact: Its 2010 eruption sent an ash cloud over Europe that grounded most air traffic for six days.

blurb: One of Japan's oldest hot springs, in Matsuyama, centred on a grand wooden bathhouse from 1894.
fun_fact: Its main building, Dōgo Onsen Honkan, is said to have inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away.

blurb: A town on the shore of Lake Victoria in northern Tanzania, a quiet base near the western edge of the Serengeti.
fun_fact: Julius Nyerere, Tanzania's first president, was born in Butiama, a village in the hills near Musoma.

blurb: A Gnawa village at the foot of the Erg Chebbi dunes near Merzouga, known for its drum and iron castanet music.
fun_fact: Its people descend from West Africans brought across the Sahara; Gnawa music is now on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

blurb: A green valley village in the High Atlas south of Marrakech, with olive groves, a lake and walks to Berber villages.
fun_fact: The road on from here over the Tizi n'Test pass leads to Tin Mal, the 12th-century mosque of the Almohads.

blurb: Sea caves at Cape Spartel near Tangier, where the Atlantic surges in through an opening in the rock.
fun_fact: Legend says Hercules slept here before his eleventh labour; the sea opening looks like a map of Africa.

blurb: Granite boulders near Tafraoute painted blue, pink and red, scattered across a bare Anti-Atlas valley.
fun_fact: They were painted in 1984 by the Belgian artist Jean Vérame, and have since been repainted.

blurb: Olive orchards around a large pool on the edge of Marrakesh, with a green-roofed pavilion and the Atlas behind.
fun_fact: The pool and orchards were laid out by the Almohads in the 12th century.

blurb: A riverside town on the Okavango, facing Angola across the water, the hub of Namibia's Kavango region.
fun_fact: The river flowing past it later vanishes into the sands of Botswana, forming the Okavango Delta.

blurb: A small town in Damaraland, a base for the Petrified Forest and the rock art of Twyfelfontein.
fun_fact: It was the capital of the Damaraland homeland before Namibia's independence in 1990.

blurb: A ridge-top hamlet of lodges on the trail from Phedi into the Annapurna range, with forest and mountain views.
fun_fact: The trail beyond leads into the Annapurna Sanctuary, a glacial basin ringed by peaks over 7,000 m.

blurb: The forested hills on Kathmandu's northern rim, with day hikes to Shivapuri peak and the Nagi Gompa nunnery.
fun_fact: Its springs are a main source of Kathmandu's drinking water.

blurb: A stone village on the Annapurna Circuit, the headquarters of Manang district, with hot springs by the river.
fun_fact: It is the capital of Manang district, yet sits at about 2,670 m with Annapurna II towering above.

blurb: A 6,476 m trekking peak south of Everest, climbed after a long trek through the remote Hinku valley.
fun_fact: From its summit you can see five 8,000 m peaks at once, including Everest, Makalu and Kangchenjunga.

blurb: The 'blue town' of Vesterålen, a bridge town on the Sortland Strait where buildings are painted in shades of blue.
fun_fact: The blue paint is an art project begun in the 1990s; Hurtigruten ships call here every day.

blurb: A tiny fishing hamlet on Lofoten's north coast, open to the midnight sun over the sea.
fun_fact: By the shore stand a ruined German radar station from the war and a stone sculpture called 'The Head'.

blurb: A farm on Vestvågøy in Lofoten where a Viking chieftain's longhouse was found and rebuilt as a living museum.
fun_fact: The original longhouse was 83 m long, the largest Viking Age building found in Scandinavia.

blurb: Inca ruins at Limatambo on the road west of Cusco, with a long terraced wall of trapezoidal niches.
fun_fact: It was a tambo, a rest stop on the Inca road from Cusco, which gave Limatambo its name.

blurb: Lowland Amazon rainforest near Puerto Maldonado, with river lodges, giant otters and clay licks full of macaws.
fun_fact: Every morning parrots and macaws gather on its riverside clay cliffs to eat the clay, probably for its salt.

blurb: A red-brick cathedral from the French era in central Ho Chi Minh City, next to the old Central Post Office.
fun_fact: All its red bricks were shipped from Marseille, and they have kept their colour without paint.

blurb: A perfect volcanic cone on the Bolivia-Chile border, rising over Laguna Verde and visible from San Pedro de Atacama.
fun_fact: Its summit crater, near 5,900 m, holds one of the highest lakes in the world, with tiny creatures living in it.

blurb: The last stop before Annapurna Base Camp, at about 3,700 m below the fishtail peak of Machapuchare.
fun_fact: Machapuchare has never been officially climbed to the top: it is sacred to Shiva and closed to climbers.

blurb: An island of vineyards, olive groves and beaches, a 40-minute ferry ride from Auckland.
fun_fact: It is the second largest island in the Hauraki Gulf, after Great Barrier Island.

blurb: A short bush walk near Rotorua to falls on the Kaituna River, also a rafting spot.
fun_fact: Its 7 m Tutea Falls is the highest commercially rafted waterfall in the world.

blurb: Iceland's quiet east: steep fjords, small fishing villages, reindeer and few crowds.
fun_fact: It is the only part of Iceland with wild reindeer, descended from animals brought from Norway in the 18th century.

blurb: A natural stone arch over the Las Cuevas river near Aconcagua, stained orange by mineral hot springs.
fun_fact: Darwin visited it in 1835; a spa hotel built beside it was destroyed by an avalanche in 1965.

blurb: A colourful apartment block in Vienna with uneven floors, onion domes and trees growing out of the rooms.
fun_fact: Hundertwasser took no fee, saying it was worth it to stop something ugly being built there.

blurb: A baroque palace and formal gardens in Salzburg, with the fortress framed across the river.
fun_fact: It was built in 1606 by Prince-Archbishop Wolf Dietrich for his companion Salome Alt, mother of his children.

blurb: A Benedictine monastery in Salzburg's old town, with a baroque church, cliff catacombs and an old cemetery.
fun_fact: Founded around 696, it is one of the oldest monasteries in the German-speaking world.

blurb: Red rock outcrops by a turquoise salt lake on the Atacama high plateau, with volcanoes behind.
fun_fact: At about 4,000 m, vicuñas graze on the shore and flamingos feed in the salt lake.

blurb: A narrow finger of Namibia reaching east between Angola and Botswana, with rivers, floodplains, elephants and hippos.
fun_fact: Germany got it in 1890 to reach the Zambezi; it was named after the German chancellor Leo von Caprivi.

blurb: Santiago's founding square, with the cathedral, the old post office, palm trees and street chess players.
fun_fact: It was laid out by Pedro de Valdivia when he founded the city in 1541.

blurb: A huge park on Mendoza's western edge, with a lake, rose garden and the Cerro de la Gloria monument.
fun_fact: It was designed by Carlos Thays, the French-born landscaper behind many parks in Buenos Aires.

blurb: Pablo Neruda's house in Valparaíso, stacked up a hill with sea views and full of his odd collections.
fun_fact: It is named after Sebastián Collado, the Spanish builder who began it and died before finishing.

blurb: The yellow house on Getreidegasse in Salzburg where Mozart was born in 1756, now a museum.
fun_fact: Mozart's family lived on the third floor until 1773; his childhood violin is on show.

blurb: A vast adobe sanctuary south of Lima, sacred long before the Incas, with a Sun Temple facing the sea.
fun_fact: Its oracle drew pilgrims from across the Andes; Hernando Pizarro looted it in 1533.

blurb: Peru's Amazon frontier region on the Bolivian and Brazilian borders, reached via Puerto Maldonado.
fun_fact: It holds parts of Manu and Tambopata, among the most biodiverse places on Earth.

blurb: A small village in west Iceland where the saga writer Snorri Sturluson lived; his round bathing pool survives.
fun_fact: Snorri was murdered here in 1241, in the cellar of his own farm.

blurb: A geothermal beach in Reykjavík where hot water warms a lagoon in the sea.
fun_fact: Golden sand was brought in and hot water piped in, so the lagoon reaches 15 to 19°C in summer.

blurb: A greenhouse town in south Iceland built on hot ground, start of the walk to the Reykjadalur hot river.
fun_fact: Its geothermal greenhouses are warm enough to grow bananas.

blurb: A geothermal farming village in south Iceland, home of the Secret Lagoon, a hot pool in the open air.
fun_fact: The Secret Lagoon (Gamla laugin) was built in 1891, making it Iceland's oldest swimming pool.

blurb: The temple in Lumbini over the spot where the Buddha is said to have been born, beside a sacred pool.
fun_fact: Emperor Ashoka marked the site with a stone pillar in 249 BC, which still stands next to the temple.

blurb: An open-air museum in Takayama of old farmhouses moved from the Hida mountains, with steep thatched roofs.
fun_fact: Several are gassho-zukuri houses, with 'praying hands' roofs like those of Shirakawa-go.

blurb: Hokkaido's second city, gateway to the Daisetsuzan mountains and the flower fields of Biei and Furano.
fun_fact: It holds Japan's official record low temperature, -41.0°C, set in 1902.

blurb: A temple on the slopes of Mount Misen on Miyajima, with stone Jizo statues, prayer wheels and lanterns.
fun_fact: It is the head temple of Miyajima, said to have been founded by the monk Kūkai in 806.

blurb: Ancient pilgrimage trails through the forested mountains of the Kii Peninsula to the three Grand Shrines of Kumano.
fun_fact: It is one of only two pilgrimage routes on the UNESCO World Heritage list, with the Camino de Santiago.

blurb: One of the three Grand Shrines of Kumano, with a red pagoda framed by Japan's tallest waterfall.
fun_fact: Nachi Falls drops 133 m, the tallest single drop of any waterfall in Japan.

blurb: A small park on the slopes of Mount Meru near Arusha, with forest, a crater, lakes, giraffes and colobus monkeys.
fun_fact: It is one of the few Tanzanian parks where you can walk with an armed ranger, and the start of the Mount Meru climb.

blurb: A big film studio on the edge of Ouarzazate, with sets of ancient Egypt and old Jerusalem you can tour.
fun_fact: Gladiator, Kingdom of Heaven and parts of Game of Thrones were filmed here.

blurb: A white shrine on a boulder above Aroumd on the trail to Toubkal, a pilgrimage site for Moroccans.
fun_fact: Only Muslims may cross to the shrine of Chamharouch, said to be the king of the djinn.

blurb: A village in the Draa Valley known for its green-glazed pottery and an old Sufi library.
fun_fact: Its library holds old Qurans, some written on gazelle skin.

blurb: An oasis town in the Anti-Atlas, with palm groves, mud-brick villages and few tourists.
fun_fact: The hills around it are rich in prehistoric rock engravings of animals from a greener Sahara.

blurb: The rose town on the road between Ouarzazate and the Dades Gorge, where rosewater is distilled.
fun_fact: Each May it holds a rose festival to celebrate the harvest of the Damask rose.

blurb: A small two-tiered pagoda temple on an island in Phewa Lake, Pokhara, reached by boat.
fun_fact: It honours Barahi, a form of the goddess Durga believed to guard the lake.

blurb: A quiet Sherpa village on a terrace above the Dudh Kosi, off the main Everest trail, facing Ama Dablam.
fun_fact: It is home to the Khumbu Climbing Center, which trains Nepali climbers and mountain workers.

blurb: The pyramid peak above Everest Base Camp and Kala Patthar, 7,161 m high.
fun_fact: George Mallory named it: Pumori means 'unmarried daughter' in Sherpa.

blurb: The royal square of Patan (Lalitpur), packed with Newar temples, courtyards and the Patan Museum.
fun_fact: Its stone Krishna Mandir, built in 1637, is carved with scenes from the Mahabharata and Ramayana.

blurb: The elegant 6,812 m peak of the Everest trek, with a hanging glacier below its summit.
fun_fact: Its name means 'mother's necklace': the ridges are her arms and the glacier is the dablam, a charm box.

blurb: Imja Tse, a 6,165 m trekking peak above Chhukung, often climbed after Everest Base Camp.
fun_fact: Eric Shipton's party named it Island Peak in 1951, as it looks like an island in a sea of ice.

blurb: A sunny harbour city in the Bay of Plenty, next to the beaches and summit walk of Mount Maunganui.
fun_fact: Its port is the largest in New Zealand by cargo volume.

blurb: An old gold-mining town in the Inangahua valley on the West Coast, with heritage buildings and bush walks.
fun_fact: In 1888 it became the first town in the southern hemisphere with a public electricity supply.

blurb: A small West Coast settlement south of Westport, once a gold-rush town, now known for caves and glow-worm tours.
fun_fact: In the 1860s gold rush it was a busy town with dozens of hotels; few traces remain.

blurb: A tiny gold-rush town near Hokitika, start of the West Coast Wilderness Trail cycle route.
fun_fact: Richard Seddon, New Zealand's longest-serving prime minister, started his political career as its mayor.

blurb: New Zealand's largest unmodified wetland, a tidal lagoon on the West Coast for kayaking and birdwatching.
fun_fact: Nearby is the only nesting site in New Zealand of the white heron, the kōtuku.

blurb: A slender waterfall in beech forest beside the Haast Pass highway, a few minutes' walk from the road.
fun_fact: It pours out of a hanging valley, left high above the Haast River when glaciers deepened the main valley.

blurb: Small ponds beside the Milford Road in Fiordland that reflect the Earl Mountains on calm mornings.
fun_fact: The sign by the lake is written upside down, so it reads the right way in the reflection.

blurb: A forest lake on the Milford Road, ringed by red beech and moss, with a short nature walk.
fun_fact: The beech forest around it is home to rare native birds such as the mohua, or yellowhead.

blurb: A hill above Lake Tekapo with a university observatory and wide views over the turquoise lake.
fun_fact: It lies in the Aoraki Mackenzie Dark Sky Reserve, one of the largest in the world.

blurb: A dark, still lake near Franz Josef, reflecting the Southern Alps, good for kayaking.
fun_fact: Its water is stained dark by tannins from the forest, which makes for mirror-like reflections.

blurb: A green hill above central Wellington with a lookout over the harbour, city and airport.
fun_fact: Its forest was used to film the hobbits hiding from a Black Rider in The Lord of the Rings.

blurb: A dark, split volcano near Rotorua, visited on guided walks to the rim of its crater.
fun_fact: Its 1886 eruption destroyed the famous Pink and White Terraces and buried several villages.

blurb: A free public park in central Rotorua with steaming pools, bubbling mud and hot foot baths.
fun_fact: The ground is still active: in 2001 an eruption here threw mud and rocks across the park.

blurb: A valley near Rotorua born in the 1886 Tarawera eruption, with steaming lakes and a walk down to Lake Rotomahana.
fun_fact: It holds Frying Pan Lake, the largest hot spring in the world.

blurb: A scenic railway from Dombås down Romsdalen to Åndalsnes, past the Troll Wall.
fun_fact: It crosses Kylling Bridge, a stone arch high above the Rauma river, and loops through a horseshoe tunnel.

blurb: A deep valley in western Norway between sheer walls, ending at Åndalsnes and the Romsdalsfjord.
fun_fact: Its Troll Wall is the tallest vertical rock face in Europe, about 1,000 m high.

blurb: The 24.5 km tunnel linking Aurland and Lærdal on the road between Oslo and Bergen.
fun_fact: It is the longest road tunnel in the world, with three blue-lit caves inside to keep drivers alert.

blurb: An open-air museum in Lillehammer of nearly 200 old buildings from Gudbrandsdalen, including a stave church.
fun_fact: It began as the private collection of a dentist, Anders Sandvig, who bought old houses from 1887.

blurb: The border town between Peru and Bolivia south of Lake Titicaca, a stop on the bus from Puno to La Paz.
fun_fact: It sits on the Desaguadero River, the only river flowing out of Lake Titicaca.

blurb: A small Inca ceremonial site by the Urubamba at km 104, start of the one-day Inca Trail to Machu Picchu.
fun_fact: Its stone fountains and baths were likely used for ritual cleansing before reaching Machu Picchu.

blurb: A pre-Inca cemetery in the desert near Nazca, where mummies sit in open tombs with their hair still intact.
fun_fact: The dry desert preserved them for about 700 years; looters scattered bones before it was protected in 1997.

blurb: A bohemian corner of central Santiago, with cafés, bookshops, small museums and Cerro Santa Lucía.
fun_fact: It is named after the 19th-century writer José Victorino Lastarria.

blurb: One of Valparaíso's colourful hills, with steep lanes, murals, cafés and funiculars down to the port.
fun_fact: It was settled by British and German merchants in the 19th century and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage area.

blurb: The park around Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, from rainforest to moorland to summit glaciers.
fun_fact: Kilimanjaro is the highest free-standing mountain in the world, rising about 4,900 m above its base.

blurb: A laid-back sandy beach north of Hoi An, with seafood shacks and bars under the casuarinas.
fun_fact: Erosion has eaten away much of nearby Cua Dai beach, so An Bang has become Hoi An's main beach.

blurb: Cham brick towers on a hill in Nha Trang, still an active temple, above the Cai River.
fun_fact: Built between the 7th and 12th centuries, it honours Yan Po Nagar, the mother goddess of the Cham.

blurb: The mountain above Tromsø, reached by the Fjellheisen cable car, with views over the city, islands and northern lights.
fun_fact: You can also climb about 1,200 stone steps to the top, laid by Sherpas from Nepal.

blurb: A long valley in eastern Norway from Lillehammer towards Dombås, with old farms and roads to the mountains.
fun_fact: It gave its name to Gudbrandsdalsost, Norway's sweet brown cheese.

blurb: A suspension bridge over an arm of the Hardangerfjord, opened in 2013, with a path for cyclists and walkers.
fun_fact: Its 1,310 m main span was the longest of any bridge in Norway when it opened.

blurb: A valley on the Oslo-Bergen route, with ski resorts like Geilo and Hemsedal.
fun_fact: It is famous for the hallingdans, a folk dance where the dancer kicks a hat off a pole held high.

blurb: A village near Sucre known for its Sunday market and the colourful weaving of the Yampara people.
fun_fact: Each March it holds Pujllay, a festival marking an 1816 victory against the Spanish.

blurb: Vienna's grand boulevard around the old town, lined with the opera, parliament, city hall and museums.
fun_fact: It was built from 1857 where the city walls stood, after Emperor Franz Joseph ordered them torn down.

blurb: The imperial library in Vienna's Hofburg, with a baroque State Hall full of frescoes and old books.
fun_fact: Its State Hall holds about 200,000 books, including the library of Prince Eugene of Savoy.

blurb: Kanazawa's old samurai quarter, with earthen walls, narrow lanes, canals and the Nomura family house.
fun_fact: In winter the walls are wrapped in straw mats called komo to protect them from snow.

blurb: The valley of the Colca River around Chivay, with pre-Inca terraces, hot springs and villages in colourful dress.
fun_fact: Its terraces were built by the Collagua and Cabana peoples, and many are still farmed today.

blurb: A vast moss-covered lava field on the Ring Road near Kirkjubæjarklaustur.
fun_fact: It was formed by the Laki eruption of 1783, whose famine killed about a fifth of Iceland's people.

blurb: The great mosque and university in the medina of Fez, founded in 859, with green-tiled roofs.
fun_fact: It was founded by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, and is often called the oldest existing university in the world.

blurb: A volcanic area near Mývatn with the Víti crater lake, steaming lava fields and a geothermal power plant.
fun_fact: In 2009 a drilling project here hit magma by accident at about 2 km depth.

blurb: Japan's fourth largest city, home of Toyota, a rebuilt castle, Atsuta Shrine and miso-rich food.
fun_fact: The golden shachihoko on its castle roof are mythical tiger-headed fish meant to protect it from fire.

blurb: The heart of the central Serengeti around the Seronera River, with resident lions, leopards and big herds.
fun_fact: It holds the park's main airstrip and visitor centre, and big cats live along its river all year.

blurb: A fishing town on Eyjafjörður north of Akureyri, with whale watching and the ferry to Grímsey.
fun_fact: Each August it holds the Great Fish Day, when the town serves free fish to tens of thousands of visitors.

blurb: A big Shinto shrine at the top of Gion in Kyoto, glowing with lanterns at night.
fun_fact: It runs the Gion Matsuri, Kyoto's month-long July festival, which began in 869 to calm a plague.

blurb: An oasis village south of San Pedro de Atacama, built of white volcanic stone, with orchards in a ravine.
fun_fact: Its bell tower from 1750 is built of liparite, a pale volcanic stone.

blurb: A cluster of yellow fishing cabins on stilts in Lofoten, between Hamnøy and Reine.
fun_fact: Its cabins are old rorbuer, built for visiting fishermen during the Lofoten cod season.

blurb: A remote caldera in Iceland's highlands, holding deep blue Öskjuvatn and the warm Víti crater.
fun_fact: NASA astronauts trained here in 1965 and 1967 before the Moon landings.

blurb: A small coral island off Pemba with clear water, mangroves and some of Tanzania's best snorkelling.
fun_fact: Its name is said to come from 'msala', Swahili for prayer mat, after a legend of a prophet who prayed here.

blurb: A remote Maasai area east of the Serengeti, on the road to Lake Natron.
fun_fact: It is a game-controlled area where Maasai herders and wildlife share the land.

blurb: A remote park in western Tanzania with huge buffalo herds, packed hippo pools and few visitors.
fun_fact: In the dry season hundreds of hippos crowd into the shrinking pools of the Katuma River.

blurb: The walled capital of the old kingdom of Mustang, a Tibetan town on a high desert plateau.
fun_fact: Its king kept his title until 2008, when Nepal abolished the monarchy.

blurb: A hill town with a palace-fort on a ridge, the birthplace of modern Nepal.
fun_fact: Prithvi Narayan Shah set out from here to unite Nepal in the 18th century; the Gurkha soldiers take their name from it.

blurb: A river island in the Mekong near My Tho, with orchards, coconut workshops and narrow canals.
fun_fact: In Vietnam the Mekong splits into many branches, which gives it the name Cửu Long, 'Nine Dragons'.

blurb: A 5,421 m mountain near La Paz reached by road, with views of Huayna Potosí and Lake Titicaca.
fun_fact: It had the world's highest ski lift until its glacier disappeared in 2009.

blurb: A city in northern Peru, gateway to the tomb of the Lord of Sipán and the pyramids of Túcume.
fun_fact: Pope Leo XIV served as bishop of Chiclayo before his election in 2025.

blurb: A rainy island in southern Chile with wooden churches, houses on stilts and its own myths.
fun_fact: Sixteen of its wooden churches are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

blurb: A fishing town on the Varanger Peninsula by the Barents Sea, known for winter birdwatching.
fun_fact: Steller's eiders and king eiders winter in its harbour, drawing birders from all over Europe.

blurb: Norway's easternmost fjord, between the Varanger Peninsula and the Russian border.
fun_fact: Unlike most Norwegian fjords it is wide and open, and it stays ice-free in winter.

blurb: A Mekong Delta river market near Cai Be, best early in the morning, among orchards and workshops.
fun_fact: Each boat hangs samples of its goods from a tall pole, so buyers can see from afar what it sells.

blurb: A glacier tongue of Vatnajökull near Skaftafell, with blue crevasses, popular for glacier hikes.
fun_fact: It was a filming location for Interstellar and Batman Begins.

blurb: A geothermal area in Iceland's central highlands on the Kjölur road, with hot springs and a natural pool.
fun_fact: The outlaw Fjalla-Eyvindur is said to have hidden here in the 18th century; his shelter is still shown.

blurb: A climb of about 500 steps near Tam Coc to a dragon-topped summit over rice fields and karst peaks.
fun_fact: Múa means 'dance': legend says Tran kings watched dancers perform in the cave at its foot.

blurb: A tall red rock cleft in the Quebrada de las Conchas, a short scramble from the Cafayate road.
fun_fact: Beside it is the Anfiteatro, a natural rock amphitheatre with such good acoustics that it hosts concerts.

blurb: A quiet adobe village in the Calchaquí Valleys of Salta, with a white colonial church.
fun_fact: It is named after the water mills that once ground grain here.

blurb: A winding mountain road from Salta to Cachi, climbing through green valleys to the Piedra del Molino pass.
fun_fact: Beyond the pass it enters Los Cardones National Park, full of giant cardón cacti.

blurb: A town north of Windhoek with two big woodcarving markets.
fun_fact: It is the seat of Herero chiefs, and each August Herero people gather here in traditional dress.

blurb: A small waterfall of vivid blue water rushing into a cleft, reached by a riverside walk.
fun_fact: Its blue colour comes from fine glacial silt in the water.

blurb: One of Iceland's tallest waterfalls, dropping 122 m into a canyon near the volcano Hekla.
fun_fact: Its name means 'high falls'; its smaller neighbour falling beside it is called Granni, 'neighbour'.

blurb: A milky blue geothermal lagoon near Lake Mývatn, a quieter northern answer to the Blue Lagoon.
fun_fact: Its mineral-rich water comes from a geothermal borehole at nearby Bjarnarflag.

blurb: A narrow strait near Bodø with one of the world's strongest tidal currents, forming whirlpools four times a day.
fun_fact: Up to 400 million cubic metres of water rush through a 150 m wide gap at up to 40 km/h.

blurb: A wild sandy beach between steep mountains on Lofoten's north coast, reached only on foot.
fun_fact: Two surfers spent a winter here in a hut built from driftwood, filmed in North of the Sun (2012).

blurb: A 1960s shopping complex in Tokyo packed with anime, manga, figures and vintage toys.
fun_fact: When it opened in 1966 it was a luxury address, and celebrities lived in its upper-floor flats.

blurb: A 97 m waterfall near Lake Chūzenji in Nikkō, at its best in autumn colours.
fun_fact: It is the only outlet of Lake Chūzenji and one of Japan's three most famous waterfalls.

blurb: A trail village of lodges on the Poon Hill trek, before the long stone staircase up to Ulleri.
fun_fact: The climb from here to Ulleri is said to be over 3,000 stone steps.

blurb: A cluster of lodges in bamboo forest deep in the Modi Khola gorge, on the way to Annapurna Base Camp.
fun_fact: Above here the trail crosses avalanche zones that sometimes close it in winter and spring.

blurb: A lodge stop at about 3,200 m in the Modi Khola gorge, the last before Machapuchare Base Camp.
fun_fact: From here the gorge opens into the Annapurna Sanctuary, a ring of peaks over 7,000 m.

blurb: An island joined to Ha Long City by road, with the main harbour for Ha Long Bay cruises.
fun_fact: Its port is the main departure point for overnight boats into Ha Long Bay.

blurb: Sung Sot, one of the largest caves in Ha Long Bay, with huge chambers of stalactites.
fun_fact: French visitors called it the 'Grotte des Surprises', and its Vietnamese name, Sửng Sốt, means 'amazement'.

blurb: Colourful hot springs in Beppu made for looking, not bathing: blue, blood red, bubbling mud and a geyser.
fun_fact: The Blood Pond Hell gets its red colour from iron oxide and clay in the water.

blurb: A canyon of red, green and white rock in the hills north of San Pedro de Atacama, with rock art nearby.
fun_fact: The colours come from minerals: iron gives red, copper green, and salt and gypsum white.

blurb: A red and white communications tower in Minato with observation decks over the city.
fun_fact: At 333 m it is taller than the Eiffel Tower, which inspired its design.

blurb: The main Buddhist temple of Nikkō, with three gilded giant statues in its Sanbutsudō hall.
fun_fact: It was founded by the monk Shōdō Shōnin in 766, centuries before the Tōshōgū shrine.

blurb: A large pagoda in My Tho mixing Vietnamese, Chinese, Khmer and French styles, with giant Buddha statues.
fun_fact: It was founded in the 19th century and rebuilt with arches in the French colonial style.

blurb: Tokyo's youth fashion district, with crowded Takeshita Street of crêpes, costumes and street style.
fun_fact: On Sundays young people used to dress up in cosplay on the bridge to Meiji Shrine.

blurb: A fishing village north of Agadir with one of the longest surf waves in Africa.
fun_fact: Fishermen still pull their boats up on the beach right beside the surf schools.

blurb: A palm-lined gorge in the Atlas foothills near Agadir with green pools to swim in.
fun_fact: The area around it is known for argan trees and for honey from the mountain villages.

blurb: A steaming volcanic crater above Noboribetsu, with boardwalks over sulphur vents and boiling pools.
fun_fact: It feeds Noboribetsu's onsen, producing about 3,000 litres of hot water a minute.

blurb: A quiet shrine near Yanaka in Tokyo, with a tunnel of red torii and azaleas in spring.
fun_fact: Its buildings from 1706 survived both the 1923 earthquake and the wartime bombing.

blurb: Japan's oldest and largest museum, in Ueno Park, with samurai armour, scrolls and Buddhist art.
fun_fact: Founded in 1872, it holds dozens of objects listed as National Treasures.

blurb: A wide waterfall on the Jökulsá á Fjöllum, a short walk upriver from Dettifoss.
fun_fact: The same canyon holds three falls in a row: Selfoss, Dettifoss and Hafragilsfoss.

blurb: A Colca Valley village with a white baroque church, hot springs and Wititi dancers on the plaza in the morning.
fun_fact: The Wititi dance of the Colca Valley is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

blurb: A Colca Valley village with the white church of Santa Ana, below the smoking Sabancaya volcano.
fun_fact: Its church has been damaged many times by earthquakes and tremors from the nearby volcano.

blurb: A pair of lighthouses at the tip of the Reykjanes Peninsula, good for birds, seals and northern lights.
fun_fact: The old lighthouse from 1897 stands near the newer one from 1944, one of Iceland's tallest.

blurb: An alpine park with New Zealand's highest mountain and longest glacier, and easy walks like Hooker Valley.
fun_fact: Edmund Hillary trained here for Everest; about 40% of the park is covered by glaciers.

blurb: The river on the edge of Chitwan National Park at Sauraha, with canoe rides past crocodiles and sunset views.
fun_fact: Two crocodiles live here: the mugger and the rare gharial, which eats only fish.

blurb: A basalt sea stack shaped like a drinking dragon off the Vatnsnes Peninsula in north Iceland.
fun_fact: Legend says it is a troll caught by the sunrise while trying to destroy the convent at Þingeyrar.

blurb: Restored moai platforms on the edge of Hanga Roa, the best sunset spot on Easter Island.
fun_fact: One of its moai, Ko Te Riku, is the only one with its white coral eyes put back.

blurb: An ahu site near Hanga Roa's airport, with stone walls fitted so finely they recall Inca masonry.
fun_fact: Thor Heyerdahl saw that stonework as proof of contact with South America, a theory most experts reject.

blurb: A salt lake on Bolivia's Altiplano, crowded with pink flamingos, on the lagoon route south of Uyuni.
fun_fact: Its name means 'stinking lake', from the smell of sulphur.

blurb: A valley in Nagano where wild snow monkeys bathe in a hot spring pool in winter.
fun_fact: These macaques are the most northern-living non-human primates in the world.

blurb: The river through eastern Tokyo, with water buses, cherry trees and the Skytree beside it.
fun_fact: Its summer fireworks festival dates back to 1733.

blurb: The largest glacier in the Alps, a river of ice over 20 km long seen from the Jungfraujoch and Eggishorn.
fun_fact: Where its three ice streams meet, at Konkordiaplatz, the ice is about 900 m thick.

blurb: Switzerland's capital, a medieval old town of arcades and fountains in a loop of the Aare river.
fun_fact: Einstein worked out his special theory of relativity while living in a flat on Kramgasse.

blurb: A rugged volcanic range between the Atlas and the Sahara, crossed on winter treks past nomad camps.
fun_fact: Its Aït Atta nomads fought one of the last battles against French rule here, at Bougafer in 1933.

blurb: A village of mud-brick kasbahs on the south side of Jbel Saghro, a quiet base for treks.
fun_fact: The hills around it hold rock engravings of animals and hunters thousands of years old.

blurb: Hanoi's biggest covered market, at the edge of the Old Quarter, selling everything from fabric to food.
fun_fact: Built by the French in 1889, it was largely rebuilt after a fire in 1994.

blurb: The capital of Honshu's northernmost prefecture, known for apples, seafood and the Nebuta festival.
fun_fact: At its August Nebuta Matsuri, giant lit floats of warriors are paraded through the streets.

blurb: A village in a sheer glacial valley of the Bernese Oberland, with dozens of waterfalls and trains to Wengen and Mürren.
fun_fact: Staubbach Falls, dropping almost 300 m beside the village, inspired a poem by Goethe.

blurb: A glacier on Mount Balmaceda reached by boat from Puerto Natales, in Bernardo O'Higgins National Park.
fun_fact: It once reached the fjord, but has retreated so far that it now hangs high on the mountain.

blurb: A glacier ending in a lagoon of floating ice, on the boat trip from Puerto Natales.
fun_fact: A short path leads from the boat to its lagoon, where icebergs drift below the glacier front.

blurb: A bright turquoise lake below snowy peaks in Huascarán National Park, a classic day hike from Huaraz.
fun_fact: The hike climbs to about 4,600 m, so it is often used to acclimatise before longer treks.

blurb: The bridge across the Waitematā Harbour, linking central Auckland to the North Shore.
fun_fact: Extra lanes clipped onto its sides in 1969 were built in Japan, so locals call them the 'Nippon clip-ons'.

blurb: A colourful art centre in Whangārei with a golden dome and wavy floors, built to Hundertwasser's design.
fun_fact: Hundertwasser lived in New Zealand for decades; the centre opened in 2022, long after his death in 2000.

blurb: The gateway to Vietnam's far north, start of the Ha Giang Loop through karst mountains and minority villages.
fun_fact: Its Dong Van Karst Plateau is a UNESCO Global Geopark.

blurb: A small town near the Chinese border with an old quarter of stone houses and a Sunday market of hill peoples.
fun_fact: Nearby, the Ma Pi Leng Pass road runs along a cliff high above the Nho Que river.

blurb: A big high lake on the Altiplano road between Arequipa and Puno, with flamingos, alpacas and trout farms.
fun_fact: At about 4,200 m it drains through the Cabanillas River towards Lake Titicaca.

blurb: A hilly city on Lake Geneva with a Gothic cathedral, a steep old town and the lakeside quarter of Ouchy.
fun_fact: A night watchman still calls out the hour from the cathedral tower every night, a custom kept since 1405.

names: Salinas and Aguada Blanca National Reserve
blurb: A high Andean reserve between Arequipa and the Colca Valley, with vicuñas, flamingo lagoons and volcano views.
fun_fact: It protects the springs and lakes that supply much of Arequipa's water, below Misti and Chachani.

blurb: A ski area above Queenstown with views over the Wakatipu basin, and mountain biking in summer.
fun_fact: It opened in 1947 as one of New Zealand's first commercial ski fields, and it offers night skiing.

blurb: A Māori village on the shore of Lake Rotorua, with a carved meeting house and a Tudor-style church.
fun_fact: In St Faith's Church, an etched window shows Jesus in a Māori cloak who seems to walk on the lake behind.

blurb: The southern tip of the Americas, a rocky headland where the Atlantic meets the Pacific, reached by boat or plane.
fun_fact: It is named after the Dutch city of Hoorn, home of Willem Schouten, who first sailed round it in 1616.

blurb: A wide bay in west Iceland scattered with islands, rich in seabirds, seals and strong tidal currents.
fun_fact: An Icelandic saying holds that its islands are too many to count; estimates run to about 3,000.

blurb: A small island off Iceland's north coast, crossed by the Arctic Circle, home to puffins and one village.
fun_fact: It is the only part of Iceland inside the Arctic Circle; a giant stone ball marks the moving line.

blurb: A broad fjord and valley in north Iceland known for horse breeding, river rafting and turf houses.
fun_fact: Its Glaumbær farm has turf houses that were lived in until 1947.

blurb: A lakeside town in Patagonia's Lake District, with Alpine-style buildings, chocolate shops, ski slopes and hikes.
fun_fact: It is Argentina's chocolate capital, a tradition brought by Swiss and Italian immigrants.

blurb: A mountain forest park near Da Lat on the Langbiang Plateau, with pines, mossy forest and treks.
fun_fact: It includes Lang Biang mountain, named in legend after two lovers, Lang and Biang.

blurb: Austria's third city, on the Danube, with an old town, the Ars Electronica Center and the Pöstlingberg hill.
fun_fact: It gave its name to the Linzer torte, one of the oldest known cakes, with a recipe from 1653.

blurb: A valley of the Danube between Melk and Krems, with vineyards, apricot orchards, castles and abbeys.
fun_fact: It is a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its apricots and dry white wines.

blurb: A tiny wine town in the Wachau with a blue baroque abbey tower and a castle ruin above the Danube.
fun_fact: Richard the Lionheart was held prisoner in its castle in 1192 on his way home from the Crusades.

blurb: A lake village on the Wolfgangsee with a cable car up the Zwölferhorn.
fun_fact: Mozart's mother was born here, and his sister Nannerl later lived in the same house.

blurb: A clear lake in the Salzkammergut, ringed by mountains and the villages of St. Wolfgang and St. Gilgen.
fun_fact: A rack railway climbs from the shore to the Schafberg summit, with views over many lakes.

blurb: A pilgrimage village on the Wolfgangsee, with a Gothic church and the famous White Horse Inn.
fun_fact: Its church holds a winged altar by Michael Pacher from 1481, a masterpiece of late Gothic art.

blurb: A wide turquoise waterfall on the Paine River between lakes Nordenskjöld and Pehoé, an easy walk with views of the Cuernos.
fun_fact: The water is milky blue from glacial flour, fine rock ground down by the glaciers upstream.

blurb: A long milky blue lake below the Cuernos del Paine, coloured by glacial flour.
fun_fact: It is named after the Swedish explorer Otto Nordenskjöld, who led an Antarctic expedition in 1901-04.

blurb: A small Atacameño village on the road to the Miscanti and Miñiques lagoons, with old farm terraces.
